chapters.title: Strangers in the Sacred Space
paragraphs: By order of the government, a new land survey was about to take place in the village. The official who was to come for this purpose was named Klassiper. The Erumathramadam was being cleaned and prepared as his place of stay.

Kodanthara Moothassan, one of the community leaders, rushed over upon hearing the news. The temple administration was under the authority of the community leaders known as the ‘Sthanikars’. The most important place in the village was the temple itself. Moothassan asked the temple administrator, “What is it, Kanakku Pillai, for whom is the Erumathramadam being prepared?”
“For Klassiper.”
“In that case, what is his caste?” Moothassan inquired.
“Most likely a Sudra.”

“If so, what will the Namboothiri elders and the others do if they come face to face with him?” Moothassan’s question was not one to be dismissed lightly. Until now, the Erumathramadam had only ever been given for the stay of Brahmin priests, the Thantris. This was something unheard of in practice. But the order from the Tahsildar’s office stated that accommodation must be provided for Klassiper. Kanakku Pillai, who managed the temple affairs, had already received word that the incoming official was a Sudra and that he was someone required by Ponnu Thampuran.
“In that case, the madam must be cleaned thoroughly,” Moothassan was compelled to say.

Mani, Kunjudevi, and Kunnukki polished the floor with cow dung. They too knew that Klassiper was close to Ponnu Thampuran. Kunjudevi, when she was a little girl, had seen Ponnu Thampuran at Ambalappuzha. That grandeur—

It was indeed a sight to behold. Along with him was the Thampuratti Amma. Draped in a silk saree, adorned with gold ornaments, the image of her walking by remains vivid in memory even now. Thampuratti Amma’s complexion was like burnished gold—there was no telling where the gold ended and her skin began. Even today, Kunjudevi remembers it. Kunjukki was a singular woman; she would oppose anything, anywhere. No matter who said what, she had to speak against it.

“We are women, they are women too. Just as life grows in our wombs, it grows in theirs as well,” Kunjukki retorted. “Once the lamp is put out, what difference does color make? All women are the same. After death, when buried, they rot; if burned, they turn to ash.”
“Speak a little softer, Pottachi. You’re talking about the lady of the Ponnuthampuran house. Be careful, you might lose your head,” it was Kunjilakshi who said this.

But Kunjukki paid no heed to any of that. The other women, unable to bear those words of royal sacrilege, turned away. They feared what might happen if someone else overheard and reported it to those close to the Thampuran when the Classiper came.

Just then, Kuruppachan arrived there. The Erumadramadam had to be kept very clean. Someone important to Ponnuthampuran was coming to stay. The Asan instructed the women to mix ash with cow dung and polish the floor. The women whispered among themselves that the morning temple naivedya prasadam had been given. There was one person in the village who truly knew the taste of the morning naivedya prasadam—he was the Moothassan. Everyone working at the temple knew that if you gave that prasadam, you could win over the Asan.
The officer came to inspect the place where the Classiper would be staying. Moothassan and the administrator took the upper cloth from their shoulders and tied it around their waists.

When the community leader, Kodantra Moothasaan, himself came directly and pointed out the place where the classiper was staying, the officer felt satisfied. To clear his doubts, the Asaan asked the officer:
"Who is this classiper?"
"The land survey is coming, Kuruppae. He is the one concerned with that," replied the officer.

It seemed the Asaan understood. The officer explained further that henceforth, the tax would have to be paid in cash, and that was the reason for the survey. It was news that made one tremble. Until now, only a share of the produce from the land, the rajabhogam, had been given as tax. That was the way it had always been. But now, it would not be so. The tax must be paid in money! On which land does money grow?

Kuruppasaan asked, "Would Ponnuthampuran issue such an order? Is he not the visible deity of the farmers?" The officer’s opinion was that all this was not happening with the Thampuran’s knowledge, but was the work of the Talavayi.

From now on, the lands would be measured and a fixed amount of money would be set as tax. The collection would be done by the taluka office clerks. There would be no need for the tandalkaran or the measurer anymore. If the tax were in paddy, all these people would be needed.

The officer also hinted that there was no longer any compulsion that the next person to hold office must be his son-in-law, by hereditary right. For generations, the office had remained with the Mulleppilli family. Kuruppasaan wondered if the glory of family institutions was fading away.
"What if we don’t pay the tax?" Kuruppasaan asked.

The officer had no doubt. If the tax was not paid, confiscation measures would be the punishment. For every child in the family, this was a hardship. Land surveys had happened before as well. Some stories told by Achoman Mama lingered in the Asaan’s memory. The Vettikkattu paddy fields had once belonged to the Kodantra family...

Sarvemoolam’s story would be narrated in detail by Kodanthra Achoman Kuruppu. It was a good story. The “Karanavar”—the head of the family who managed the household under the marumakkathayam (matrilineal) system—was the protagonist. He would be the maternal uncle of the family members. After him, his nephew would inherit the position of Karanavar. Kuruppachan pondered over this. In those days, the Karanavar of the family was Idramankonthi, who would lease out land to those interested in farming. Land was not to be left fallow. That was the custom of those times. Kuruppachan could not recall the name of the official who, in those days, drew up the contract deed for the agricultural land. The then “thandalkarars” (land agents) would seek out suitable people and bring them before those officials. Then, the land would be leased out to them. Five hundred marakkals of paddy field were registered in Idramankonthi’s name.

The Kodanthra family, at that time, did not have the manpower or wealth to cultivate so much land. By paying a bribe of seventy “rashis”—that is, seven hundred silver chakrams—they managed to reduce it to a hundred. The land, situated by the river and blessed with fertile silt, was rich and bountiful. Thus, the Vettikkattu paddy field came into the possession of the Kodanthra family.

Every family had its own story like this. Whenever something had to be said about a family, Achomanmama would begin to recount its tale. The way he would retell the stories he had heard in his youth from the present elder was always engaging. Whether on the verandah of the house, on the field embankment, or under the mango grove, wherever the story was told, there would always be people eager to listen to Achomanmama. If not, he would send for them and gather an audience before beginning his tale. If those stories had been written down, they too would have become a Purana—an Achoma Purana.
Achomanmama knew nothing of family affairs. Poor man, he spent his life telling stories and passed away.
The Mulleppilli family too had its own story. Achoman...
Kuruppasan remembered the story that uncle had asked him to tell.

It was a story connected to the old land survey. When Achomak Kuruppu began to narrate it to Kodantra Moothakuruppu, Kuruppasan too started recounting the tale, and the officer’s face fell slightly. He feared that some shameful detail about his own family might emerge from it.

On that day, the contract registration officers roamed the entire village, searching out and bringing in eligible people. No one could escape, whoever they were. Was it not a royal order? Each family was allotted as much extra land as they could manage. Even then, there was land left over. Only one karanavar, with great confidence, told the karyasthar that it was possible to write and take more land than what was strictly allowed. The reason: he was under the special grace of Hanuman. That was why he had such courage.

Even after that, land remained. There was no need to do anything more to the soil. It was good, fertile earth, layered with rich alluvium. The seasons brought sun and rain in their turn. All that was needed was to sow the seed. The five elements themselves seemed ready to yield a thousandfold. All the people here had to descend to the earth and work, so that they might eat. That was why Ponnuthampuran had established the system of leasehold contract registration. If so, letting the land lie idle was a mistake—a crime. The karyasthar was troubled by this, and as he pondered, he thought of the Mulleppilly family. A family with plenty of gold, silver, and influence. Once, they had earned their wealth working in the trade of the white men.

The karyasthar summoned the karanavar of the Mulleppilly family. Because they had written and taken a little more land that day, the permanent position of authority in the Mulleppilly family came to him.
With the new land registration, the Mulleppilly family’s position of authority would be lost. This land registration brought both good and ill to the people. Asan

He pondered. But, whatever the nature of the order, if the officer implementing it thought carefully, he could ensure that the farmers would not be harmed. The officer had realized that the Asan was a man of knowledge. Perhaps it was the clarity gained from hearing the story. The officer left.

The Asan went and sat on the sloping bench of the Ezhupura verandah, where discussions on various matters were held. He was troubled by the thought that this land registration might bring confusion to the whole village. Yet, perhaps, it might prove beneficial to the Mangalaseri family. There, the sons-in-law were hefty fellows, numbering twenty or twenty-five. They were not lazy when it came to work. Even now, without asking anyone, without seeking permission, they cunningly took over the wastelands and cultivated them. Yet, year after year, the family did not have enough rice for their expenses. No matter how much land was written over to them, they would cultivate it.

The Asan suggested an idea to the administrator. “Let’s ask for and acquire as much land as can be registered in the name of the temple. If it’s for the temple, there will be no tax. We must keep the classifier happy. It’s not for our own benefit, is it? Isn’t this for a noble cause?”

Balathol Mukundar arrived there. He was a prominent Brahmin. For fifty years, he had served as the chief priest in the temple. He had come to inquire upon hearing that the Erumathramadam was about to be given for a Shudra to stay in.

“That madam is meant as a place for Brahmins visiting the temple to stay overnight. Can Shudras be allowed to stay there with their families? What is this Kuruppu? Is Kuruppu of the Kodantra clan or not? Do you not know the rules of the clan and the laws of dharma?”

Before Balathol Mukundar’s question, Kuruppu Asan faltered. Yet, he replied humbly, “This has become a matter that must be done for the village. The person coming is an officer from Ponnuthampuran. If he is not properly attended to, the villagers will face trouble. Even the karisal forest will be registered, and everything—”

If the settlement is decided, all the farmers will end up leaving the village. If you please the Classifier, you will get many benefits.” Hearing what the Moothassan said, the Namboothiri’s thoughts turned in another direction. After all, they would not levy taxes on the temple or Brahmin property. He must get vast tracts of land registered in his family’s name. With this matter in mind, he returned to his house to consult with his sons.

The Classifier and his family arrived from Thiruvananthapuram. They settled in the Erumathra Madom. Kochu Pillai, the Classifier, was a handsome man. With his tuft and the heavy gold earring he wore, and the mundu tied around his waist, anyone who saw him walking by would stop and take a second look before moving on. But his wife, Kunjulakshmi, was dark-skinned and stout—a veritable black ogress. For a man who looked like a celestial Gandharva, his wife was like a Kurathi woman. There was no match between them at all. Yet, they had grown fond of each other. To the young men in the village, it was a wonder. How could this Gandharva be so enamored of this black ogress!

The Classifier began his land survey work. With the Tandalkaaran and the officer following him, he went from house to house, climbing up and down, and started preparing the register of information. The villagers began to understand what this land survey was all about. He was going to assess taxes. From now on, taxes would have to be paid in cash instead of paddy. If there was any deficiency regarding the land registration, the Classifier had to be pleased. For that, one had to go and meet the Classifier in person and do what was necessary. The first to meet him in person and offer a gift was Mangala Cheri Ravipillai. Oil, sugar, large bunches of Nendran bananas, vegetables—he brought all these together in abundance.
That offering was bundled into small parcels. Not only that, but there were also two sovereigns of gold jewelry, wrapped and hidden in silk cloth.

When the surveyor, Klassiper Kochupillai, went to the Idakkara house to measure and verify the land of Kochumichar on the left bank, Kochumichar stood there, dumbfounded and open-mouthed. The Kochumichar family knew about Kochupillai. It was Kochumichar who had been taking the coarse, red parboiled rice, called variyarisi, to Ponnuthampuran for the royal feast. For thirty-six years, he had been traveling to Thiruvananthapuram once a month without fail. The rice that Kochumichar carried was cooked and served to the five Thampurans who had left the village. Because of this, he knew many stories from the palace.

“Is Subbaiyan Swami still there?” asked Klassiper Kochupillai, slightly taken aback. Subbaiyan Swami was the one who used to cook for the Maharaja. He was also the one who measured and received the variyarisi that Kochumichar brought. Thus, he and Kochumichar were close. In Thiruvattaaru, Subbaiyan Swami had his first sambandham in a great Nair house. It happened on the Maharaja’s orders. Even before the engagement sari was given, the woman was already pregnant. After the childbirth, she told Swami not to come that way anymore. Kochumichar, who knew all these stories, bewildered Kochupillai by asking, “Does Swami still go to Thiruvattaaru?” and other such difficult questions.

Those who overheard this conversation said that Kochumichar was enjoying the fruits of having teased the surveyor. Kochumichar had no fear. Klassiper could do nothing to him. If he went to Thiruvananthapuram and saw Subbaiyan Swami just once, that would be enough—after that, the surveyor’s authority would not touch him. It was only by catching hold of Subbaiyan that even the Maharani, along with—
Through the Maharaja, anything could be accomplished.

Klassiper knew the stories that would strip away the honor and respect that existed in the town today. Kochumichar knew those stories as well. Kochumichar would tell those tales to everyone who came and went from his house. After that, Subbayyan Swami had yet another marriage. Swami married Bhavathi, who had been a wet nurse in the house of one of the Maharaja’s wives. She had a daughter—a dark-skinned girl. Swami had to act according to Bhavathi’s wishes. In the meantime, the son of the steward of the Kilimanoor palace joined the palace as a clerk. He was a handsome young man. Anyone who saw him would think he was some young prince. Bhavathi’s daughter set her eyes on that clerk, Yandan. She told her father, “This man is enough for me.” That was the way she spoke. The reason was, her father was Subbayyan Swami, the cook of the Madappalli. If he said something, even the Maharaja would not object. Thus, for Kunnu Lakshmi, who was like Karumbutham, the daughter of a maid who did the sweeping and cleaning, her husband became Kochupillai—a man as handsome as Kandavarnan and of a high caste. Those who had gathered around Ponnuthampuran heard this story about Kochupillai’s honor being lost. Kochumichar’s daughter-in-law, Paru, also listened to this story from her hiding place. She too understood why Karumbutham had become Kandavarnan’s wife.

Klassiper’s closest attendant was Devadi Mullakkaran. He went from house to house, informing everyone of the latest development. From now on, those who wished to offer gifts should not bring anything grown on the hills. All the rooms in Erumathramadam were filled with fruits and vegetables. They were rotting, spreading their stench everywhere. Nothing seemed suitable to the townspeople. Therefore, Erikkillathu Pappu announced that from now on, the offering should be two sovereign gold coins stamped with the horse seal.

The Panikkar received an order from Mullakkaran; in the same way, he gave instructions to everyone. Pappu Panikkar was a good man who managed his family as best as he could with what he had. The price of two sovereigns of gold coins was one hundred and forty rupees. Panikkar was stunned. The command had come from Devide Mullakkaran. Who could dare refuse or speak against it?

A few days later, with a necklace strung with a hundred horse-emblem gold coins, Kunju Lakshmiyammai came to the temple. Among the old coins, there was one called Nagarasi. Once she had obtained the horse-emblem coin and grown tired of it, Kunju Lakshmiyammai began to desire a Nagarasi as well. Who else but Mullakkaran could fulfill his wife’s wishes? But in which family could a Nagarasi made of pure gold be found? Devide Mullakkaran went from house to house, searching. There were very few who had even heard of the Nagarasi.

Kuruppachan remembered a story he had once heard. It was a very old tale. In the Pullattu family, a pond was dug in the southwest corner. The head of the family at that time was Idyathikaimal. As they dug the pond, a spring burst forth from the muddy earth. In that bubbling water, a large bronze pot emerged, rolling and tumbling. It was a treasure guarded by spirits. The workers, frightened, ran away. Idyathikaimal leapt into the pond. He spat out curses, and after four spits, the gushing water subsided. Kaimal seized the pot and lifted it. In his confusion, afraid it might slip from his hands, he spat into the treasure itself, defiling it. Later, it took ten men to lift and carry the treasure pot into the house. Inside were many Nagarasis. But on the tenth new moon, Idyathikaimal coughed up blood and died. Even today, the Pullattu family is said to lack the blessing of progeny.
Now, the present head of the family, Ittirachikkaimal, has only one sister and two children in that household. The Nagarasi was given as a gift to the wife of Klassiper...

Even though Cheyya Mullakkaran insisted greatly, Ittirachikkaimal paid no heed to it. Mullakkaran too did not tire. He registered one thousand and five hundred marakkals of karisal land in the name of Pullattrukkaimal. Let us see how Pullattrukkaimal, who had only a single son-in-law, would cultivate so much land! Let the Pullattru family be ruined by paying taxes. That was Mullakkaran’s stubbornness.

Kuruppachan did not forget to register many good lands in the name of the Devasthanam and have them exempted from taxes. In the hilly region, one hundred and seven level fields connected to the paddy reservoir came under the Devasthanam’s account. No one else wanted the land that belonged to the Pulayars. If their clan deity, Marutha, became angry, they would have to die coughing blood. Just as with Brahmin property, if anyone laid hands on Pulayar property, it would only bring ruin. Dharmasastha need not fear Marutha. That is why all the lands, including the Pulayar settlements with tall, palm-like coconut groves, were registered in the name of Dharmasastha. None of the Pulayars knew anything about this.

Klassipper and his wife’s daily temple visit had become an important event in the village. The grandeur of their procession was something everyone would stop to witness at least once. When they went to the temple, there was always a doubt whether Dharmasastha would be present or not. The reason was, to register lands in the name of Dharmasastha, the final approval of Klassipper was needed. What would Klassipper and his wife pray for in the sanctum of the deity? That marital flag had not yet blossomed. It was certain that Kunjulakshmiyammai prayed for a child. Except for Nagarasi, she had obtained everything she desired. But she did not have a living child. The goldsmith, Thattachari Samimoopar, had advised her to have a child made of gold crafted. In the village, this became a subject of ridicule here and there.
She would only sleep with that golden child lying beside her.

There were still a few others who had not made their offering to the Classiper in person. In their names, lands unsuited for cultivation were added to the register as a way of settling the matter—this was what the Mullakkaran went around telling all the farmers. Everyone cursed him, placing their hands on their heads in despair. But the Mullakkaran paid no heed to any of it. He bore no grudge against anyone. The system of land registration had come into effect. Everyone had to cooperate with it. That meant everyone had to make their offering to the Classiper. As was customary, the Mullakkaran always did whatever pleased the superior. For ten generations or more, the family of the Devideek had served as permanent Mullakkarans. With this land registration, that office would come to an end. Since the settlement had to be paid in cash, the Mullakkaran was no longer needed. Not only that, the Mullakkaran’s family would have to give up even the house they lived in and stand out on the street. The present Mullakkaran had no heirs. Only his aged sister remained with him in the Devideek family. According to Unnooliyamma, it was the betrayals the Mullakkarans had committed against the villagers, generation after generation, that had wiped out their lineage.

Unnooliyamma thought back to the old days. In her youth, there had been eighteen people in this family. All of them had left her. Except for her younger brother Paacharan, every night after serving rice, she would sit beside Unnooliyamma and say, “I feel like my breath is being drawn out, Paachara.” They say that if a thousand hearts curse someone in anguish, the result is a death where the breath is snatched away. Not just the one who sinned, but the others in the family as well…

This situation is oppressive. Ever since Pacharan became the Mullakkaran, thousands have cursed him with tears. Even before that, the sins of six or seven generations of Mullakkarans had been circling that family. Unnooliyamma would be praying that, at least from now on, no one’s curse should ever take hold.

But what could Pacharan do? Now, the officer is coming to conduct a higher inquiry into the land matters. If the villagers have any complaints, the officer is coming precisely to hear them. It is the responsibility of the classiper to please the officer and send him back satisfied. That is, it is the Mullakkaran who must collect and present the gifts for the officer. Moreover, this means an extra share is needed. Now, what words could be used to win over the villagers? If they failed to give the officer his gift, the blame for that failure would fall upon the Mullakkaran.

Where to accommodate the officer—this was discussed by the community leaders: the elder Kodantra Moothassan, Seerattak Kaimalan, and Konnothu Pillai. They deliberated together. They cleaned the upstairs house on the southern side of the temple. They set up the Subramanjak cot and made it ready. They stitched and spread a velvet mattress. For cooking, they brought in Sankaran Annaavi. The arrangements to impress the officer were, in one way or another, completed.

In the front, two servants in uniform; at the back, two sword-bearers gripping their swords. Along the path, villagers stood with cloths tied around their waists, heads bowed, lips sealed, in respectful silence, to witness the officer’s arrival. The inquiry lasted three days. No one had any complaints about the pattam land registration. Even so, would anyone dare to bring a petition while Devidi Mullakkaran was present? The classiper, Kochupillai, was greatly praised by the officer, who then departed.
When he left, the village presented the officer with a gold ring from Idangali as a token of their esteem. This must be called nothing but the Mullakkaran’s cleverness.

But this incident left Kunjulakshmi’s heart somewhat shaken. She could not bear the sight of her husband standing humbly bowed before the superior officer. The value of the Classifier had diminished the moment the superior officer arrived. She measured within herself the pride of position that would have been hers, had she been the wife of a superior officer. At the time of her marriage, she had almost told her father that the man destined for her must be a superior officer. Her mother too had been ready to agree to her wish. If Ponnuthampuran’s cook Subbaiya Swami and Bhavathi Pillai set their minds to something, what could not be achieved? Now, there was only one way forward: to transform Kochupillai into a superior officer. That was Kunjulakshmi’s desire. She shared this wish with Kochupillai. For Kochupillai, such a lofty promotion was far beyond his own aspirations. But if Ponnuthampuran willed it, even this could come to pass. Even greater things could happen. Kunjulakshmi revealed her thoughts: what if Kochupillai made an attempt, just once, to go as far as Thiruvananthapuram? If needed, she was ready to bear the expenses for it. The money earned from the Classifier’s work was sufficient for that.

On full moon nights, the fragrance of parijata flowers drifts through the Kodantra compound. A scent found nowhere else on earth. In that vast garden, there are seven serpent worship shrines. There are great mango trees that rise up, touching the sky. The Kodantra kalari hall was the main training ground for martial arts in the village. Nangaiyar had seen the old influence of that family. Though she was but a servant there, it was in that household that Nangaiyar was born and raised. Now, the only remaining female descendant in that house, Kochu Pennu Kunjammai, was raised by her.
It was Nangaiyar. It must be said that Kunjamma was not born of her womb.

It was in the house in the eastern garden that the eldest Kuruppu Asan resided. In those days, it was in this house that the elder Asans lived together with their wives. The present elder Asan, Ittikkuruppu, had no wife. Though he had once married a woman, that union did not last long. His wife, Ittichiri, had passed away. Left alone in the house, sleeping by himself night after night, the Asan had grown old. He had a younger brother—Ayyappa Kuruppu—who was to be the next head of the household after the elder Asan.

It did not seem that the elder Asan realized that his daughter-in-law, the young woman Kunjamma, had reached marriageable age. Due to his responsibilities measuring temple lands, the Asan scarcely had time to stand upright and take stock. But did not the family need an heir? For this family to endure, Kunjamma must bear a child. Not only that, but in the Kodantra compound, the wandering of the Gandharvas had begun. It had not happened for a long time; now it had returned. Nangaiyar knew this was a sign that the family was about to have descendants. The Gandharvas came only to see a maiden like Kunjamma. Now, Kunjamma must be married to some Brahmin. In Kodantra, it was customary for women to have Brahmins as their husbands. Nangaiyar, standing hidden by the doorway, spoke of this matter to Kochu Asan. To appease the Gandharvas, a Gandharvan song performance must also be arranged. Nangaiyar knew all the old customs. Kochu Asan replied that he would speak to his uncle.

Without delay, a young Pattar, Seshaiyyan, arrived from Thiruvananthapuram. After consulting with the elder Kuruppu, it was Kochupillai who had summoned Seshaiyyan. At an auspicious hour, Seshaiyyan tied the thali around the neck of young Kunjamma. That day, after the evening puja at the temple, Seshaiyyan arrived at Kodantra, to sleep at his mother-in-law’s house. The elder Asan too...

Kochachasan and the others received the Brahmin with respect. Seshayyan only left after eating the namaskara rice at the temple. In Kodanthayil, there was a separate madam for Brahmins to sit and eat. The elder Kuruppu had offered Seshayyan the special privilege of cooking his meals there if he wished, but Seshayyan had no interest in that. After the elder Kuruppu had gone home, the priest explained his difficulties to Nangaiyar. If he was given, without hindrance, the rice, coconut, oil, and other things needed for his daily use, that would be enough. It would be a help to a Brahmin family in Thiruvananthapuram. “I will manage with the naivedya offerings for the gods,” he said. Nangaiyar agreed to this.

Seshayyan went into Kunjammai’s room. After a while, he came out, clutching his waistcloth, twisted and bunched, and ran out the door. It was as if a wrestling match had taken place. Kunjammai too was gasping for breath. Why did the priest run out in fear? Nangaiyar could not understand. Had the priest strangled the Gandharvan? Was there a Gandharvan’s presence in that room? That was the room where a newly married woman lay. The Gandharvan’s presence could be anywhere else, but not there.

The frightened and exhausted Kunjammai lay down in Nangaiyar’s lap and slept like a little child. Nangaiyar sat there, motionless, gazing at that innocent face. Seshayyan, lying on the outer veranda, heard the fluttering of a night bird’s wings and cried out in terror. His fear would not leave him. Nangaiyar’s nose caught a scent. Was it the fragrance of parijata flowers on the wind? Or the mingled aromas of sandalwood and seven other perfumes drifting together? No. This was not a day for the Gandharvan’s mischief. Or was it the fault of the old room? All around, Nangaiyar thought she could hear faint moaning sounds. Perhaps they were the sighs of the ruined lives of the Kodanthara Kunjammais who had passed away.
Once, in Kodantharayil, when a Kunjammai was to be married, her intended husband brought a Tulu Brahmin—

He came. That Kunjammai had a lover, so when her maternal uncle brought the Tulu Brahmin, she told him directly to his face that she did not want him. With a single kick from her uncle, Kunjammai’s story ended.

This is the tale that Nangaiyar’s maternal grandmother used to tell. Though that Kunjammai was beautiful, the Gandharvan did not come to her. The Gandharvan did not desire beauty; what he wanted in a woman was the scent of honey. Nangaiyar, as her little daughter Kunjammai slept in her lap, bent down and inhaled her. It was a unique fragrance. Kunjammai’s breast-bud was dark. How many months does it take for a breast-bud to darken?

It was a night thick with darkness. After twenty-four naazhigai had passed, at Kodanthurai, on the peak of the mamathu, the crescent moon shone bright. Only then would dawn break. Nangaiyar sat with Kunjammai lying in her lap, waiting for the day to lighten. When Kunjammai awoke, she described to Nangaiyar all that had happened in the night. As soon as that Pattar entered, he asked questions. “How many months for me?” he asked, and I got angry. I said the Gandharvan would strangle and kill him. Then, outside, a scent was noticed. The sound of footsteps was heard. He asked what the Gandharvan would look like. I explained in detail.

That day, Kunjammai spoke more than usual. With her hair tied thickly in a knot, adorned with tulasi flowers, anointed with eight kinds of fragrances, smeared with kasturi, wearing blouse and angavastram, with a gentle smile—thus was the Gandharvan. It became certain to Nangaiyar that Kunjammai had seen the Gandharvan in person.

Kunjammai continued her story. The Pattar shook his head, sang a low, moaning song, and asked me if the Gandharvan was someone staying at the Erumathra madam. I reached out and grabbed his throat. He stuck out his tongue, his eyes rolled in panic, and even after I remembered myself, I did not let go. I too became frightened. Even as she told this, the fear had not left Kunjammai’s face.
The name of the Kalasi who stayed at the Erumathra madam—
Nangaiyar thought about what Kochupillai had said—that Kunjammai resembled Gandharvan. Yet, her heart insisted that it must indeed be Gandharvan.

The next day, before dusk, Seshaiyyan came to Kodanthur. There were scratch marks from nails on both sides of his scrawny neck. He did not come inside. Standing outside, he called for Nangaiyar. He took the rice and other provisions, bundled them in a cloth, and left.

Kodanthur Kuruppu, Seerattakaimal, and Konnotthu Pillai together arranged a job for Seshaiyyan at the temple. The work was to cook the offering rice for the hereditary trustees of the temple and for the devotees who came for darshan. The wage was three marakkal of paddy per month. In addition, there was profit to be made by selling the leftover rice each day. Once or twice a month, he would go to the Erumathramadathu. Whenever she went there, Kalasipper would be a little startled. Seshaiyyan went there only to ask for money. Kalasipper, afraid that if he quarreled with the Pattar and opposed him, his Gandharva secret would be exposed, would give whatever money the Pattar asked for; this was something Kunnulakshmi did not know. In this way, Seshaiyyan put down roots in that village. The daily allowances at Kedanthra, the monthly wage from the temple, the profit from selling leftover rice after performing the temple rituals, and above all, the considerable sum he collected every month from Kalasipper—thus, Seshaiyyan was earning income from various sources. At night, his sleep was in the house of Sakthi, whose fortunes were rising in the temple.

Sakki had once been married to someone. That man was gone. Since then, no one had even bought her a piece of cloth. No one recognized her as a woman. No one even spoke to her. She was not beautiful. But

Seshayyan understood her worth. Chakki was not one to make a fuss. Only she and her aged mother lived together. After the night pooja, Seshayyan would go to Chakki’s house with the leftover rice and betel leaves for the old mother. The mother had grown fond of this new connection. But how long could this go on? At an auspicious time, in the presence of four people, the mother wished that Swami should give the girl a betrothal sari and tie the thaali, making the relationship formal. Seshayyan was somewhat startled. Not only that, he explained that he truly loved Chakki, but if he married her properly, he would lose every single privilege and benefit he received in the Kodanthur family. Whether he should cast aside all those privileges and tie the thaali for Chakki, or continue his relationship with her without formal marriage—this was the question Seshayyan posed, and the mother could not answer.

A new generation was born in the Kodanthur family. Kochu Pennu gave birth to Kunjammai—a girl child as precious as gold. People thought that never before had such a beautiful girl been born in that village. The elder Asan leapt with joy. For the child’s longevity, he conducted many rituals, including the Mrityunjaya homam. He had a horoscope written for her.

That year, agriculture throughout the village was poor. Most families, every year, would borrow from the granary of Ganapathi Ayyar Swami in Mangombu at an interest of two for ten, to cover farming and household expenses. When agriculture failed, it became difficult to repay that year’s loan. Then, Swami in Mangombu would refuse to give more paddy loans. Even in Kodanthur, there was no paddy left for their own needs. Because of the rains, there was no way to boil and dry the paddy already in hand. Even in such circumstances, Seshayyan came every day to collect his share. Because of this, for the next day’s needs...

Even if it was just rice, Nangaiyar would measure it out and give it as soon as Seshaiyyan arrived. The reason: if a Brahmin’s curse befell them, its consequence would be the destruction of their lineage. In the Kodantra household, there was only one female heir. Yet Seshaiyyan paid her no heed.

The blended fragrance of kasturi, punugu, and rosewater mingled and spread throughout the Kodantra compound. Milk was poured at the serpent worship shrines. It was the season of Gandharva wanderings. The Gandharvan appeared in the form of Kochupillai. It seemed as if the child, who would stay awake for long hours and begin to play, knew exactly when the Gandharvan would arrive. Kunhammayi would be entranced watching Kochupillai lull the child to sleep. In those days, it was not customary for fathers to lift and fondle their children. Children grew up even without fathers. Even Kunhammayi, the young woman, had no memory of her own father. She had only heard it said that her father was a Brahmin. The Brahmin’s lodging in Kodantra was where he had stayed. After Kunhammayi’s mother died, he too left. After that, he had no place there.

In the Seeratta family too, there was a lodging for Brahmins. At any given time, five or six Namboothiris and Pattars would stay there. In Seerattai lived the husbands of the Kunhammayis. There were seventeen Kunhammayis there—old women, middle-aged, and young women. Siruthak Kunhammayi was the eldest among them, eighty years old. She was the aunt of the present Moothakkaima. Siruthak Kunhammayi had borne seven children. The eldest among them was to become the next head of the family. Her husband was Ganapathippotri. Even now, he stayed in the lodging. But once Siruthak Kunhammayi closed her eyes, Ganapathippotri would have to step down. After that, he would have to spend his days in his birth home. The privileges he had enjoyed in his wife’s family would not be available in his own. Yet, he would have to go. The children would not say, “Father, don’t go.” In every family, it was the same.

Nothing of the sort happened. Even though Siruthakunjammai’s children knew that Ganapathippothri had left the Seerattai house carrying the tin box, they did not come to see her. There was talk that, while living as Siruthakunjammai’s husband, Ganapathippothri had only managed to acquire less property than what she had in her birth home, and that the money for the rituals to be performed until her death, as well as for her remaining days, was kept in that tin box. Yet, every day, Ganapathippothri would pray that he should die before Sirutha.

Another group of officials came to finish the land survey work. They were the measurers. The leader of that group was a Tamilian named Nagampillai. His job was to measure the land according to the rules, verify it, fix the boundaries, set the stones, prepare the sketch, and assign the survey number, all with practiced experience. He did not stay for long. A dispute arose between Klassip Perkku and Nagampillai. The farmers, complaining that the boundaries were not fixed according to proper procedure, met Klassip Perkku in person and expressed their difficulties, but it was of no use. Nagampillai thought that Klassip Perkku had no authority over him. He too had to receive his share of bribes. But there was no Devidamullakkaran to collect and hand it over to him. In all, there was only a single errand boy.

He lived in that village. Paruthikkattu Othai, he stayed at the Konnotthu cattle shed. Even though a stout woman would sweep and clean it thoroughly, it was still a filthy cattle shed. The class leader, Erumathra Madathil, lived in regal comfort. No one cared about Nagampillai. He had settled his own scores with the villagers. Every boundary in the village became a matter of dispute. Because of the class leader’s land registration, Nagampillai’s boundaries could not be established. There was not a single farmer who did not have a complaint. The villagers began to realize the class leader’s inability to curb the Tamilian’s audacity.

In the end, Devadimulakkaran advised the farmers to offer gifts to Nagampillai as well. In this way, he resolved the complaints of those who made offerings to Nagampillai. Along with this, every day at dawn, even before the crows began to caw, people started gathering at the Konnotthu cattle shed. Paruthikkattu Othai was overjoyed that the villagers had begun to support Nagampillai.

The local leaders—Kodanthara Kuruppachan, Seerattak Kaimalan, and Konnotthu Pillai—gathered and discussed. It was the responsibility of the community leaders to resolve the quarrels that had broken out all over the village. They decided to make the house next to the temple, the upper-storied house where Nagampillai was staying, more comfortable for him. The expenses for him and his group were added to the temple’s accounts for paddy expenditures. With such privileges granted, Nagampillai felt a certain clarity. Whenever he and his group arrived or departed, the villagers began to stand up and greet them with folded hands. The authority of the class leader seemed to be waning. Now, Surveyor Nagampillai was the powerful leader. But it was still the class leader who had amassed wealth.
Only Othai faced a difficulty. The upper-storied house where Nagampillai stayed was within the temple walls. Christians were not allowed to enter there. Nagampillai’s place of stay, the Konnotthu...

When he was at the oil press, people would come circling around Outhai, seeking his attention. That good fortune has now slipped from his grasp. For many generations, Outhai’s family had been rooted in that village. Long ago, it was a Christian family who brought and supplied the coconut oil needed for the temple; Outhai was descended from them. The Paruthikkattu house, belonging to the temple, had been set aside for that family to reside in. It was the Paruthikkattu sons-in-law who supplied the required punna oil and coconut oil to all the houses. Now, there are ten Christian families in the village.

Since Nagampillai arrived, Outhai no longer had time for the oil press. Even with his wife Orodhai and his son Varkki working day and night at the press, they could not supply all the houses with the oil they needed. Outhai had the honor of marrying off both his daughters into good families. He had laid down a great burden in life. Now, he had only one wish left: to build a church in the village. It was for permission to acquire land for this that he continued to serve Nagampillai so devotedly.

There was no oil in the house of Konnothu Pillai for soaking the wicks. When Outhai delayed in supplying it, a farmer from there came and threatened that Outhai’s hut should be set on fire as punishment. Yet Outhai paid no heed to this. His confidence lay in the fact that Konnothu Esaman was obedient to his own master, Nagampillai.

Mangalacheri Iravippillai had newly registered a thousand marakkals of karisal land in his own name. It was Nagampillai who had helped him in this. However much land the people of Mangalacheri already owned, it never seemed enough to them. The reason was that...

There are numerous heirs in the family. None among them can afford to remain idle without work. For the marshy lands where farming had never been practiced until now, only a few days were needed for them to clear the forest and level the ground. The able-bodied men of Mangalacheri, together with fifteen agricultural Pulayas attached to the temple, joined hands to mark the boundaries of that karisal land, fenced it, ploughed it, and made it ready for sowing. Ravipillai gave that land the name Mangalacheri Karisal.

The people of Mangalacheri belonged to a caste slightly lower than the Nairs. There was no connection with Brahmins there. The number of women in that place was steadily increasing. Not even the head of the household, who provided for their expenses, knew exactly how many men, women, and children lived in the family. Such was their abundance and growth. Now, there were chiefly two matrilineal lines there. One was the line of Ravipillai’s mother, the present head of the family. The other was Madhupillai, the son of Ravipillai’s grandmother’s younger sister’s daughter, who would be the next head. The twenty-six people descended from Ravipillai’s mother’s line, and the thirty from Madhupillai’s mother’s line, all lived together as one family. The head of the household could not even identify many of them individually. Yet, it was he who had to provide the monthly measure of rice needed for the expenses of everyone in that family.

Ravipillai’s wife was Kochunnyamma. She was from Vaipparacheri. In the Mangalacheri family, the wife of the head of the household enjoyed special respect. She was addressed with reverence as Periyamma—Great Mother. For generations, the Periyammas of Mangalacheri had come from the Vaipparacheri family. All of them had been good women. In times when women from other families became Periyammas, the women of Mangalacheri lived in tears and distress.

In the days of Kunjanda Pillai Mama, Pachaalathu Kodhai was the Periyamma of the household. By holding the office of Periyamma, she had managed to secure wealth for her own birth family. She drowned the women of Mangala Cheri in tears. Listening to her pillow-side incantations, Periyamma Mama would not give a single thing for the household expenses for months on end. The women shriveled from hunger. Valiyamaani Paatti, unable to bear the suffering, spoke directly to Periyamma’s face. “Let the men go and join them, let’s see what happens, all of you are only after your own enjoyment.”

The day after Kunjanda Pillai Mama died and the funeral rites were completed, Pachaalathu Kodhai went to her birth home. She had to go—there was no other way. Once a husband dies, the wife has no place in her husband’s house. In her own family, she lay starving. Many years later, on one occasion, she came to Mangala Cheri. Though she had once tormented and oppressed them greatly, seeing their old Periyamma lying in hunger, the hearts of the women of Mangala Cheri were moved. Valiyamaani Paatti spoke to the then head of the family and made the necessary arrangements so that Periyamma would be given an annual allowance for her expenses.
There are hundreds of such stories about the Periyammas.

It was always the responsibility of the Periyammas to make known the needs of the women in the family to the head of the household and to see that they were fulfilled. Kochunjiyamma was in the habit of carefully seeing to all these matters. In the midst of all this, she troubled Iravippillai by asking for something needed for the happiness of the family. In Mangala Cheri, the marriages of eleven girls had to be arranged. The eldest among them had already turned fifteen. Any further delay would only bring shame to the family. But Iravippillai was already engaged in a major undertaking, wasn’t he! He had to cultivate the new karisal land. This was an enterprise that would require great expense. The harvest...

Afterwards, with the opinion that the wedding could be conducted with great pomp once everything was settled, Kochunnyammai did not agree with Iravippillai. She argued on behalf of the women in the family. In the end, Iravippillai consented to conduct the girls’ weddings immediately and finish the matter.

But Thampi Muraikkaran Madhupillai did not agree to this. He told his elder brother that it would be enough to hold the wedding after the harvest was over and the yield was in hand. Was that not Iravippillai’s original thought as well? It was Kochunnyammai who changed that idea. Not only that, the current situation of the family was such as well.
“I have decided. The wedding must be finished immediately. There are eleven unmarried girls in the family. If we keep delaying, something untoward might happen,” Iravippillai resolved.

But Madhupillai was not ready to give in. It was a large family. After calling six community elders and discussing, it was decided to conduct the wedding soon. The expenses would be high. The family had already sunk into heavy debt after preparing the Mangalacheri karisal land for cultivation. How much more could be borrowed from Swami in Mangombu to manage both these matters together? Madhupillai again insisted that the wedding could be held after the harvest.

It was only due to the power of his wife’s pillow-side counsel that Madhupillai found the courage to stand before the elders, argue, and calculate. Madhupillai’s wife, Kochumaniyammai, had a motive to bring down Periyamma’s authority a little. Periyamma was fond of the women of Mangalacheri. They too liked Periyamma. But in their estimation, Kochumaniyammai was a jealous woman. She wanted to prove that even a wedding fixed on Periyamma’s word could be stopped. That was what she was trying to achieve through her husband.
Iravippillai did not withdraw, thinking of the expenses. For the agricultural expenses, the paddy needed would have to be borrowed from Mangombu…

He borrowed money from Swami. The day the sowing was done in the Mangalacheri karisal fields and the day the wedding pandal post was planted happened to be the same. Kochumaniyammai did not participate in the pandal post planting ceremony. That event marked the beginning of a rift between the Karanavars and the matrilineal relatives of Madhupilayi.

Four days after the sowing in the new karisal land of Mangalacheri, the entire field had a certain sourness. Being karisal land, there was an acidity to it. That place had once been a great forest. Legend had it that the forest was destroyed by a wildfire. Half-burnt, huge trees lay buried beneath the soil. The head Pulayan opined that if water was let into the field and soaked thoroughly, enough for the paddy crop to be submerged, the acidity would be neutralized. But in a thousand-makkal field, to pour water and keep it standing, one had to roll heavy logs day and night, treading them constantly. It was a great expense, but it had to be done. Yet, not a single rough man from Mangalacheri came forward to roll the logs. The reason was that all of Madhupilayi’s matrilineal relatives had gone to work in other fields in Mangalacheri. The water that was poured had to be left to dry up by itself. With no one to operate the six-yard rollers and tread the field, the roots of the paddy seedlings rotted and the plants wilted. Iravippillai had calculated that he would reap gold from virgin soil. But that karisal land had no richness. It was land scorched by forest fire. And now, not only that, but the help of Madhupilayi’s matrilineal relatives was also lost. Iravippillai’s heart burned with worry.

Meanwhile, the wedding that took place shattered the familial bonds of that household. Iravippillai had an elder brother, Pappummaavan. By age, it was Pappummaavan who should have been the karanavar. But he was not fit for it. How could Pappummaavan, who was both reckless and wayward, be the karanavar? He had married a girl from a poor family—a Chaanakathara Kochukoathai, and Pappummaavan too...

He was staying at his wife’s house. Every month, Iravi Pillai would personally go to the family house and hand over the paddy for his expenses. He never interfered in any of Pappumma’s family matters.

But for the upcoming wedding, who would stand at the forefront and perform the ceremonial decorations as the senior aunt? Kochumani insisted that, as the wife of the eldest uncle, Kochukothai Akka should be the one to take on the role of the senior aunt. This was Kochumani’s ploy to push Kochunnyammai aside in one stroke. Madhu Pillai too understood his wife’s intention. The men and women from her side of the family supported her. Iravi Pillai’s maternal relatives opposed this. After all, it was Iravi Pillai who provided the expenses. The one who measures out the rice is the responsible uncle. Therefore, at the wedding, the first place of honor as the senior aunt should go to his wife, Kochunnyammai. The argument continued without resolution. The women in the family split into two factions. The discussion reached a deadlock.

Kochumani was filled with excitement. She went to Chanakathara and urged Kochukothai Akka to accept the responsibility of the senior aunt. But it was a matter that would incur great expense. The senior aunt could not go to the ceremony empty-handed. She would have to bring six bronze platters heaped with neyyappam. Where would they get all that from? Pappumma’s husband and wife were living on nothing but the fifteen marakkal of paddy Iravi Pillai gave them each month, barely enough for their gruel. Kochumani agreed to bear the cost of making the neyyappam. Whatever happened, she was determined to make Kochukothai the senior aunt of Chanakathara. Kochumani pressed her again and again. At last, Kochukothai agreed.

But Pappumma’s husband was not ready to oppose Iravi. He knew well that if they made an enemy of Iravi, even their daily gruel would be at risk. Remembering this, Kochukothai too hesitated to take on the responsibility of senior aunt.
She renounced her desire for the title. The scheme that Kochamanyiamma devised to bring down Kokachunnyiamma thus failed to bear fruit.

In the end, it was Kochunnyiamma who assumed the responsibility of Periyamma—the eldest, most respected matriarch. Next in line was Kochu Kodhai of the Chanakath family. Kochumani was relegated to the third position. In every ceremony, Kochumani would quarrel and jostle with Periyamma for prominence.

When it came to the delicacies and offerings that the Periyammas were expected to prepare and bring, Kochumani would always bring twice as much as Kochunnyiamma, both in quantity and in other matters. Yet, on several occasions, Kochunnyiamma outshone her in quality.

The wedding was conducted smoothly and concluded well. However, a rift arose between the matrilineal kin of Iravippillai and those of Madhu Pillai, leading to a split between the two factions. It would be accurate to say that Madhu Pillai’s wife, Kochumaniamma, was the one who divided members of a single family into two separate groups. Just as a new stretch of karisal land is fenced off and cultivated, Madhu Pillai now found the courage to demand an account from the head of the family for the losses incurred. This had never happened before. Iravippillai’s heart burned with anxiety as he saw these signs of the family’s impending disintegration.

Amidst all this, those aligned with Madhu Pillai began to nurture a desire—to break away and form a new social branch, to live separately. If that were to happen, Kochumani’s wish to become the Periyamma of Mangalacheri would also be fulfilled. Within a week, Iravippillai shriveled and withered like pickled mango left too long in brine; he took to his bed.
Klassipperu’s wife, Kunjulakshmiyamma, became pregnant. No one expected to see a little child born to that household. Thus, at Klassipperu’s residence in Erumathra—

Every day at the madam, only acts of piety took place. Service to the Bhagavathi, Ganapathi homam, ritual foot-washing and anointing of Brahmins—such were the daily observances. The utmost care was taken in the service of the pregnant woman as well. Kunjulakshmi wished for a girl child. Kochupillai, on the other hand, desired a boy. The reason for this was that in Kodanthurai, he already had a daughter. If Kunjulakshmi bore him a son, Kochupillai would then have both a daughter and a son. Whom should the child resemble? Whether boy or girl, Kochupillai did not particularly wish for the child to be like Kunjulakshmi. He had not married that dusky beauty out of any great desire.

In Seelandhippillai’s house, a special responsibility now fell upon Kalyaniyammai. In that village, Kalyaniyammai was renowned as a skilled midwife. She had to bathe Kunjulakshmi with oil and herbal paste. Before the sun rose in the east, Kalyaniyammai would arrive at the Erumathramadam. Kochupillai would wake up very early and stand on the stone step at the threshold, as if waiting for someone. If Kalyaniyammai was delayed, she would hurry in, breathless, and stand before Kochupillai, then dart away to the north side like a startled fawn. The air would be filled with the fragrance of kasturi. The gandharva in Kochupillai’s heart yearned to possess her. In Kalyaniyammai’s mind, Kochupillai became a veritable Manmatha, the god of love. Her visits always took place at dawn.
One day, in the brightness of early morning, as she leaned on her walking stick, weakened, he said to his beloved, “Shall I tie the thali for you?” She gave no reply.

Kunjulakshmiyammai’s body was swollen with dropsy; the swelling was compounded by breathlessness. Kalyaniyammai, who had attended the births of many, now found herself pressed by another task amid her duties as a servant: copying out the palm-leaf manuscript of the Gita Govinda. For two days, from the Grantha Library at Seelandhippillai’s house...

She had begun to write out what she had painstakingly sought and collected. On every palm leaf, she drew pictures of Radha and Krishna with her stylus. For whom was this beautiful copy being prepared? Once, a Sanskrit scholar had married her. He had gone away somewhere. When he left, had he remembered to take with him the manuscript she had copied? No one knew. When Kalyaniyammai copied out the manuscripts for others, she never discussed wages with anyone. It was the hereditary occupation of the women of the Seelandhippilli clan. For some days now, no one had asked her to copy any manuscripts. For whom was she making this copy now?

Before the end of the month, Kunjulakshmiyammai was seized by labor pains. The pain was intense. The physician was in the village. It was midnight. Not a single star in the sky. The physician gave her a greenish herbal juice and told her to rub it like a salve. Even so, the child was not born. The pregnant woman writhed and twisted in agony. Kalyaniyammai felt her belly. The child did not move within. When she rubbed with hot water, the child stirred. The water pot broke. The skilled midwife massaged her belly again. A woman’s longing for life was taking human form and coming towards the earth. But it came in a hideous, repulsive shape. A mass of blood. A sharp head on top. Closed eyes. She cut the umbilical cord and separated the child. There was no life in it. “Why isn’t my baby crying?” the mother asked in a feeble voice. At that moment, Kalyaniyammai felt a movement in her own belly. Something was stirring.

The women all said that the punishment Kunjulakshmi received was for wringing the village dry and amassing wealth. Without much delay, after finishing the land measurement work, Klasipper Kochupillai and his family left that village and returned home.

Generally, that year the harvest had been quite good. A sense of satisfaction filled the whole village. Every granary in the Devasthanam was brimming with paddy. There was not enough space to store all the grain. After setting aside what was needed for the temple’s annual expenses and the costs of cultivation, it was thought that the surplus paddy could be sold and, with the proceeds, an elephant could be bought. Some felt that it would suffice even if a golden umbrella were purchased instead. Should it be an elephant? Or a golden umbrella? A great debate arose within the village. In Veluchovan’s toddy shop, this question led to quarrels and even fistfights. Among the temple sweepers, the argument escalated into mutual abuse and shouting matches. Each person’s secret liaisons and hidden stories came to light and were publicly aired. At the temple’s first-of-the-month meeting, the main topic of discussion was this: should they buy an elephant or a golden umbrella? There was another matter that needed to be resolved at the first-of-the-month meeting. It had been a year since the Vezhapra family had been ostracized from the community. During a previous first-of-the-month gathering, the head of the Vezhapra family had defiled the communal feast rice prepared for all the community members after the puja, by touching it. The Vezhapra family were Pallichanmar, the palanquin bearers for the rajas. Though they were Nayars, the other community members would not touch them. For the head of the Vezhapra family to defile the communal rice by his touch was an act of arrogance, and he was punished for it. The Vezhapra family was cast out from the community. Even if someone died in the ostracized family, no one from the village would attend. No one would even speak to them. It was a harsh punishment. Now, a year had passed. It was time to bring a resolution to lift the ostracism. The penance required for this had to be determined by Seelandhippillai Paramu Vathiyar, the most learned man in the village and the spiritual guide to all. Paramu Vathiyar decreed that, without fail, twenty marakkals of land—enough to yield the paddy required to provide a daily midday meal in the temple for a Brahmin—must be leased to the Devasthanam.

A penance was ordained. The head of the Vezhapra family consented to it. With that, he was freed from the constraints of the village council. Thus ended the social meeting of the great men of Kodantra. But among the people of Seerattakkai, a debate arose—did they want an elephant for their community, or a golden umbrella? They stood divided on this question. Some demanded an account of the temple’s income and expenditures.

At Mangalacheri, it was Mathupillai who first asked the community leader for such an account. Even in the community of Konnothupillai, certain disputes arose. The opinion of the Seerattakkai and Konnothupillai factions was that the villagers had no right to interfere in the administration of the temple. According to them, it was enough if the community leaders decided the temple’s affairs. But Kodantra Moothassan, the leader of another community, did not agree. What was wrong in making the accounts known to them? If possible, both the elephant and the golden umbrella should be acquired. But the Seerattakkai were not ready to submit to the villagers in this way. What right did the villagers have to question the community leaders or to instruct them?—this was the question of the Seerattakkai.

Yet, it happened. Just as the head of the Mangalacheri Mathupillai family was questioned, so too were the community leaders asked for accounts. There were villagers who sided with Mathupillai. This became a turning point in the history of the temple, something never even imagined before. Perhaps, it was a sign of changing times.

In Seelanthipillai, everyone—men and women—was literate. The women there had two main occupations. At any given time, one among them would be a midwife. The other occupation was copying palm-leaf manuscripts. They were hereditary experts in this. Any Purana could be copied there. One could even purchase a copy for a price. It was a source of income for them. The women there walked about in white mundus. They were beautiful. Even at home, they wore gold ornaments. They adorned their foreheads with pottu. Their lips...

They are reddish in complexion. No one there is of dark color. When they walk, a fragrance wafts in the air. Yet, they are of a lower caste. No respectable men would mingle with them or touch them. But wherever they go, in any house, they are served food as one would serve honored guests.

It was Kalyaniyamma who brought all the midwives seen in the village from Karuppayi to the earth. She was the nurse for everyone. The manuscripts copied by Kalyaniyamma are held in special affection in the village. The letters are clear, the script is well-formed, and there is not a single error.

In the southern house of Seelandhipillai, there are manuscripts that have been collected and preserved for generations. These are authoritative texts on medicine, astrology, research, mantra, tantra, and all such subjects. It is a family from which great debaters, physicians, astrologers, and epic scholars have been born. From ancient times, higher learning in the village meant studying under the gurus of Seelandhipillai.

The present head, Paramu Vathiyar, is a man of great ability. He is the guru for everyone in the village. The current generation in the village is one that pays him respect. Before this, Paramu Vathiyar was an accountant in a pepper godown in Alappuzha. His manager was Krishnankovindan. Krishnankovindan’s wife was Vaaryanthara Kochittuliyamma. She had four brothers. All of them lived together as a joint family in Vaaryanthara.

Once, when the plague that spread through the Alappuzha region struck, Kochittuliyamma’s four brothers and her husband Krishnankovindan died. That lady became destitute. She had no kin in that village. Her ancestral family was far away, in Malabar.

In Malabar, in the Kaplangattu Mana, there was a Nair family belonging to a class that lived by serving others. In that family was a maiden—her name was Kochidvoori. She captured the heart of a young Namboothiri from the south who had come to that house. They fell in love. At one time, as if they were united...

They ate rice from the same vessel. For a Shudra woman, such an act was enough to shatter Brahminical sanctity. There was a severe punishment for this sin. Unable to bear the prospect of her family being excommunicated from their caste, Kochittuli left her village with her lover, Unni Namboothiri. They settled in Thiruvambadi, in the Alappuzha region. Thus began the Varyanthara family. The only surviving descendant of that family was Kochittuli. Her husband, Krishnankovindan, was her visible deity. The brothers were treasures of affection. When all of them died, Kochittuli was left alone.

At that time, Seelandhipillai Paramu Vathiyar, then a young man, brought Kochittuli to his own village. He found a house for her in the paddy fields belonging to the Devasthanam and settled her there. Paramu Vathiyar married that woman. Through Kochittuli, Paramu Vathiyar had a daughter. That daughter too was married off, and she too gave birth. The beloved child, Kunnumalu, was the very life of Paramu Vathiyar; for Kunnumalu, grandfather meant everything.

Suddenly, the news spread through the village: Paramu Vathiyar was going to Kashi. With a small bundle, Vathiyar set out from Seelandhipillai. It was a journey from which he would not return, a final pilgrimage after seeing his family one last time. What could have caused him to make such a sudden decision? The previous day, while Vathiyar was looking through some astrological manuscripts in his grantha room, his sister Kalyaniammai came and stood before him. Usually, sisters did not stand in front of the head of the family. Thus, until that moment, Vathiyar had not known that Kalyaniammai was pregnant. She, who had been living apart from her husband, was now with child! Seeing Kalyaniammai with her swollen belly, the self-respecting Paramu Vathiyar lost himself in anger. He grabbed the thick staff lying nearby and, like a wild—

With a shout, he leapt before his sister. At first, she staggered back, unable to withstand the blow, and stood behind. Like the fierce Rudra himself, Vathiyar struck a second time, reaching out. Now, Kalyaniyammai had no room left to retreat. Afraid of heights, she let the knot of her sari, which was wrapped around her swollen belly, come undone. Pregnant women do not tie their saris tightly. Vathiyar was forced to turn away. The cane fell to the ground.

The news spread through the village like wildfire— Paramu Vathiyar is going to Kashi. No one could persuade him to withdraw from his decision. From Seelandhipillai’s house, Vathiyar set out and sat in the bhajan hall at the temple. For seven days, he performed bhajans there. All the elders and disciples came to Vathiyar, bowed before him, and offered their dakshina. Once a man has resolved to go to Kashi, it is a sin to tell him not to go. Even his wife, Kochittuli, did not agree to see him in person and send him off on his pilgrimage. Neither his daughter nor his granddaughter—no one had the right to stop him.

It was true, as Kalyaniyammai said, that she had not meant to shame her uncle, but had loosened her clothes out of a desperate will to live. But to the question of whose child she was carrying, she never gave an answer, no matter who asked. To all who questioned her, her only reply was, “I loved a man.”

After seven days had passed, some began to wonder why Vathiyar had not yet left for Kashi. There was something weighing heavily on Paramu Vathiyar, something yet unfinished. It was not about his family, wife, or children. It was the fear that the palm-leaf manuscripts preserved in Seelandhipillai’s house might be destroyed. To whom could he entrust their protection? The only one who knew how to safeguard them was Kalyaniyammai. But how could he tell her?
At last, Vathiyar summoned one of his disciples and—

He spoke. “Tell that Chandali to keep the grantha bundles safe.” Having issued this command, the priest gathered all the gold, silver, and gold coins he had received as dakshina, placed them in the temple treasury, and, without telling anyone, set out on his journey to Kasi. A journey from which he would not return.

From the first to the tenth of Chithirai, there would be the grand Padeni street play at the temple. Each night, after the evening puja, for those ten days, the thullal dance would take place. From the second day onwards, there would be performances of chovan, geethangal, parayan, and kakkan thullal dances. All the happenings of the past year in the village would be presented in these thullal dances, in a satirical manner.

Like the time surveyor Nagampillai bought toddy and gave it to someone, and then caught a crow. The dispute in the temple about whether an elephant or an umbrella was needed. The way Seerattakkaimal treated the community leaders with utter contempt. The sons-in-law of Mangala Cheri leaving their own community and forming a new family of their own. The Konoth family, having run out of rice for expenses, secretly ferrying away a boatload of paddy from the devasthanam at midnight—everything was revealed through the stories woven into the thullal performances.

Even the matter of who the celestial lover was that made Kunjamma pregnant in Kodanthurai—everyone came to know that it was none other than the classic pair, Kochupillai. The kakkan thullal enacted that story thus:

Holding up a child’s figure made of straw in the lamplight, Kakkan asked his wife: “Woman, who does this child resemble?” “It looks like you,” she replied. Kakkan looked closely. “This is not mine.” “Then whose is it?” “From the waist up, he’s as handsome as the classic master. From the waist down, like Seshaiyyan Swami.”
“How can a child belong to two people?”

“In these times, that’s how it is,” said Kaakkathi. “She’ll make him the son of Gandharvan.” “Yes, yes. All day, it’s survey work. At night—Gandharva’s work.” Everyone understood where that work had taken place.
chapters.summary: When government official Klassiper arrives for a land survey, Kodanthara Moothassan and the villagers prepare the sacred Erumathramadam, sparking debates about caste, tradition.

chapters.title: Passing of the Keys
paragraphs: Konnothu Valyachan lay on his deathbed. He would never rise from this bed again. His breathing had grown labored. Only a few days ago, Kodanthra Moothassan had died. In the hour of his death, Konnothu Valyachan and Seerattakaimal had stood by his side. They watched, eyes brimming with tears, as those eyes closed for the last time. Kodanthra Moothassan had lived as a good man; he walked the righteous path. With his death, there was no one left in the village who could taste and identify the subtle flavors of the temple’s morning naivedya prasadam. Now, in Kodanthra, the Moothassan was Ayyappakuruppu; he was the son-in-law of the deceased Moothassan. Likewise, when Konnothu Valyachan died, Kallaraykkal Raman Pillai would become Konnothu Valyachan. Konnothu and Kallaraykkal were two branches of the same family. In either Konnothu or Kallaraykkal, the eldest by age would become Konnothu Valyachan. The administration of both branches would rest with that person. Kallaraykkal Raman Pillai now sat by the bedside of the dying elder, watching without blinking. Seerattakaimal was also there beside him. The sorrow of impending solitude was plain on his face. In the span of a single life, yet another companion was about to depart.
Amidst his labored breaths, Konnothu Valyachan reached beneath his pillow and felt for something. A heavy bunch of keys—the keys to the devasthanam treasury, the rice granaries—

That was the key-bunch of all such things. Earlier, it had been under the charge of Kodanthra Moothassan. When Moothassan was on his deathbed, he handed it over to Konnothu Valyachan. Now, everyone gathered there was eager to know to whom Konnothu Valyachan would entrust it next. In due course, Konnothu Valyachan handed it over to Seerattakkaimal. The reason was that, among the living leaders of the community, the eldest now was Seerattakkaimal. With tears in his eyes, Kaimal extended both hands and received it.

When Konnothu Valyachan was dying, Raman Pillai, the next in line in that family, had expected that the key-bunch of the Devasthanam treasury would be given to him. Similarly, when Kodanthra Moothassan was on his deathbed, Ayyappakuruppu had hoped that the key-bunch would be entrusted to him. But the older generation always has little faith in the new. The elders think the younger generation is irresponsible. It has always been this way. Everyone says the coming generation is worse. Yet, generations move forward.

Now, Seerattakkaimal became the owner of the Devasthanam treasury keys. When Konnothu Valyachan died, all six community leaders had gathered together. It was as if a minor chieftain had left his land.

After Konnothu Valyachan’s death, it was the Kallaraykkal faction that gained importance. The reason was that it was the head of the family who measured out and gave them the paddy for their expenses each month. When Konnothu Valyachan was the head, the women of the Kallaraykkal faction had never eaten their fill. Now, with Kallaraykkal Raman Pillai as the head, the Konnothu faction was lying hungry. There was not enough paddy in the family to measure out as per the accounts. Earlier, whenever there was no paddy for household expenses, Konnothu Valyachan would bring paddy from the Devasthanam granary. After all, in those days, the key was in Konnothu Valyachan’s hands.

It was so. Now, it is in the hands of Seerattakkaima. Raman Pillai was left floundering, without even a handful of paddy for expenses. There was only one way out: to borrow from Ganapathi Ayyar of Mangombu. But the late head of the family had already borrowed heavily from Swami. Swami had finally declared that if he were to give any more paddy, some arrangement would have to be made. The debts incurred by the previous generation were not small. The elder generation, which claimed that the younger had no responsibility for these debts, had already sunk the family deep into debt—this realization was unbearable to Raman Pillai. Yet, for the time being, he considered how to rise and stand on his feet. Unless some properties were mortgaged to Swami, Swami would not lend any more. The last remaining tract, known as Naatrangkaal Naru—forty acres—was mortgaged to Swami, and thus the debts left by the previous generation were cleared. He also borrowed paddy for the present needs.

One of the best lands in the village was Naatrangkaal Naru. That land, belonging to the Konoth family, was now mortgaged to Swami of Mangombu. The deed was executed according to the new land measurement regulations. Paruthikkaattu Ozhathai Maappillai took the land on lease from Ganapathi Ayyar to cultivate it. It was the old surveyor, Nagampillai, who recommended Ozhathai Maappillai to Ganapathi Ayyar for the lease. If Nagampillai spoke, Ganapathi Ayyar would not refuse. Swami would provide the seed paddy. But Ozhathai Maappillai did not begin the cultivation alone. His son Varkki, Anthoni of Aatrukkadal, Mathayi of Kol, and ten other Christians joined together, dividing the shares among themselves—thus it became a collective farming effort. They had sons, daughters-in-law, and enough people to work for them. Many changes began to emerge; some felt that the times to come would be completely different.

Four or five generations ago, a Brahmin named Thanu Ayyar came from Tamil Nadu to Kuttanad as a cloth merchant. He settled in Mangombil and conducted his trade from there. Over time, through the price of goods given on credit, he managed to accumulate an income of four thousand marakkals of paddy. Where could he store four thousand marakkals of paddy? There was no way to take it back to his native place either.

Seeing the Brahmin’s predicament, the hearts of some farmers softened. In those days, there was a system for borrowing paddy needed for agriculture. All the farmers would borrow paddy on credit from the Swami; at an interest of two for every ten. As soon as the harvest was over, everyone would measure out the principal and interest together and give the paddy back to the Swami. That account grew larger and larger. The paddy was abundant and of good weight. Thanu Ayyar brought his family to Mangombil and settled them there. He built a large house to live in. Many generations passed.

Now, all the farmers are clients of Ganapathi Ayyar; not only for agriculture, but even for household expenses, the arrangement is the same. When the land survey was completed, the first registered deed was in the name of Konothu Pillai. When Ganapathi Ayyar read the deed, he felt a sense of security. It was not like the old palm-leaf records. The property had a land survey number. The deed had strength. Yet, another matter troubled the Swami. All the old people were dying one by one. Would the younger generation be as bound to their word as the elders had been? Would they develop the same Brahmin devotion as the old ones? The generation is changing. Land survey has come into effect. That is a change. Have people changed as well? All this must be watched over.
The new clients, year after year, measure out the paddy they borrowed as loans and repay their debts. Yet, no one’s debt ever truly ends. Paddy piles up in the house, endlessly, never to be cleared.

Instead of simply collecting the debts owed to him, Swami’s intention was to have the lands transferred to his name. He would visit the debtors at their homes. In this way, the lands of many families had gradually come under Swami’s name. Swami’s thirst for land only grew stronger. Just as Konothupillai had mortgaged his paddy field of young seedlings to Swami, so too did many others, from whom Swami took over their lands by having them written in his name.
Seerattakaimal would bring eight thousand marakkals of paddy to Swami’s house. Now, if this Kaimal were to die, the next heir would be Kittunnik Kaimal, whom Swami did not consider to be trustworthy.

Kittunnik Kaimal had marital ties with the Aatrithara family. He was a man who showed no hesitation in transferring property from his own family home to his wife’s family.
