It had become customary to harvest paddy from the fields and take it to one’s own family home. But the head of the family had decreed that he was not to enter the ancestral house. So, he stayed at his wife’s home. Until then, the Seeratta family would not eat rice without bathing if they so much as touched anyone from the Aatrithara family. Kittunnik Kaimal paid no heed to such untouchability. Those who broke this rule would be cast out from the family. In many families, such lesser sons-in-law had begun to appear. They would take paddy and coconuts from their own family home and deliver them to their wife’s house, and some had even started living there and running their families from that house. How could one expect Brahmin devotion from those who flouted such customs and traditions? All these were signs that the age of Kali had reached its peak. Swami feared that once the time of the family heads had passed, these people would not measure out the paddy owed to him. For this reason, Swami insisted to Seerattakaimal that the land and its produce should be mortgaged or sold to settle the debt. Kaimal too felt this was only fair. When there is debt, the property...
No respect. In this way, some lands belonging to the once-prestigious Cheerat family came into the possession of Ganapathi Iyer.

In Kodanthara, the present mistress is Ayyappakuruppu’s wife, Agavur Nani—a woman of rare beauty. She is now the Ammaavi—the respected lady—of Kodanthara. The art of the pillow-charm, which could keep Ayyappakuruppu bound within the walls of the house, was a skill she possessed. He would fulfill her every wish. It was only by borrowing money from Swami at Mangombu, pledging two thousand marakkal of paddy, that he bought fifteen marakkal of land in his wife’s name. Until that day, no husband had ever bought property for his wife’s family. This was an act in violation of family law. To make matters worse, Ayyappakuruppu had taken a loan with interest to commit this transgression against social custom. Such was the power of the pillow-charm.

Nangayyar had become bedridden. She lived on only for the sake of her youngest daughter, Kunjamma. Kunjamma, for her part, lived in a world of her own with her child. It was the hope that her Gandharvan would one day return that kept Kunjamma alive. Ayyappakuruppu had developed a special affection for Kunjamma’s daughter, Thripurasundari. The reason was that it was through this girl, and her descendants, that the Kodanthara family must endure. But because Agavur Nani was now in the Kodanthara house, Ayyappakuruppu forgot his own sister and her daughter. The secret that Thripurasundari’s father was neither Gandharvan nor Seshaiyyan, but rather Kochupillai, who had come in the guise of a Kalasip, was revealed to Ayyappakuruppu only by Agavur Nani herself. She was also the first to notice that Seelandhippillai Kalyaniyamma’s son, a handsome, fair-skinned boy, bore a resemblance to Thripurasundari. She told her husband this as well. After that, he lost all affection for his sister and the other family members.
None of this was known to Kunjamma. That simple woman—
She lived on, dwelling in a dream world where only she and her celestial lover existed.

For the first time in the village, a government school was established. Seelanthippillai Kalyaniyammai enrolled her son Kesavan in that school. The teacher was a Tamil Brahmin. Kesavan was a lively boy. Swami predicted that he would study well and become a great officer. That was Kalyaniyammai’s wish too; she wanted Kesavan to study and become someone important.

The temple festival had begun. On the fifth day of the festival, the abhisheka pedestal, the golden umbrella, and other sacred objects were to be brought out. But Seerattakaimal, who held the keys and was entrusted with opening the great treasury to take out these items, had not arrived. Even when someone was sent to call him, he paid no heed and did not set out. In the end, the chariot procession took place without the abhisheka pedestal and the golden umbrella. Villagers from all six communities gathered, and it turned into a great commotion. Yet, Seerattakaimal remained unmoved. He could not bring himself to go along with the new, inexperienced holders of the temple offices. That was the reason for his absence. The villagers knew that if, at least by evening before the procession began, the treasury was not opened and the abhisheka pedestal and other items were not handed over, they would not spare the temple office-bearers.

Some even suspected that the office-bearers had stolen the abhisheka pedestal. In the end, Kodantra Ayyappa Kuruppu, Konathu Ramanpillai, and Mangalacheri Madhupillai together broke open the lock of the treasury in the presence of the villagers and brought out the pedestal and the umbrella. The treasury was then secured with a different lock. In response to this action by the office-bearers, Seerattakaimal filed a case. It became an incident that shook the entire village. The one who played a significant role in this was Mangalacheri Madhupillai. He too was one of the office-bearers. Some said that Kodantra Kuruppu and Konathu Pillai had together created the office-bearer position for Mangalacheri Madhupillai.

They left. Mathu Pillai, who had relinquished the responsibilities of the family head, was now a man whose vigor had faded with the cold. From now on, he would be the rightful keeper of the key to the treasury. The bunch of keys that had been with Seerattakkaima no longer had any use. She had stopped coming to the temple. Her body had grown weak. Her mind was worn down. The affairs of the family were being managed only by her son-in-law, Kittunnikkaimal.

Those who benefited from this arrangement were the women of Kittukkaimal’s household. Their only thought was to help the Aatrithara family as much as possible. The women of the Seeratta family were the ones who would now bear the hardship.

Once the festival flag was hoisted, only the women of the birth families of the Sthani households had the privilege of walking on the upper floors of the mansions. The women of other families would watch the festival from the lower parts of the mansion, as was the custom. But this time, contrary to tradition, the wives of the Sthani men also took their places on the upper floor. Agavoor Nani, Aatrithara Paappi, and Kadammattu Kochikki watched the festival from the mansion’s upper floor. Though the young women of the Kodantra, Seeratta, and Konnotthu Sthani families were also on the upper floor, none of them possessed their former glory. Among themselves, they gossiped about the follies and scandals of their uncles and brothers.

Now, it was Agavoor Nani who received the first honors. Everyone noticed that she wore some of the old ornaments. Where had Agavoor Nani obtained these old jewels? In the Kodantra Ettukattu house, there was a room that had never been opened. Ayyappa Kuruppu and Agavoor Nani together broke open its ancient lock. Inside was a chest. In it, a great many old ornaments—the jewels worn by the Kodantra women of the previous generation. Agavoor Nani claimed them all as her own. The true heir, Kochupennu Kunjamma, knew all about this.

In the Ettukattu house of Konnotthu as well, there was a similar room—one that no one ever opened. There too, old ornaments were said to be kept. The women of the Kallaraikkal branch gathered together and deliberated. Had Ittiraman Mama perhaps taken possession of the old ornaments from the Konnotthu room? Were they not rightfully theirs—who could they ask about it? Raman Pillai of Kallaraikkal and Ittiraman Pillai would not speak to each other. In Konnotthu, there were now two branches—each had gone its separate way. Ittiraman Pillai insisted that the property too must be divided accordingly. Ever since the case where the temple treasury lock was broken, and Ittiraman Pillai had stood as a witness against him, Kallaraikkal Pillai bore an unending grudge toward him. Ittiraman Pillai reproached Kallaraikkal Pillai, saying that the women of the Konnotthu branch were not even given enough paddy to fill their stomachs. Years had passed since the Seeratta hut was thatched. Ittiraman Pillai also accused him of selling off family properties without count. Kallaraikkal Pillai justified himself, saying that he had sold the properties only to pay off the debts incurred by the previous heads of the family. The dispute dragged on endlessly. They would not even look each other in the eye.

That year, after the harvest, Ittiraman Pillai declared firmly that half the yield from the fields must be measured out to the Konnotthu branch; otherwise, he would not agree to measure out the paddy owed for Ganapathi Iyer’s loan. Many tried to mediate, but he would not relent. In the end, it was with seven hundred marakkals of paddy that Ittiraman Pillai returned from the fields.

In this situation, though Raman Pillai hesitated to go to the Konnotthu household, he had no choice but to go. All the women of his branch insisted upon it. His wife, Kadammattuk Kochikku, too, longed to open the unopened door in Konnotthu and see what lay within. Like the old ornaments of Agavur Nani, she too harbored a desire for all the ancient jewelry.

He wanted to try and see for himself. In the end, Raman Pillai went to Konnooth. Idthiraman Pillai, who belonged to that family, was not there. The women of the Konnooth branch were surprised. After a long time, the head of the family was visiting them. The house was not thatched; it was soaked and ruined. The eldest Kunhammayi of Konnooth spoke of their hardships. “Tell everything to your Idthiraman Pillai—” Kallaraikkal Raman Pillai said nothing more. Using the excuse of wanting to see the soaked and ruined house, the head of the family went inside and found the inner room. Inside the room, there was yet another room. Emptiness! For the old jewels, the Kadampattu Kochakki and the Kallaraikkal Kunhammayis had both sweated and given themselves names in vain.

During the temple festival, while the village procession and the Kaliyattam dance were taking place, Kodanthara’s young daughter Kunhammayi’s eyes searched for someone. Among the group of boys holding flags behind the dancers, Kunhammayi saw her Gandharvan. With his hair tied in a kudumi, fair and tinged with red, Gandharvan had come as a beautiful boy. Before the idol was brought to the eastern side of the mansion, there would be a solo drum Kaliyattam performance. From the upper floor, Kunhammayi watched him. In the second row of the flag bearers, he danced with exuberance. Kunhammayi did not see the Kaliyattam. She did not hear the sound of the drums. She was floating in a world filled with the fragrance of jasmine and kasturi. Nangaiyar, noticing the change in Kunhammayi, grew afraid. She realized that some confusion of memory had overtaken her. The child, Thripurasundari, sobbed and cried. Her daughter’s weeping pulled Kunhammayi back into this world. Kunhammayi gathered her daughter in her arms, kissed her, and closed her eyes. Yet, she did not fully return to earth. For a long time—

Long, lingering kisses. Not her daughter, but someone else had been held within her arms. The child cried out at the top of her voice. Even as Nangaiyar bent over her, she did not loosen her grip on the child. Then, fainting, she collapsed, her head resting in Nangaiyar’s lap, lying there like a newborn babe. Kunjammai imagined that Kodantra Gandharvan had come as a boy, holding the flag and the umbrella, dancing and leaping for the sake of the Kodantra family. In truth, it was Seelanthippillai Kalyani Amma’s son, Kesavan.

The mango season arrived. In every grove in the village, children would run about, gathering mangoes. It would take only a quarter of an hour to fill a basket as wide as a chest. Such was the season when mangoes fell in abundance. In the Kodantra compound, to the south of Gandharvan’s temple, there stood a mango tree that soared skyward. One day, no children came there. Only a single child—Seelanthippillai Kesavan. He was the first to come and gather mangoes.

A thick, long tuft of hair was tied to the left. A royal leaf was tucked into it. He wore a spotless white cloth that gleamed. His body was fair, tinged with red, beautifully formed. Kodantra Kunjammai stood transfixed at the sight of him. She felt as though Gandharvan himself had come as a handsome boy to gather mangoes. Kunjammai stretched out her hand and called him to come up to the verandah. Kesavan, frightened, ran and hid. Kunjammai broke down and wept. Would Gandharvan, dressed in enchanting clothes and anointed with fragrant sandal, never come again at night? Was the child who ran behind the festival dancers, waving the flag, and who now wandered the groves gathering mangoes—was he Gandharvan?

Kunjammai grew weak and despondent. She told Nangaiyar the story of how she had seen Gandharvan. Kunjammai waited, hoping Gandharvan would come again to the mango grove. The child Thripurasundari too waited, longing to see Gandharvan.

Kesavan told his mother about the incident that had happened while he was picking mangoes. It was when he was gathering mangoes in the Kodanthur estate—a pale, thin woman had fixed her gaze on him and beckoned him with an outstretched hand. Kalyani Amma corrected his suspicion that it might have been a yakshi. The name of the Kochu girl, Kunjamma, came to Kalyani Amma’s mind as she recalled the matter—she had given birth to a child as golden as a gold ornament. She knew whose features that child bore. Without realizing it herself, Kalyani Amma told her son, “My son, you have a sister.” But Kalyani Amma did not openly say that the child in Kodanthur, Thripurakandhari, and her own son Kesavan, both had the same father—Kochu Pillai of Classipar.

Some people had started calling Paruthikkattu Olathai, the oil-mill man, as “Olathe Mappillai.” The respect he gained was because he had become a farmer. Olathai had taken six and a half acres of Natrankal land on lease from Ganapathi Iyer, for the sake of his son. At first, it was a share-cropping arrangement with ten people, including his son Varkki. Before starting share-cropping, Olathai had explained everything to everyone: after the harvest, the first thing to do was to measure out one thousand two hundred and one marakkals of paddy as rent to Ganapathi Iyer. As sublease, two hundred marakkals of paddy had to be given to Olathai. When taking land on lease and then subleasing it to another, there should be some profit for him. Those two hundred marakkals of paddy would be just enough for his old age and for the expenses of his wife, Oorothai. All these years, Oorothai and Varkki had kept the family going by working the oil mill. Varkki blamed Olathai, his father, for idling away his time and wandering about without working.

He would say it. There was no fault in what he said. But it was only because he believed that, in his old age, he should no longer get involved in such matters, that Nagampillai came forward to help Outha. It must be mentioned that it was Surveyor Nagampillai who stood as guarantor for Outha to take four hundred nal of land on lease from Ganapathi Ayyar.

However, Kolil Mathayi, one of the shareholders, felt that asking for two hundred marakkal of paddy as lease was a bit too much. He expressed this opinion openly. Because of this, Outha and Mathayi ended up quarreling among themselves over the matter. The first crop yielded a good harvest. All ten shareholder-farmers, along with their wives and children, worked together to complete all the agricultural tasks. As a result, everyone made a good profit. Once the first crop was harvested, Kolil Mathayi and Vattathara Peeli took their share and separated.

A few days before that, at Changanassery, Mathayi and Peeli happened to meet Kunjachan. This Kunjachan had married Mathayi’s aunt’s daughter. He had recently bought some land in the eastern foothills and was engaged in farming there. He was acquainted with some white planters who had established large estates. East of Palai, Kunjachan had cleared and leveled vast forests and started rubber cultivation. He was another wealthy man. Following Kunjachan’s advice, Mathayi and Peeli started a joint business. They would buy paddy from Kuttanad at a low price, transport it by boat, and sell it in the hill regions like Pala for a good profit. On their return from selling rice, they would bring back timber logs from the forest by boat. The business that Mathayi and Peeli started flourished greatly. Now, it was they who determined the price of paddy in Kuttanad.
Outha Mappillai felt no envy at Mathayi’s growth. But Mathayi was a deceiver.

The old man knew about it. It was Mathayi who went to Ganapathi Iyer’s residence and revealed that, without Iyer’s knowledge, Outha had taken a sublease for two hundred marakkals of paddy from the partners. Swami called Outha and questioned him to find out if this was true. Outha broke into a sweat. Swami had always believed Outha to be a man of his word. He measured the lease properly and honestly. But the thought that Outha had made a profit from it without his knowledge pained Swami. Still, Swami gave his permission, reasoning that the lease Outha had obtained would ultimately benefit Outha himself. He also advised him to keep a close watch on those in the partnership group. Ganapathi Iyer’s words were clearly directed at Mathayi, and Outha understood this. The eight partners who were present also dispersed. Now, only Outha’s son Vakki and Andhoni from Aatrukkadal remained as partners in farming.

That night, Outha could not sleep. He saw a great danger looming before his eyes. With every passing day, Mathayi was becoming wealthier. Even Kallaraykkal Raman Pillai, from the Konnoothu branch, now borrowed money for his needs from Mathayi. Kallaraykkal Raman Pillai was once a man of great means. He had built a house for his wife’s family. He had repaired the Kallaraykkal house. All of this was done with money borrowed from Mathayi. In this situation, if the need arose, Kallaraykkal Pillai might have to transfer the rights to the four hundred naatrankaal fields to Mathayi’s name. If he cleared the debt owed to Ganapathi Iyer, this could very well happen. This was what filled Outha with fear. There was only one way to escape this predicament: in any way possible, he must acquire the rights to the four hundred naatrankaal fields. Outha went straight to the kolath and met his guardian deity, Nagampillai.
He offered himself as surety for ten thousand marakkals of paddy, and—

Nagampillai wrote a deed for Swami, granting the land to Olathai. Olathai returned, handed over the deed of surety given by Nagampillai, and borrowed all the paddy from Swami. Selling that paddy for a good price and turning it into cash, he went to Kadammattu and met Kallaraikkal Pillai. Without delay, two deeds were registered at the Alappuzha Registrar’s Office. One was the registration of ownership of the Natrankal Four Hundred in Olathai’s name; the other was the registration of the mortgage deed by which he pledged the ownership he had acquired to Nagampillai. That night, the journey of Kunjunji from Paadi to Paruthikkadu was a long one. Everyone he met along the way, Olathai stopped and told, “From now on, the Natrankal Four Hundred belongs to Olathai.”

When he reached home, Olathai’s son-in-law garlanded a prize cow with a plate-garland. Along with it, the trumpet blared as if for a parade of soldiers. In the midst of that exuberant celebration, there was even a doubt whether Olathai had given his prize cow a kiss.

In the village—the best land, the Natrankal Four Hundred, the largest property of the Konnoth family, land that had been mortgaged and written over from Konnothu Pillai to Ganapathi Iyer; land that Iyer Swami had longed to make his own. But now, without even Swami’s knowledge, it had come into the hands of Chekkaatti Olathai. It was news so unbelievable that even the villagers could not accept it; not even Olathai’s son, Varkki. “From now on, the Natrankal Four Hundred belongs to me. After my death, it will be yours,” Olathai said, tossing the registration deed before Varkki.

Ganapathi Iyer suffered great humiliation at having been thus deceived by Olathai. Taking the paddy from his own hands and selling it, Olathai had, without anyone’s knowledge, twisted into his own grasp the ownership of the land from his own ancestral property. The ingratitude of Konnothu Pillai, who wrote the deed without asking or telling him anything, was also something Swami could not forgive.

He could not bear it. In the Konnot family, the old heads of the household had never behaved in such a manner. They had always been bound to truth. When the four-hundred para of paddy field was mortgaged to him, Raman Pillai—the present Konnot Pillai—had been a good man. How suddenly had the heads of this family turned into schemers, devoid of Brahmin devotion? Ganapathi Iyer cursed Konnot Pillai from the depths of his heart! He cursed Othayi as well. Yet, even Swami doubted whether a Brahmin’s curse would have any effect on a Christian.

But the greatest blow fell upon Mathayi at Kol. With the hope that he could one day write the deed for the four-hundred para field, Mathayi had continued to lend money to Raman Pillai whenever he needed it. Now, that land had fallen into Othayi’s hands. To recover his money, Mathayi went to Raman Pillai’s wife at the house behind the cattle shed. He insisted that it was hard-earned money, and that it must be returned to him at once. The money had been borrowed with the promise that it would be repaid with the next harvest’s paddy, or, if that was not possible, by writing over the land itself. With the four-hundred para field already transferred, Mathayi knew that there was no longer any large land left in Raman Pillai’s name. All the remaining large holdings belonged to the Konnot branch. Still, Raman Pillai insisted that he was the head of the Konnot family, and that he had the right to sell or mortgage any land under Konnot’s possession. But Mathayi knew those were empty words. If he could only recover the money he had lent, that would suffice for Mathayi. After all, the money given to Othayi was still there—he could use that to settle his own debts! Mathayi pressed him. “I don’t have the money to pay you now,” said Kallanaykkal Raman Pillai, firmly.

Mathayi did not relent. “Is this the way you speak? Is this proper? Just now we got the money from selling four hundred seedlings. And yet you say there is no money in the house? Is that how the people of this household should talk? I have starved and saved that money, and now it must come to me.”

In business, it was Vattathra Peeli who saw even greater progress than Mathayi. He parted ways with Mathayi and started his own business. It flourished. Peeli’s eldest son, Thoma, became the owner of plantations in the eastern hills. He became a wealthy man. He also felt that he should do a little farming in the countryside. In Mangombu, he took on lease one thousand five hundred marakkals of land belonging to two Swamimars. Mundampadam was the name of that great paddy field. It was the largest tract of land in the village. It lay on the riverbank. For some time, agriculture had...

Uncultivated land lay fallow. No one except Thoma dared to lease such a vast expanse and attempt farming upon it. The reason: Thoma alone possessed the necessary funds. In a matter of days, he hired laborers and had a fence built all around. It was a low-lying paddy field. To drain water from such a large field by the old method—rolling the urulai and turning the vadakkayiru—would have taken months. But how swiftly Thoma, employing the new mechanical method, drained the water! The villagers saw, for the very first time, water being pumped out by an engine. They gazed in awe at this marvel. The engine worked by burning firewood. Its noise could be heard from a great distance. If this mechanical method became the norm, there would be no more need for urulai or vadakkayiru.

Thoma also introduced a new custom in paying wages to the laborers. Instead of the usual payment in paddy, he paid them in cash. Paddy could be found anywhere, but it was money that everyone lacked. The agricultural laborers of the village were eager to work in Thoma’s fields. Never before had such a clear, systematic method of paid labor been established. Where did Thoma get so much money? Only a few in the village knew that story.

Thoma had married Kunjjeli by paying a dowry of three hundred chakrams. At that time, Kunjjeli was emaciated, her chest sunken, her cheeks hollow, her eyes deep-set—nothing but skin and bone. Now, that same Kunjjeli had grown plump and beautiful to behold. The clothes she wore were brought from the city. She now looked like the wife of a white sahib. Thoma had become an important man. During their time living in the eastern hills, Kunjjeli had borne four children. The fourth died soon after birth. That child’s hair was copper-colored. Surely, it must have been the child of a white sahib.

When it was born, it was a difficult delivery; there is even a story that it was killed in the womb. Such things, the villagers say, are quite common in the wild. One day, the white sahib came to Mundampad to inspect the agriculture. The whole village ran to see the spectacle. For many, it was the first time they were seeing the sahib. Some thought, “It is by paying tribute to this white man that our Ponmudampuraan rules this village.” A few reflected on this: this man is trying to change the customs of the village; from now on, only if we learn his language will we get government jobs. But only a handful in the village understood such things. After the sahib finished his meal at the bungalow and came to inspect the farming at Mundampad, he boarded the boat, taking Kunjjeli by the hand and seating her beside him. Neither the presence of Thoma nor the crowd of villagers was any hindrance to the sahib’s amorous pursuits. That moonlit night, Kunjjeli walked alongside the sahib through the bunds of Mundampad’s fields. Her left hand was wrapped around the sahib’s waist.

Paloothra Kunjan was a temple farmer. He had even forgotten to get married. The reason was that all his time was taken up by the temple’s agricultural work. During the farming months, the sun itself would rise only after Paloothra the farmer had gone to the fields. He was angered by the landlords taking the temple’s paddy for their own families. He got an opportunity to express this. That year, he argued before the landlords that all the temple’s lands must be sown. Three thousand marakkal...

There was no paddy in the temple storehouses for sowing in the fields. With even that gone, it was because of the thefts carried out by the landlords that Paluthra opened his mouth. Apart from these three—Kodanthra Ayyappa Kuruppu, Seeratta Ittunni Kaimal, and Konothu Raman Pillai—there was a fourth landlord as well: Mangalacheri Madhupillai. When Paluthra told Madhupillai the measure of paddy he had taken for his family, Madhupillai leapt up in anger. He left only after threatening to teach that laborer a lesson. When Paluthra recited the accounts of the paddy the other landlords had taken, they hung their heads in shame. However the accounts were tallied, only enough paddy for cultivating half the land remained in the temple stores. The landlords decreed that it would suffice to farm only that much. The cultivator opposed this. Kunjhan declared that, with whatever paddy was available, he would plough and cultivate the entire land. For the Pulayas who worked the temple lands, he paid half their wages daily and farmed the whole stretch. That year, the harvest was good. Once the reaping was done, he had promised the Pulayas that he would give them the remainder of their wages in full. The Pulayas had come to trust Paluthra Kunjhan. To them, Kunjhan was a god they could see with their own eyes.

But when the sheaves were gathered in the fields, the landlords came and seized the harvest. As usual, boatloads of paddy were sent to the landlords’ houses. The rest of the paddy was taken to the temple storehouses. The paddy needed to pay the Pulayas their remaining wages was required by Kunjhan. The landlords did not give it. The betrayal of trust that the Pulayas had to endure shook Kunjhan to his core. He could not bear that sorrow. Kunjhan used to sleep on a rope cot on the veranda of the temple’s great paddy granary. One dawn, Kunjhan did not wake up. To have betrayed the trust of the Pulayas, who had placed their faith and love in him—
It seems that his heart broke from what befell him, and life departed from his body.

Konnothu’s elder, Kallaraykkal Raman Pillai, was painted as a villain by Ittiraman Pillai, who filed a lawsuit against him. From then on, Konnothu Pillai could no longer sell or transfer any land; he could not take loans; he could not intervene in temple affairs. The court’s order barred him from everything. Hearing this news, Mathayi’s mind was thrown into turmoil and distress. When Konnothu Pillai had said he would write off small plots of land as payment for the money he had borrowed, Mathayi had refused to accept it. Now, Konnothu Pillai did not have the right to sell even an inch of land. Konnothu Pillai himself could not bear it. He went in person to his associates, the Sthanis, to ask for help. The ten Karana elders of Pullarathu Kudumbam, who had once stood by Konnothu Pillai in times of need, felt a desire to help him. But if Ittiraman Pillai came to know of it, he would turn even those loyal to him against him. When he went to see Mangalacheri Madu Pillai, he learned that the latter had fallen into an even greater predicament. In the conflict with Madu Pillai, Ravippillai had weakened and fallen bedridden, and before his death, he had mortgaged some lands belonging to Mangalacheri to Ganapathi Ayyar. Those lands were the rightful inheritance of Madu Pillai’s branch of the family. Based on the mortgage deeds executed by Ravippillai, Ganapathi Ayyar had calculated the principal and interest and had issued a demand for payment. The court’s peon had come with the summons. Madu Pillai refused to accept the summons. Still, now he would have to go to court, or else he would have to settle Ganapathi Ayyar’s debt with principal and interest. It was said that Ravippillai had taken the loan at the request of his wife, Vaiparacheriyil Kochunnyammayi. Madu Pillai and his wife Kochumaniyammayi together had betrayed Ravippillai and his branch of the family for these very reasons.
Kochunnyamma took her revenge in return.

When the sixteenth-day rites after Iravippillai’s death were completed and Kochunnyamma returned to her natal home, she went carrying with her the property she needed to spend the rest of her days. She had already made the necessary arrangements for this even before Iravippillai’s death. This was a heavy blow to Madhu Pillai and the branch family members. Now, for the debts Iravippillai had taken, it was Madhu Pillai who would have to climb the steps of the court.

When the law came into effect that would portray Konothu Valyachan as a wrongdoer in the eyes of the court, Ganapathi Iyer was shaken. From now on, in every family, sons-in-law would file suits just to tarnish the reputation of the family heads. It was the family heads who had borrowed thousands and tens of thousands from the monastery. All debts, principal and interest, must be settled without delay, a warning bell sounded for the Swami. He began to file urgent suits in the courts against all the family heads. There was not a single family head who did not receive a summons based on the suits filed by Ganapathi Iyer. That was how Madhu Pillai too received a summons. Madhu Pillai was a tough man. The same tough man who had pushed aside and neglected Iravippillai. But now, even such a man as Madhu Pillai did not know what to do. The family heads were astonished—where had his pride and arrogance gone?

The court peon came even to Kodanthara. Ayyappakuruppu had thought that since he had no sons-in-law beneath him, there would be no one to come and ruin his name. But he too received a summons. Ganapathi Iyer had filed a suit for fifteen thousand marakkals of paddy and the interest on it. Kuruppu could not understand how to settle this debt. Of the Kodanthara family’s property, only the farmhouse and a few fields remained now.
There was not a single family the court peon had not visited.
The whole village was caught in the web of Ganapathi Ayyar.

Each householder clutched whatever papers they could find and ran about here and there. Before going to court, some went to see the Swami in person. There was no place for truth in the village. The community had lost its leaders. Families had lost their patriarchs. Brahmin devotion had vanished. In this situation, the Swami insisted that both the principal and the interest of the loans he had given must be repaid to him.

A summons came for Kanakkulathu Pappupillai as well. There was no one as upright and truthful as Pappupillai. Every year, he would take paddy from Ganapathi Ayyar, and without fail, he would return both the principal and the interest, measured out properly. On a hundred marakkal of land by the riverbank, Pappupillai had been farming. The yield was always excellent. The five hundred marakkal of land adjacent to this belonged to the Swami. He had leased it out. Every year, the Swami would demand from the lessee half as much again as was customary for five hundred marakkal. If the hundred marakkal by the river were added to this five hundred, cultivation on the five hundred would flourish. If that could be arranged, the lessee said, he would increase the rent. From that day on, the desire to take possession of Pappupillai’s hundred marakkal of land arose in the Swami’s mind. With this aim, he filed a praadu (suit) in Pappupillai’s name as well. A praadu for one thousand five hundred marakkal of paddy. That year, Pappupillai owed only the eight hundred marakkal of paddy he had taken. Even that was to be paid only after the next harvest. Honest Pappupillai, not understanding the matter, went to the math and met Ganapathi Ayyar. With many people gathered around, Pappupillai asked why a praadu had been filed in his name when he owed nothing outstanding. The Swami argued that there was no false accounting in the math.
“You have been dealing with the math for many years, haven’t you? Every year, you measure out four or five marakkal less paddy…”
They might have come. That shortfall of paddy and the interest due on it might also be there. The moment Papupillai heard Swami’s words, a chill ran through his body. He could not contain his anger.

“How dare you speak like this? Are you even a Brahmin? In Pandinadu, you were just a Maravan who lived with us. Lower than a Paraiyan! At least a Paraiyan has his word of honor. A Maravan doesn’t even have that. Bah! You and your sanctity, your vows!”

Papupillai’s voice was loud. The whole village could hear it. He was a man who minded his own business, who ate what he earned, and never spoke unnecessarily. Yet now, Papupillai called Ganapathi Ayyar a Maravan. Ganapathi Ayyar was hearing such words for the first time in his life. The whole village was abuzz with this talk. Ganapathi Ayyar, who had filed cases against everyone in the village, now found Papupillai to be a man worthy of respect in everyone’s eyes. After this incident, which shook the entire village, Ganapathi Ayyar never stepped out of his residence, the madam. Now, all dealings and transactions were handled by his son.

In the Kodantra estate, the serpent worship shrines multiplied day by day. Because of this, the entire forest had turned into a wild thicket. The corner pillars of the Ettukattu house had rotted and crumbled, the beams had slipped, and the house had sunk down. Only the kitchen section of the northern wing still had a thatched roof. Nangaiyar had grown old, her body trembling with age. Kochupennu Kunjammai always seemed to be looking at something in the distance. Even when there was a loud noise, Kunjammai wouldn’t notice.

One day, when Nangaiyar could not find Thripurasundari, she went searching for her in the fields. There, next to Gandharvan’s temple, she saw her daughter standing and gazing at something. A little distance away, two snakes were entwined together—one male, one female.

They were writhing like snakes. Watching snakes writhe is dangerous. Even after reaching adolescence, Thripurasundari had not yet developed the understanding to grasp such things. Nangaiyar seized her and pulled her away. From now on, there would be an increase in egg-laying snakes in that field. Such was the dense wilderness in that compound. Just like Gandharvan’s temple, even the Kodantra Ettukattu house would become invisible to the eye. There, the jackals would howl. The death-announcing kalan hens would build their nests atop the trees. In time, the next generation would speak of how once there had been a house there.

It was in the room adjoining the Kodantra kitchen that Nangaiyar, Kunjamma, and Thripurasundari would sleep. Nangaiyar in the middle, mother and daughter on either side. All night, the oil lamp would burn. The two, mother and daughter, would not let Nangaiyar roll over and sleep as she pleased. Both would sleep clinging to her. On a stormy midnight, above the roar of the wind, a cry was heard. Only Nangaiyar awoke. She thought it was the wailing of Yama’s messengers. Dawn broke. The world was silent. The sound heard in the night was only that of a mango falling from its stem in Kodantra. The next morning, Nangaiyar did not wake from the sleep she had gone to the previous night. Thripurasundari and Kunjamma tried to rouse her, calling out. She did not move. Neither of them understood what death meant. Thripurasundari ran to the hut and called for the midwife. Upon hearing the news of Nangaiyar’s death, the people of the community gathered. They cremated her in the Kodantra compound. Kunjamma and Thripurasundari did not weep or wail. Thripurasundari did not even know how to cry. Perhaps Kunjamma’s tears had dried up.
Where to shelter that mother and daughter now became the concern of the eldest asan’s wife, Agavur Nani.

It happened. In the ruin of the family, Agavur Nani too bore her share of shame. Yet, after enduring so many torments, her heart too had grown weary. From the eight-pillared house, now overrun by the wilds, she took Kunjamma and her daughter and went to her natal home. The elder Kuruppu took no notice of any of this. He filed a case against Ganapathi Ayyar’s accounts. He argued that the accounts kept by the Swami were not correct, and that none of the repayments of the loan had been entered by the Swami. What he said was true. But for the amounts repaid, there was no written receipt. Ganapathi Ayyar won the case.
It became a case of summary execution; they had to vacate and leave. At every stage of the proceedings, first Kunjamma, and then Thripurasundari, died. Agavur Nani was sent to her family by him.

Many years passed. Every morning, the elder Kuruppu of Kodantra would go to the temple, to the threshold of the great kitchen. Seshaiyyan would take a handful of rice and place it on a lotus leaf for him. At noon, he would receive the rice offered as naivedyam during the midday puja. These were the privileges of the heir in the position of sthani. Even though the house of Kodantra had fallen, the elder Kuruppu continued to receive the privileges of the sthani until his death. The reason for this was that, in all matters, the signature of the Kodantra Kuruppu’s approval was required.
The Trimurthis! That was how the village called them. Kunjhan of Uppamparambu, Paman Karthaavu of Mukkol, and Ittunnan of Sudhoorathu—they were all of the same age, companions.

In his youth, Kunjhan worked in Mangalacheri as a farmhand. There was a time when Kunjhan had taken a hundred marakkals of land belonging to Mangalacheri on lease and was cultivating it. At that time, Ravippillai too...

Together with his wife Kochunnyamma, they spoke to Kunjhan. “Kunjha, you should buy a sari for that Nani girl and marry her.” Nani was living in Vaiparacheri; she was the daughter of Kochunnyamma’s sister. Kunjhan refused, saying he belonged to a lower caste. There was a reason for this. He had fallen in love with a girl in Mangalacheri—Devi, a relative of Iravippillai, had taken a liking to him. But could Kunjhan, a farm laborer, ever marry a girl from Mangalacheri? In the haze of an evening, the helpless lover asked his beloved, his voice faltering, “What should I do, Devi?” Devi replied, “It’s enough if you always desire me.” Kunjhan could not bring himself to defy Iravippillai’s command. At the next Avani month, at the Aravathu stone in Vaiparacheri, Kunjhan gave Nani a sari and tied the thali around her neck. But Kunjhan never once went to see Nani. Every night, Nani waited for him. Each day she went to the temple and poured out her sorrows to the gods. She prayed for her husband. But he never came to her. Kunjhan’s farming prospered. Iravippillai was a support to him. After Kunjhan tied the thali for Nani, he never went to her again—Kochunnyamma once told Iravippillai about this. What could Iravippillai do! Kunjhan could not forget Devi either. Meanwhile, a Sthaninayar from Kodupunna gave Devi a sari and tied the thali around her neck. Kunjhan stood in pitiable silence, unable even to arrange for a wedding feast. Devi stood like a stone and accepted the sari. What was there in accepting a piece of cloth? There was another man in her heart. When the uncle of the man who gave Devi the sari died, he became the head of that family. From then on, Devi had to act with the responsibility of being the eldest woman in the household. As her husband, he brought her to his family…
He left. Devi did not.

The era of Eravippillai had passed. The days of Madhupillai’s glory too had faded. In Mangalacheri, the women had fallen into dire hunger. When he thought of Devi’s condition, Kunjhan could not bear it. She had thought only of herself; even when her husband came to fetch her, she had not gone. If only she had responded to the call that day and gone with her husband, how prosperous her life might have been! It was Ittunnan’s opinion that Kunjhan should build a house and rescue Devi. But Kunjhanpillai’s own thought was that, except for the bond of the coin he had given her with the sari, it would not be right. Even after so many years, the coin waited for him.

As for the family of Paraman Karthavu, they had already been outcastes. The family bore the respectful title of Marakkan Karthavu. Paraman Karthavu had served as the overseer for the Konnotthu family. There was a woman there who waited for Karthavu—a Kunjhamma named Kalikkunjhamma. Karthavu would fulfill her every wish. Through Paraman Karthavu, she became pregnant. But during childbirth, Kalikkunjhamma died. Though there had once been a man named Vayaran Potri, who was considered her relative, there was no one who did not know that the father of that child was Paraman Karthavu. They named the child Lakshmi. It was a name chosen by Karthavu himself. He brought and gave the child everything she needed. For the child Lakshmi, Karthavu was very dear. But she would never call Paraman Karthavu “father”; nor did anyone teach her to do so. When Lakshmi grew up, he gave her a sari. Children were born to her as well. The Konnotthu family had shattered. For Lakshmi and her children, Paraman Karthavu continued to bring the monthly rice for their expenses.
But in the Konnotthu family, all the other women…

When the family was starving, could Lakshmi and the children alone eat rice separately? The paddy that the landlord brought and gave would be finished within two or three days. After that, it was nothing but hunger. When he saw his daughter and children, their eyes sunken and faces pale with exhaustion from not eating, Paraman’s throat would tighten. With a heavy heart, he would tell all this to the landlord. For this, Kunjan Pillai suggested a remedy: “You build a house at the Eriyetra property. Then take her and the children there and look after them.” Paraman found his friend’s advice acceptable. Thus, at Eriyetra property, another branch of the Konnoth family came into being.

Ittunnan’s story was even more interesting than this. Ittunnan was a wiry, sharp-tongued man, with a nature that cared little for others. He had married three times. The first woman he married by giving her a saree did not like him. On the day he gave her the saree, after finishing his supper, Ittunnan went to her house. She did not open the door. She had rolled up the mat and left it outside—a sign that she did not want him. Without a word, Ittunnan turned and went back. The second woman he gave a saree to, he rejected when he found out she had another secret relationship. These experiences gave Ittunnan a few principles. One must ask and find out what a woman’s wishes are. Whether man or woman, once married, one must live by the rules. If he gave a saree and took her, she must remain his until her death. He could not leave her and go away. Ittunnan spoke of things he had never mentioned before. A few days later, Ittunnan found a woman who suited his principles—Araykattu Kochunani. Between them, there was a good…

A perfect match. Sankaran, a man worthy of strength. It seemed as though the gods had created him solely for Kochunani. Like him, she too was dark, sturdy, and short in stature. Kochunani had never loved anyone before. No one had ever loved her either. He took her with him. They lived as an independent family. Until then, such a thing had not existed in practice in that village.

All the old glories of the landlords had faded away. Now, only the three previously mentioned men, known as the Trimurthis, were the leaders of that community. Whatever the issue in the village, people would go to Uppamparambil Kunjhan Pillai. Not Kunjhan Pillai alone, but the Trimurthis would gather, discuss, and make decisions together. If they joined hands, there was nothing they could not accomplish. Those who disregarded them would face punishment as a result. Everyone feared them. Those who had once been mere wage laborers had now become equals to the landlords. The rough old trees had begun to wither, and the stunted, neglected trees below had started to grow and flourish, forming a canopy. Now, all three enjoyed good income, both in paddy and in cash. They also had generous hearts, willing to help others.

There was not even enough rice for the daily charity meal at the temple. There was no one to manage the accounts. If an administrator could be found to run things on an advance payment, agriculture could be revived. There was only one person fit for that role: Uppamparambil Kunjhan Pillai. But who would go and say it to him? The oldest man in the village was Therumathu Kondikkuruppu. Though he was nearly a hundred years old, he still came and went for daily worship at the temple. The decline of the temple pained the old man. One day, Kondikkuruppu went to Uppamparambil and said to Kunjhan Pillai, “Kunjhu, you must take up the administration of the temple.” Kunjhan Pillai knew that touching the temple administration was like putting his hand in fire. He tried to withdraw and escape. But when the elder Kondikkuruppu insisted, he agreed. The Trimurthis gathered.
They made their decision only after much deliberation. Thus, Kunjan Pillai, who had been a ploughman, became the administrator of the temple. That year, the temple’s agricultural lands yielded well.

The most mischievous boy in the class was Kesavan. Sheelanthippillai Kalyaniyamma lived solely for her son. In Kesavan’s class, there was a girl studying—her name was Kochu Devi. Kesavan liked Kochu Devi. He would tell his mother about the affairs of his friends. Whenever he spoke thus, Kalyaniyamma felt his face would glow. Once, he asked his mother, “Amma, where is my father?” Without any hesitation, she replied that he was far away, in Thiruvananthapuram. Then, one day, he asked, “Who is Kochu Pillai?” Kalyaniyamma told him that was his father’s name.

Kalyaniyamma wanted to know more about her son’s friend. When he said she was a good girl, she became eager to see the girl her son liked. Kalyaniyamma, who yearned for love wherever she might find it, had found none. Only disappointments had come her way. Yet, her heart had not been shaken by despair. Her face always remained bright.
Kesavan moved on to the sixth standard. His schooling at that school was over. He found a job. He dreamed of a life where he would marry Kochu Devi and live with her.

Kochu Devi had an elder sister—Kochutti. They had decided to give her in marriage to her maternal uncle’s son. But her mother’s brother, Kochunni Nair, did not agree to this. He had resolved to give her to someone else. From somewhere in the east, he brought a dark, sturdy man named Achoman. He was a relative, but everyone felt he was not suitable for Kochu Kutty. He looked like a sugarcane stalk.

Who could dare speak against the Karanavar? Nothing could happen in that house against the wishes of Kochunni Nair. Kochukkutty’s coming-of-age sari ceremony was conducted with great pomp and splendor. For the next Thiruvathira festival, Achoman brought a boatload of Thiruvathira seer for that family. The seer included nendran bananas, sweet potatoes, and all the customary items. Usually, the Thiruvathira seer brought from relatives’ homes would be handed over to the women of the family. But Kochunni Nair locked it all away in a room.

The next day, with a bunch of nendran bananas, a single betel leaf, and four rolls of tobacco, Kochunni Nair went to the stone house where the Konnothu Valyachan was staying. He told him that he had come to invite the community leader to attend the eldest daughter-in-law’s Thiruvathira. The man at the stone house could not believe it. How many years had it been since anyone in the village who respected the swamis had disappeared? Kadukkathra Kochukalyan also went with affection to invite the Konnothu women for the Thiruvathira.

None of the Konnothu women now had husbands. There was no Thiruvathira fasting there anymore. Among the Konnothu women, it became a subject of debate whether or not to go to the Kadukkathra Thiruvathira. The Kadukkathra people were of a lower caste. The Konnothu women were untouchables to them, forbidden to mingle. The Kadukkathra people did not even have the right to call the Konnothu women to their house.

In earlier times, for the Thiruvathira festival in the Konnothu family, women from all the families in that community would come. Anyone could mingle with the Konnothu people. Now, because of hunger, should they mingle with the Kadukkathra people? “Even if the elephant is thin, can it be tied in the cowshed?”—that was the question of some of the women. Some others thought, “At least for one day, we will get to eat our fill,” and were willing to go. Not only that, but for cooking and serving, only in Konnothu...

The Kadukkathra men would discuss among themselves that the Kunjammas were needed. At those times alone, it seemed there was no fault in it. According to some Kunjammas, there was nothing wrong in eating food cooked by anyone, whoever it might be.

Amidst all this, another problem arose. One among the group of Kunjammas became pregnant. Her name was Suttikkunjamma. The Brahmin who had given her a saree had left her, and it had been two years since then. He had left because he had to lie in hunger, with no way out in sight. The Devasthanam boatman became close with Suttikkunjamma along with Kunjangarasaar. Every evening, Kunjangarasaar would secretly bring her whatever food he could manage.

Despite all this, her periods stopped. She told Kunjangarasaar about it. Kunjangarasaar was of a lower caste; not only that, but for the Parisalotti Konnooth family, this was a disgrace. Kunjangarasaar went somewhere and found the Brahmin who had once given her the saree and brought him back. The Brahmin stayed with Suttikkunjamma for two nights, sleeping with her, and then left again. Thus, Suttikkunjamma’s honor was preserved. For this, Kunjangarasaar spent fifty panam. After that, Suttikkunjamma gained a certain courage—a courage born out of hunger. Lying on an empty stomach, she bore a child. She kept saying that she had decided to run away with Kunjangarasaar. If anything like that happened, it would be a great disgrace to the Konnooth family.

The other Kunjammas pleaded with her not to go that far. Once, someone had run away before. But that had not been a disgrace. Lakshmi, along with her children, had been taken away and settled separately by their father, Paraman Karthaavu. No Kunjamma from the Konnooth family had ever run away with a man of lower caste. If Suttikkunjamma were to run away with Kunjangarasaar, the other Kunjammas said, then there would be no need to go to the Kadukkathra Poothiruvathira festival.

They made a decision. They feared that the Kadukkathra people would humiliate them. But, fortunately, Kunjangarasar did not come to take Konnothu Kunjammai away. The honor of the Konnothu women was preserved.

In Kadukkathra, the festival of Poothiruvathira was celebrated with great pomp. All the women of that community gathered together. It was the Konnothu women who cooked and served the food. At night, there were songs and dances in celebration of Thiruvathira. The Ganapathi song was sung by Seelanthipillai Kalyaniyammai. She had a unique grace in leading the steps and clapping to the rhythm. The Saraswati song was sung by Kadukkathra Kochudevi. She had a fine voice. Kochudevi was beautiful too, and Kalyaniyammai felt a motherly affection for her. When no one was watching, Kalyaniyammai would embrace her and whisper in her ear; “My son is a match for you; Kesavan is waiting for you.” Devi replied, “I am waiting too.”

A school was about to be opened in the village for the untouchable castes. The order for this had come from the taluk office. A building for it had been constructed and completed at the edge of Manikkathara. The Three Elders could not believe this news. For the lower castes to learn to read and write was against the Dharmashastras. That the Maharaja had issued such an order—surely it must be due to the influence of wicked ministers. The Three Elders gathered to discuss the consequences. When Seelanthipillai learned that Kesavan had been appointed as the teacher there, he sent for him through a messenger. They harshly forbade Kesavapillai, saying that if Parayans and Pulayans were taught to read and write, the village would be ruined, and therefore he should not accept that job. Kesavan argued, “How can opening the eyes of a few children bring harm to the village?” But Kunjanpillai said firmly, “You must not be a teacher in that school.” Kunjanpillai and Paman Karthavai—

Kesavan knew that nothing would happen in the village without confronting Ittunnan. But the reasons they gave were not clear to Kesavan. Why shouldn’t the Parayars and Pulayars be allowed to read and write? Kesavapillai was ready to stand upright and ask this question. Kalyaniyamma too shared the same opinion. Yet, she felt it was dangerous for her son to challenge those self-appointed triumvirs. Ittunnan would not hesitate to do anything. Many had advised Kesavapillai that nothing could be done without the consent of the triumvirs. But from the stories he had heard, Kesavapillai felt that Ittunnan had a heart of thorns.

It was Ittunnan who, for the first time in the village, brought a woman to live with him and established a family. It was Ittunnan who first declared that a husband and wife must live together as a family; that he should not leave her. Like Ittunnan, he too had a longing—to bring Kochu Devi to live with him and start a household. Now, just as that life was about to begin, the opportunity was slipping away. Kesavan thought that if he went to Ittunnan and told him of his predicament, he would help. But Ittunnan was nowhere to be seen in the village.

Kunjan Pillai and the Karthavu together prevented the Parayars and Pulayars from sending their children to school. Each Parayan and Pulayan had, in writing, surrendered themselves as slaves to one of the families in the Devasthanam. None of them could act against their overseer—especially not against Kunjan Pillai, the administrator of the Devasthanam. Yet, there was one Parayan who belonged to no master—Idyappan. There was no one in the village as strong as he. He feared no one. He roamed about, committing misdeeds, a ruffian and a brute. No one could control him. Among the Parayars, he stood alone. Under Kunjan Pillai’s control…

He was ready to break the rules. He insisted that his child be sent to school and taught to read and write. Ittyappan did not back down. He was a man with a straight spine, aware that he was a free man, not a slave to anyone. From that day, after taking his son to school, Ittyappan would stay there, keeping watch until school was dismissed. In the evening, he would take his son home. He was not prepared to give up. Ittyappan went to every Paraiyar hut and urged them to send their children to school. No one listened. The reason was that they were all slaves; they were afraid.

A few days later, one morning, Ittyappan left his hut and was never seen again. A rumor spread through the village that Kunjan Pillai and the Kartha had together beaten Ittyappan to death, tied up his body, and thrown it into the river. Along with that, one of the boys from Kesavapillai’s school also disappeared. A school with no children left to study. Not a single child remained. Kesavapillai expressed her distress to Ittunnan. Now that she had secured a government job, this was no longer necessary. Yet, she still had another dream: to wear a garland, to give a sari to Devi and keep her close, to protect her. There was always someone in the village who wished to give a sari to the woman he desired, to care for her and keep her safe.

Ittunnan decided to help Kesavan. When he heard Kesavapillai’s argument that it was not a crime for a lower-caste person to learn to read and write, Ittunnan was moved. But whatever was to be done, it had to be discussed with Kunjan Pillai and the Kartha. Ittunnan went to their houses to meet them. He went many times, but could not meet them. Because it was rumored that Ittunnan was about to help Kesavan, who ran a school for untouchables, they deliberately avoided him, hiding whenever he came.

They did. Ittunnan became angry. He ordered his subordinates, the low-caste workers, to bring their children and enroll them in the school. Thus, three children came and joined. It was Ittunnan himself who would bring them along; he would stand guard at the school; Kesavapillai would teach them their lessons. Kalyani Amma grew fearful that Ittunnan and Kesavan, working together, would turn the village against them. One day, Amma stopped Kesavan as he was leaving for the school. Yet, Kesavapillai went anyway. That night, sleep eluded Kesavapillai. For the first time, he had quarreled with his mother and felt deeply troubled. In the night, he stepped down to the front yard and walked about. Then, through the treetops, he saw a circle of light. Somewhere, something was burning. The next morning, Kesavapillai heard the news: someone had set fire to the Pulayar school. There was no one to put out the fire.
A few days later, an order came from the government: the Pulayar school was to be closed. Kesavapillai was also dismissed from his job.

All the Christian believers saw great progress. The foundation for everything was laid by Paruthikkattu Olatheymappillai. But the new generation did not share that mindset. Olathei’s son, Varkki, and his daughter became very wealthy. The old Olatheymappillai, now bent with age, did not like their ways at all. He would always quarrel with them, repeating his complaints whenever he saw them. In their hearts, they cursed, wishing the old man would die and be gone. Yet, they were eager to fulfill the old man’s greatest wish. A church must be built for the Christians of the village. Vattathra Peeli took up the responsibility of building the church. Olatheymappillai left his house…

It had been years since he had left. One day, a longing arose within him to walk through the village where he had been born and raised, to see it once more. After finishing his breakfast in the morning, he wrapped his cloth around him and set out on foot. As he walked, he felt as if he had regained his health once again. Along the way, he met many people. He recognized none of them. When he asked some who they were, the names he heard, the names of new houses, none of it made sense to him. None among them recognized him as Paruthikattu Olathe. He looked at the old houses he had once visited. All those who had once known Olathe Maappillai there had passed away. He went and stood on the eastern path of the temple. There, he met someone who recognized Olathe—a man called Pappuppillai, who used to call Ganapathi Ayyar of Mangombu as Maravan. The two of them spoke for a long time about how times had changed.

After that, Olathe Maappillai went to Konnothu, Kadampattu, Seerattayil, and Mangalacheri—all those places. He could not forget how things had been for those families in the past, nor the hunger of his childhood, which he had stilled with whatever gruel he could get from those houses. But his own children lived on, forgetting both the village and its surroundings. Only in the evening did Olathe return home. Those at home, not knowing where he had gone, were anxious and alarmed. As soon as he arrived, he called his son and asked for five hundred marakkal of paddy—to be distributed among the starving women in Kadampattu, Konnothu, Seerattayil, and Mangalacheri, and in the other old families. That was his last wish. Varkki agreed to give it. That very night, the old man died.

Olathe’s body was laid to rest in the new temple built in the village. Everyone’s eyes were filled with tears. Was it not the village’s own past that was being buried in that grave? Just as Olathe Maappillai had wished, the next day Varkki measured out and sent paddy to all the old families of Kadampattu, Konnothu, Mangalacheri, and the rest.

A priest had come as the bishop’s representative for Oltai Maappillai’s funeral rites. The priest told the Christians gathered there that the Parayars and Pulayars of the village must be converted, their minds changed and brought into the path of Christ. Some wondered what their caste would be if the Parayars and Pulayars became Christians. But a few days later, the effort to convert the people of that region to the path of the faith began.

Pulayars and Parayars and others converted to the new religion. Once they had received baptism, they were forbidden to worship their old gods—Madan, Marutha, and the others. From now on, there was to be only one god—Jesus Christ. After baptism, they wore the cross. Seethankan became Samuel. In this way, all their names were changed. If anyone called them by their old names—like Seethankan—they were not to respond. They followed all these instructions.

But among the old Christians, a debate arose: if a person of a lower caste became a Christian, could he be allowed into their church? The scriptures did not speak of caste differences. Yet, no one agreed to let them enter their church. In the end, a solution was found: to build a separate church for the converts. For this, they constructed a shed with palm leaves and bamboo poles.

The priest ordered that a school should be established so that the converted Pulayars and Parayars could learn to read and write, but the Christians refused. Their argument was that even if a Pulayan became a Christian, he must remain a Pulayan.

After losing his job, Kesavapillai remained inside the house. There were plenty of old books to read. At times, he would sit and daydream. The dream he saw was of a house where only he, Devi, their children, and his mother lived. Kalyaniammai could not comprehend all the thoughts her son harbored. It was a new kind of life—bringing a woman from her own home and living together as a family. Kalyaniammai could not even imagine what such a life would be like. In the village, only Ittunnan had such a household. Among the Christians too, it was the same. Whatever it was, Kalyaniammai believed that Kesavan would live his whole life with Devi, loving her.

One day, Kalyaniammai went to Kadukathra. After Poothiruvathira, Kadukathra Kochunni Nair had acquired a large walking stick—a symbol of new prestige. Since Konnothu Kunjammaimar had come to Kadukathra, a new family honor had arisen. To Mathaiyar, the mother of Kochudevi, Kalyaniammai said, "Devi is a suitable bride for my Kesavan." This had happened during the time of Devi’s birth. Devi’s mother remembered it. But Mathaiyar told Kalyaniammai directly that giving Devi, a girl from their family, to an ordinary man from the Seelandhipillai line was not fitting for their family’s honor. From the beginning, the women of that family had never been given in marriage to the men of the Seelandhipillai family. So Mathaiyar asked how Kalyaniammai had come with such an idea. Kalyaniammai’s face fell. As she rose to leave, Mathaiyar asked her to eat before going. Kalyaniammai could not refuse. She was a woman who only knew how to comply and follow. Mathaiyar did not even allow Kalyaniammai to see Devi in person.
With a wounded heart and a sense of humiliation, after finishing her meal...

Kalyaniyamma set out from Kadukkathra that day. She did not tell Kesavan about her trip to Kadukkathra to seek a bride for her son. For months, Kesavapilla had been engrossed in a great task. He was examining, one by one, the palm-leaf manuscripts kept safely in the Seelanthippilli room, sorting and categorizing them. Among them, his eyes fell upon a large bundle of family accounts written over generations. In one place, the following was written: “For the baptism ceremony of Thampi Ittikkolan’s child, expenses sent—ten marakkal of paddy.” Had there once been Christians in Seelanthippilli? Why were expenses for temple rituals recorded in the family accounts? What was the truth behind this? Kesavapilla asked Kalyaniyamma about it. She knew a story passed down through the generations. Seelanthippilli was an ancient family. Their ancestors had been Buddhists. The present Dharma Sastha temple had, long ago, been a temple to the Goddess. It was the Buddhist elders of Seelanthippilli who removed the Goddess and consecrated Dharma Sastha there. The temple belonged to the Seelanthippilli family. No one else in that village was of such high caste as they. For generations, they had been great scholars. At one time, like Rama and Lakshmana, two brothers led the family. Both were renowned scholars. Yet, the younger brother mingled with the Parangis and converted to their faith. Still, the brothers lived together under the same roof as one family. In the generations that followed, there were also Christians who had received baptism within this family. Thus, Seelanthippilli had a history of great distinction. But in later times, their caste status declined. The men of that family could no longer find brides from the families of that village. Kesavan was literate. By tradition...

He was born into a family of great scholars. Yet, he did not possess the privilege to present a sari to the goddess of the Kadukkathra family. Now, he worked as a clerk in the shop of Beerukannu Mudalali, keeping accounts.

Beerukannu’s shop stood a little distance away, on the outskirts. It was a large shop—everything from salt to camphor could be found there. From coconut fiber and pomegranate husks to gold and precious stones, all manner of goods were bought and sold in that shop. Beerukannu’s family lived in quarters attached to the shop itself. It was not a place of much bustle. Even late into the night, long after darkness had fallen, Kesava Pillai would sit in the shop, writing accounts.

One night, Kesava Pillai was preparing to leave for home when he noticed Beerukannu Mudalali in great agitation. He had filed a case against the Seeratta landlord, accusing him of wrongdoing. The verdict had come. An official from the court had arrived to seize the Seeratta fields and house and hand them over to Beerukannu Mudalali. If he wished, from the very next day, Beerukannu’s family could move into the Seeratta Ettukattu house. But a good-natured son-in-law had converted to Islam. After quarreling with the landlord of the time, he had left his home and moved out to the outskirts.

The outskirts—a place devoid of honor and humanity. There, the wind always blew like a storm. There was a reason why such a vast expanse lay desolate. It was said to be haunted. Listening to Beerukannu Mudalali’s stories was always fascinating. To Kesava Pillai, this story, like the old tale of the Seelandhipillai family, seemed almost like a legend.

The son-in-law who left Seeratta settled in that ghost-ridden, deserted land, erecting a hut with six posts. For seven years, seven months, and seven days, he remained there in meditation, without food or water. One midnight, he heard the voice of a siddha. “My son,” the siddha called to him. In Seeratta, the son-in-law had followed a siddha...

He left. He went to Pennani, converted his religion, and took the name Pareed. It was from the lineage of that Pareed that Peerukannu was born. It was out of devotion to those ancient ancestors that Peerukannu, the master, said he had come and settled in these outskirts. What he meant was that he, Peerukannu the master, had now come to own the grand eight-room house of Seeratta. The children and women of the family of the Seeratta Karana—who were once the heads of a community in the village and the local temple trustees—would have to be driven out from there. The idols of the Naga Yakshis and Naga Rajas in Seeratta would henceforth be thrown out. The sites of serpent worship would be cut down and destroyed. The kalari, once a ground for heroic games, would now become a cattle shed. The Gandharvan’s temple would turn into a mound of ashes.

Listening to the story told by the master, Kesavapillai sat there for a long time, silent. He went home and made his mother recount that story. Kalyani Amma had never heard the tale that it was the son-in-law from Seeratta who had founded the lineage of Peerukannu the master. Another story connected to Peerukannu came to Kalyani Amma’s mind. It was about Peerukannu’s birth. At that time, Kalyani Amma was a young maiden. One evening, a Muslim elder and a Muslim woman came to Seelanthipillai. Their daughter had been suffering from labor pains for two days. Two midwives had come, examined her, and given up. The delivery would not happen. Kalyani Amma was to go. In those days, Kalyani Amma would not attend the childbirths of castes lower than the Nayars. Whether it was a Namboothiri woman or a Pulaya woman, delivering a child was all the same. It was a matter of two lives. That night, as if possessed, Kalyani Amma went to the outskirts. She rendered all the necessary service to the pregnant woman. The next day, Kalyani Amma remembered how the first rays of the sun fell on the head of the child born to that Muhammadan woman.

She looked on. When she returned home in the morning, Kalyaniyammai’s mother scolded her, forbidding her from entering the kitchen. It was customary for a Nair woman who had attended the childbirth of a Muslim woman to be considered outcast. But Paramu protected her. Kalyani did not become an outcaste. The child Kalyaniyammai delivered that day is now the present Peerukannu Mudalali.

When Kesavapillai told her that Peerukannu would be taking possession of the Seeratta house and land the next day, Kalyaniyammai said, “He was born at an auspicious time. He will not be cruel. One born at a good time will not do evil”—such was Kalyaniyammai’s faith.

The next morning, Peerukannu Mudalali went to take possession of the Seeratta house and land. Amina, who had come from the court, ordered all the Seeratta Kunjammas to leave the house. The eldest Kunjamma in Seeratta was like a lotus stem—her body, nothing but a bundle of bones covered with skin, with no flesh at all. Supporting her by the arm and leading her out was a young woman, herself nothing but bones. Behind them, three Kunjammas each carried a child. The children’s bellies were sunken, their backs shriveled, their heads large, and their eyes lifeless. How had these Kunjammas given birth? Who were the men who had made them mothers? Can offspring be born where there is no flesh? None of these children seemed to have come into this world as living beings. They had neither nose nor tongue. Even their eyes did not move. As though standing in some cave, they all stood in the courtyard. There was nothing there that could be called a man. Peerukannu Mudalali, who had once boasted of belonging to the Seeratta family, now stood petrified. What was he to do with these people now? The Mudalali felt suffocated. He rubbed his chest. From the Seeratta women and the children—

No sound came from inside. They did not know what was happening. A child had been born. Peerukannu, the landlord, was shaken to his core. In that moment of trembling, he spoke without realizing it: “We must not vacate this house.” Then Amina said that, if that was so, the landlord must sign and hand over the document confirming it. He did as she asked. Only the Seeratta field he kept for himself. Leaving that house to the Kunhammis, the landlord turned and went away.

Long ago, the purakkalam—the outer fields—were, in the third watch of the night, a domain ruled by the Kollivayppu spirit, stretching its reach up to the sky. At the height of the coconut trees, in blue flames, the Kollivayppu spirit would challenge all comers. Yet, it was here that Chennan Pulayan lived with his three wives. Chennan was a bonded laborer of the Seerattakkaymal. The purakkalam bordered the five hundred marakkal of land owned by the Seerattakkaymal. It was to guard these fields that Chennan lived in the purakkalam.

Chennan’s first wife, Kunhjali, never bore children. Even though Kunhjali herself suggested that he bring home a woman who could bear children, Chennan refused. Later, it was Kunhjali who went and brought a Pulaya woman. Her name was Ulaki. Ulaki bore him a child. That was Vattathaan.

Once, during the harvest season in the five hundred marakkal fields of the Seeratta clan, fifteen Pulaya women from a distant community came to work. Among them was a beautiful woman. Her name was Kochchiri. Watching her reap was a pleasant pastime. Chennan stood behind her, and never changed his place. Kochchiri scolded the Pulaya guard who always stood behind her. Even then, he did not move from his spot.

He did not move away. After the harvest was over, they drew close and became harmonious. Kochiriyai had earlier been married off to someone. She had lived with him as his wife for a year. Then she rejected him and sent him away. Chennan grew fond of Kochiriyai. Kunjali and Ulaki approved of this. Thus, Chennan had three wives. The wages of another laboring woman now came into that household.

Three Pulaya women, and not a quarrel among them. The three would sit in a circle, with Chennan at the center. They would chat together. If someone cracked a joke, all three wives would laugh. They would eat heartily together. If not, it was as it was. In one corner of that earthen floor, they dug a little pit and created a hiding place. For namesake, a thin cloth hung as a curtain. A man with three wives needed a place for privacy, after all. Vattathaan was the only heir in the family. From one mother’s lap to another’s, he tumbled and grew up. Each mother had her own rules. Each had to give him a ball of rice. Only the finest rice would he eat. Chennan, who returned home only after dark, would check Vattathaan’s belly while he was asleep. If he sensed there was nothing in it, he would wake the boy, make him sit up, and feed him again. Vattathaan grew up. Now he had to be taught the work of the fields. But before Chennan awoke, Vattathaan would already be up and gone outside. Only after Chennan fell asleep at night would he return home. When he came home at midnight, all three mothers would feed him together.

Once, Vattathaan disappeared. He had gone off somewhere. Chennan wandered from village to village searching for him. His eyes grew weary. The wives wept themselves to skin and bone. That house was shrouded in darkness. Two months passed. One day, Vattathaan returned. All three mothers embraced him tightly.

Chennan understood. There was a smell of dried fish about him. He did not have the scent of a Pulayan. For him, the backwater was on the seashore, fishing with a Muhammadan. For the Pulayan, fishing was not a hereditary occupation. Chennan could not accept that. Vattathaan handed a bundle of money to the women and disappeared into the darkness.

Vattathaan’s master was a good man. One day, he went with his master to a place called Ponnali. His master had a house on the Ponnali seashore as well. There, Vattathaan would stay with his master. He alone would do the work of five men. He had the intelligence to finish household tasks efficiently. In that way of life, Vattathaan forgot all about his past. Once, his master asked him, “Don’t you want to marry a girl?” As his master suggested, he agreed to it.

After reciting the Kalima, wearing a cap on his head, tying a mundu around his waist, and completing the circumcision, Vattathaan’s name changed to Pareed. Now, others called him “Master.” He could sit and eat with everyone, as an equal. He and the noble landlord, Sulaiman, together led the prayers at the mosque in Ponnali. Pareed’s nikah also took place. Fatima was from Alappuzha—a poor orphan girl. But the moment Pareed saw her, his eyes went dizzy. She was so beautiful. The master gave his Alappuzha house to Pareed and arranged everything for him to run his family there.

Chennan and his three Pulaya wives went to the backwater shore in search of Vattathaan. They could not get any news about him. For those four, the grip on life loosened and slipped away. The thought first came to Kunjali. Why should one live like this? To be born a woman is only to give birth. She had not even borne a child. Barren! Even if Ulaki had given birth, she too remained barren in usefulness. There was a bastard boy—
That, too, had become a lie.

In the Ilanji forest, at night, they would heap together chaff and husks and set them alight. Four figures could be seen sitting around the fire, like statues. Even at night, sleep eluded them. On some nights, they would simply lie down and sleep right there in the Ilanji forest. That, too, was with a purpose. If they slept in the Ilanji forest, the Kollivayppu ghost would come and strike them dead. In that way, there would be deliverance from this life. Chennan would lie down, making himself an easy target for the ghost. But even the Kollivayppu ghost had its own codes. The ghost would never come near the firelight. It would not enter a house. Sometimes, the ghost would appear in the form of a bull, sometimes as a dog. Whatever form it took, they felt no fear. Yet, not once did the ghost come. Then how, indeed, was one to die and be done with it? The ghost knew them. It would not kill those it recognized. They did not know how to take their own lives.
