If they jumped into the floodwaters, they knew how to swim ashore. They would try lying down, holding their breath for a long time without letting it out. But even without their knowing, the breath would escape. They wanted only to die. Death alone would suffice.

One day, the forest river, more swollen than ever before, overflowed its banks and surged. After that, no one saw Chennan or his wives again. The hut where they had lived still stood in the backyard, just as it was. Anyone who looked that way would feel a chill of fear. The Ilanji tree stood with its head raised, like a spirit. It knew what had happened.

Past midnight, there was a great crashing sound, as though something were being shattered and destroyed. Like great boulders rolling, the springs burst forth. The sound was like a hundred people falling into the flood and struggling, trapped. No one ever swam across that forest river. Not even by boat did anyone venture there. It was said that beneath those waters, the Kasappi ghost dwelled.

The drops of holy water poured by her son moistened Kalyani Amma’s parched throat. Kesava Pillai’s tears splashed upon her chest. In that way, those eyes closed forever. That corpse was not heavy. Kesava Pillai lifted the shrouded body onto the pyre of mango wood and placed the rice in her mouth. The son lit the funeral fire. For fifteen days, he performed the rites as prescribed. He placed his mother’s ashes in a clay pot, buried it in a pit, and covered it. After a year of observance, he must immerse it in a sacred river. With that, one could find peace, knowing all that needed to be done for his mother was done.

Where would mother be now? In heaven or in hell? Kesava Pillai knew for certain she would not be in hell. How many copies of devotional stories had mother written out and copied! With devotion, without a single mistake in writing. Surely, mother must have gone to heaven!

Now, what connection remained with this life? The account books? Since he began keeping accounts in Beerukannu Mudalali’s shop, he had not even touched the ledgers. Once, there had been a desire. He was born into a family that knew how to read and write. He had even been a teacher at the Pulayar school. But he could not continue that. Why did the thought arise that he must earn ten chakrams of Sree Padmanabha coins, that is, two coins? For whom? Only for Kadukkathara Kochu Devi. Someone married Devi. After a few days, he abandoned her and left. She got a second husband. When she was four months pregnant, he too left her. Whenever he thought of Devi, Kesava Pillai’s eyes would fill.

One day, two boats full of people came to Kadukkathara. Devi, who was lying in confinement after childbirth, and all the women came out to see. Who was coming? Why were they coming? Everyone was afraid.

They were the ones who had come to seize and hand over Kadukkathra’s house and land to Kolilmathayi. The debt incurred by Kadukkathra Kochunni Nair. Kochunni Nair was not there. The man who had come from the court said there was no time to wait for him. He took out a paper and, with a practiced rise and fall of tone, read it aloud. He read out, in a loud voice, that the Kadukkathra family was to be evicted and the property transferred to Kolilmathayi. There was even the sound of a drum announcing the order. He commanded everyone to leave the house at once.

Now, the Kadukkathra family lives in a six-foot hut, fenced off in a corner belonging to the Devasthanam. The Kochunni Nair family now survives by gathering and selling green medicinal leaves from the Devasthanam fields.

The Kodanthara lineage has come to a standstill. The Konnoth family has been reduced to the ground. The Seeratta residence has passed into the hands of a Muslim. Mangalacheri is scattered and broken. In various places, the women of Mangalacheri now live in thatched huts. In Seeratta, only Kunjunni Kaimal remains as the head. For what reason does he bear this responsibility? He is simply a head in name. That is all. This Kunjunni Kaimal is dark and thin, his body covered with a dry, itching rash. He is always scratching himself here and there, baring his teeth as he does so. Perhaps it is the wrath of a serpent. The Konnoth head is Krishnapillai. Krishnapillai walks as if he might be blown away by the wind. Before the crow can descend from the tree, the Konnoth boy and the Seeratta Kaimal will climb up and sit on the Devasthanam granary platform. Neither has time to talk. Kaimal has no time for quarrels. He must scratch his body, pick at the scabs, and tear at the sores. Krishnapillai’s attention is always on chasing flies. If a fly is spotted anywhere, a slap will fall there with a crack. Not a single fly can escape from under Konnoth Krishnapillai’s palm.

Now, only six hundred marakkals of land remain under the direct cultivation of the Devasthanam. All the rest of the lands have been leased out. It is the Christians who have taken the Devasthanam lands on lease. They pay the lease rent in paddy, as per the established custom. Then, what need is there for direct cultivation? In the meantime, there were also cases filed in court against the Devasthanam.

Konothu Raman Pillai and Seerattakkaimal, who were made defendants, had signed and issued a lease deed for a hundred marakkals of land belonging to the Devasthanam to Karinjathra Cheriyan. Cheriyan did not know that Raman Pillai had been made a defendant in court over this matter. Cheriyan had obtained the lease deed by bribing Raman Pillai with fifty marakkals of paddy. Raman Pillai had done this during a time of famine. After Raman Pillai’s death, the next valyachan was Eepidikkum Krishnan Pillai. By rights, Ittiraman Pillai should have become the next Konothu valyachan. But before Raman Pillai died, Ittiraman Pillai had already died of a snakebite. “Ittiraman Pillai suffered the consequences of the betrayals committed by Raman Pillai’s family,” said Raman Pillai’s wife to Kadammattu Kochukki.

The hundred marakkals of land for which Raman Pillai had written the lease deed to Cheriyan had already been leased out by him from the Devasthanam. He did not relinquish the land. Cheriyan, making the Devasthanam the defendant, filed a suit. It was such matters, created by the sthanis, that gave headaches to the administrator Kunjun Pillai. He too had grown old. He wished to hand over the responsibility of administration to someone else and slip away. He discussed this with Krishnathirumeny of the Palathol House. Who in that village was fit to take up the responsibility of administration? Moolappadathu Govindan was a suitable person who could be relied upon. But in his own matham, the servant woman he had taken in and was raising…

When it was suggested that Kunjakki’s son was Govindan, Krishnathirumeni said no. What about Nattasseri Padmanabhan? A new man of money. Arrogant. He too was rejected. Then who? In the end, Kunjan Pillai said, “Periyavale, you must take up that responsibility.”

Now, the Palathol Math has more than three thousand marakkal of land. All of it has been leased out to Christians. They will, as per custom, pay the rent in paddy. These days, more paddy comes to Palathol Math than to the Devasthanam. Krishnathirumeni discussed the matter of taking up the Devasthanam administration with his brothers and sons. They all approved.

Seelandhippillai Kesavapillai resolved to go to Kashi. While writing accounts in Peerukannu Mudalali’s shop, his heart would grow weary. His thoughts would fly to Saranath. It would take a year to reach Saranath—a long journey, leaning on a staff, clad in the robes of a pilgrim. To die lying on the Manikarnika Ghat in Kashi—what greater blessing could there be? Once, a great man had come from the north, crossing all these paths, passing through crowds, water channels, and green meadows, and settled in this village. Another great man followed—Paramu Mama. He was a great scholar. To claim kinship with him was a matter of pride.

Kesavapillai’s heart yearned to travel from Kashi to Kapilavastu, and later to Mecca and Jerusalem. When going to Jerusalem, he could say, “The town where Thomas, the disciple of Jesus Christ, once walked is mine.” The people of his village, having heard the gospel, had changed their hearts and converted their faith. Those who converted were ostracized.

The village I cannot set aside is my own village. Even when I go to Kapilavastu, I can say it with pride. Once upon a time, I am the descendant of a great scholar who went southward from this very village. Whoever comes seeking my village, my village welcomes them. It transforms them into its own people. Is there any other village like this? Mother! My village is my mother.

Kesavapillai went to every house to bid farewell. He must remain in meditation at the temple for forty-one days. Only after that should he set out for Kashi. That is the custom. Everyone came to see Kesavapillai.

One day, Vettikkattu Nanukkuruppu came to see Kesavapillai, bringing along his daughter-in-law. From the age of fourteen, Nanukkuruppu had worked as a cook in the houses of great officials. Now, he is the cook for a judge in Thiruvananthapuram. He had taken his son-in-law, Parameswaran, with him to educate him and make him a great man. Nanukkuruppu’s wish is that Parameswaran should become a judge. It was to receive the blessings of Kesavapillai, who was going to Kashi, that Nanukkuruppu brought his son-in-law along. Kesavapillai blessed the young man.

There was no one who knew the right season for sowing in agriculture. The newly educated ones did not know how to consult the almanac for auspicious days and stars. There was no one who could read planetary positions and predict the weather. The Brahmins had become greedy. Now, what would become of the village—that was Chennanadan’s worry.

Only fourteen days remained before the journey to Kashi. When he sat alone in the lower chambers of the temple mansion, every family and every person, every mango tree of the village where he was born and raised, paraded through Kesavapilla’s memory in a long procession. In this village, even the mango trees had names. Mango season was a festival for the children. The jackfruits too had their own varieties and names. The rice cooked from Punnappuncharian’s paddy had the fragrance of ghee mixed in. It felt to Kesavapilla as if his birthplace had bound him to itself with invisible cords. Everyone in this village seemed to have affection for him. He was respected as a man who had learned four letters. He longed to build a house of his own here and live in seclusion. He did not lack the desire to reside in Seelandhippillai’s house either. In that granary house, how many priceless treasures were stored! He dreamed of bringing Kadukathra Devi along and living together in his own house. His mind settled on thoughts of Devi. Since the day he could remember, so many people had died. And with them, their memories faded away. Yet, new births followed. The story of this village was nothing but the story of lives lived and finished.

On the day before leaving for Kashi, Kesavapilla sat at home reading some scripture. His mind was restless and adrift. Someone came and stood outside. He looked up. It was Kadukathra Devi. Her eyes were brimming. Her legs were thin, her back bent, and a large-headed child lay slumped on her shoulder. Devi’s face was downcast. Tears streamed down her cheeks. Kesavapilla held back his own tears. He said, “It is all fate.” Devi turned and walked away.
chapters.summary: As Konnothu Valyachan lies dying, the symbolic passing of the devasthanam treasury keys to Seerattakaimal stirs disappointment, exposes generational divides, and sparks shifting fortunes.

chapters.title: When Justice Falters
paragraphs: A dwarf fox has taken up residence in the temple grounds and howls through the night. Such a thing has never happened before. There are those who grieve over the ruin of the temple and the village. Among them is Chennattu Kunjunayar. Along with him, there were many others who shared this sorrow, such as Kallaaru Mooppan and Sunakkulathu Kittunayar. Chennadan believes that nothing told in the Puranas will ever prove false. This is the end of the Kali Yuga. Hereafter, the lower castes will rise. Dharma and justice will falter. In the village, there is no one with as much knowledge of the Puranas as Chennadan. If he begins to speak, drawing upon the changes that have come with the times and the dharma and justice described in the Puranas, Chennadan would become a great orator.
Chennadan could not reconcile himself to the new laws and regulations regarding land boundaries that came into force after the new land measurement system was introduced.

"Do you know how land was bought and sold in the days when dharma and justice prevailed?" This was the question he posed to Kallaaru Mooppan. Tossing a bit of betel into his mouth, Chennadan continued,

"A flower and a handful of earth would be placed together on the tip of a plantain leaf, with the oil lamp as witness. The seller would hand it over to the buyer. That agreement was as if it were carved in stone—the seller sold, the buyer bought, and it was done. In those days, propriety, dharma, and justice were full to the brim. Only later did the practice of writing on palm leaves come. Now, a deed must be drawn up, and it must be registered. Is that all? Now they say what was sold was not sold, what was bought was not bought. Where is this trend going to end?"
When everything is ruined, God will take the Kalki avatar for the great destruction. The sun will fly like a dry leaf caught in a storm;
Stars fall onto the highway and whirl around; planets collide with each other. Darkness, nothing but darkness. Then, a ghostly rain begins. That will be the beginning of the next era.”

Bhagavatham and all the other Puranas—Chennadan had read and gathered the knowledge from them all. “Now, who understands if you read the Puranas? In some houses, after the night meal, there is a reading. But who truly understands what they read?” That was Chennadan’s complaint. The old man of Kallaar, who had been listening, turned Chennadan’s talk towards village affairs. In Uppamparambu, Kunjhan Pillai was considering stepping down from the temple administration. He had discussed this with Krishnathirumeny of the Palathol house. Pressured by his younger brothers, he had agreed to it. For Krishnathirumeny’s sake, his younger brother, Ganapathi Namboothiri, took charge of verifying and taking responsibility for everything kept in the temple’s rooms—the stored items, the vessels for worship, the sacred ornaments, and all else, according to the accounts. This was news that shocked Chennadan. It was not right, in his opinion, to make a man of the priestly caste an administrator. But Ganapathi Namboothiri was a clever man; most people in the village believed he would take care of everything. Chennadan did not agree. The Palathol family, he thought, were greedy for both paddy and money. Even if they swallowed the whole temple, no one would know. There were no authorities among the sthanis to question them. Therefore, he gathered everyone and discussed that the community itself should take charge of the temple administration. He called together the previously suspended meetings of the headmen, and people from six different communities gathered and spoke. For the time being, the community decided that Ganapathi Namboothiri should continue the administration. What prompted the villagers to decide so was nothing but the fact that that year’s temple festival had been conducted splendidly under Ganapathi Namboothiri’s leadership. In name only, the sthanis were Krishnapillai, who was always bothered by flies, and the dry—

Ganapathi Namboothiri did not forget to show respect and bring joy to Kunjunni Kaimal of the Soriyan family as well. The villagers felt that never before had such a festival taken place. Yet, an incident occurred that unsettled Ganapathi Namboothiri. In earlier times, the women of the Sthanikar families would watch the festival from the upper floor of the mansion, a privilege reserved for them alone. But this time, only a single woman was seen there—a Kunjammai who was related to Ganapathi Namboothiri. She was not a woman of that village. She belonged to a Madampikkal family of Chertala. Since she was Ganapathi Namboothiri’s wife, no one else went there.

But Kochudevi in the crowd could not tolerate this. She was a buttermilk vendor. She made her way towards the mansion. A flock of women followed her. In an instant, Ganapathi Namboothiri’s wife found herself caught in the midst of a group of boisterous, clamorous women, suffocated and overwhelmed. Surrounded on all sides, she feared they might pull her down and tear her away. Somehow, she managed to find a way out and descended the stairs to the ground floor. Though such an act was considered a breach of decorum, Chennadan was delighted that the bold women of the village had brought shame upon Ganapathi Namboothiri. If one were to say that Kochudevi, who first set foot among those bold women, belonged to the Konoth family, those who had seen the old Konoth Kunjammais, who were like goddesses of wealth, would not believe it.

Christian families came with sacks full of paddy to pay the lease on the temple lands. Ganapathi Namboothiri made good use of this opportunity. All the Christians who had taken temple lands on lease had also leased lands from the Palathol family. All of them had outstanding lease payments to those families from previous years. From what they brought this year to pay the temple, first the families...

The remaining dues had to be settled, so Ganapathi Namboothiri measured and only the paddy left after the current year’s lease was what the Devasthanam received. Even that was not enough for the daily needs of the temple. The property meant to be offered to the deity had been diverted to the families, and for this, Ganapathi Namboothiri earned the anger of his elder brother, Krishnan Namboothiri.

“Brother, I have heard it said that the very body of the deity will sweat. If that happens, it will not bode well for the land. Just because we perform the rituals every day, it may seem to us that it is only a stone. But it is not so. Don’t think that by settling the dues owed to us, we have become clever men.”

The deed done by Ganapathi became known to the villagers. Many believed that, as the administrator, Ganapathi Namboothiri was exploiting the Devasthanam’s property. Chennadan and the others, along with the community elders, decided to convene a meeting on the first of the month to bring this transgression to a conclusion. Amidst this, another incident stirred and unsettled the village.

One day, when the temple priest was cleaning up the previous day’s offerings, he saw swarms of insects bubbling up like foam beneath the idol. The power of the deity had waned. It was a sign of doom for the village. The first-of-the-month meeting was convened. A little fire and smoke began to rise. Many argued that the Devasthanam must come under the control of the community. But for the moment, the most important thing was to restore the deity’s power. For that, an Ashtabandha Kalasam had to be performed. But where was the money for that? Where was the paddy? No one had an answer to that.

To everyone’s astonishment, within a few days, two boats filled with paddy arrived at the Devasthanam’s granary. Whenever Ganapathi Namboothiri needed it, Mathullavan from Aatrukkadavu and Sauriyar from Paruthikkadu would each send a boatload of paddy to the Devasthanam. They were Christians who leased the Devasthanam lands for cultivation.

When Ganapathi Namboothiri came and asked, they could not bring themselves to disregard him. The Christian believers praised and extolled the efficiency of Thirumeniyan. It became yet another incident that revealed Ganapathi Namboothiri’s administrative prowess. Great Tantris came and conducted the Ashtabandha Kalasam. All the townspeople cooperated wholeheartedly. The astrologers carefully calculated and declared that the deity had regained its full power.

Now, the entire village understood clearly. A change was evident in the behavior of the people. Everyone bathed and moved about cleanly. The temple, which had lain in darkness, and its sanctum sanctorum now gleamed. There was no one who did not attribute all this to the skill of Ganapathi Namboothiri. Even Chennadan could not speak against Ganapathi Namboothiri now. However, no one in the village knew that Ganapathi Namboothiri had quietly given away some good lands belonging to the Devasthanam to Maathullav of Aatrukkadali and Sauriyar of Paruthikkadu.

Chennadan would finish his meal five naazhigai before nightfall and set out for his wife’s house. Koyilpuram was the name of his wife’s house. Kunjumalu Amma was his wife. Until halfway through the second watch of the night, one could hear the recitation of the Puranas from the house at Koyilpuram. Chennadan was a good reader. He would read and explain the meanings as well. Listening to him would be Kunjumalu Amma, their daughter, their son, and the neighboring women. One day, while the reading was in progress, two unfamiliar people arrived there—a woman and a man. In the dim light, Chennadan could not at first make out who they were. They introduced themselves as a Namboothiri from North Malabar and his daughter.

They took them in. Even though they said they were Bhavathrathan Namboothiri and his daughter Thothrakkutty Antharjanam, renowned members of the famous Kangothu family, Chennadan could not bring himself to believe it. In their faces, Chennadan saw the shade of a Muslim he had once encountered in the Eranadu and Valluvanadu regions. He suspected a case of mistaken identity. Chennadan had seen Bhavathrathan Namboothiri at the Kangothu house before. Chennattu Kunjunayar’s younger brother, Chennattu Kesavan, was a celebrated Kathakali performer in the northern regions. There was hardly a Kathakali stage in those parts where Kesavan did not perform. He was a favorite artist among the great Namboothiris of those regions. Kunjunayar, too, had traveled through the northern areas along with his brother. It was during those journeys that Chennadan and Bhavathrathan Namboothiri became acquainted.

During the Mappila communal riots that erupted in the Malabar region, Bhavathrathan and his daughter, forced by circumstances, converted to Islam and sought refuge in Travancore. Now, he was no longer Bhavathrathan, but Ahmad. His daughter was no longer Thothrakkutty, but Amina. The Mappilas had seized Bhavathrathan, cut off his sacred thread, shaved his head, made him wear a cap, and tied a mundu around his waist. They had made him eat beef. Listening to their stories, Chennadan trembled.

Yet another question remained. Even though they had changed their religion, were they not still a Brahmin man and woman? How could one receive and serve them in a Shudra household? How could one offer them food? Chennadan, well-versed in the customs and proprieties, was plunged into a great moral dilemma. In the end, he decided to lodge them in a Brahmin household. He took them to the Keelmel house.

At the Keelmel house, Govindan and his brothers pondered. Where should they seat Bhavathrathan and Thothrakkutty to serve them food? Should they be seated in the inner kitchen, in the place reserved for Brahmins, and served food there?

It was not right. Not even in the outer shed where the Nairs dined was it permitted. If the Nairs came to know that converts to another religion had been seated and served food there, they would never again sit and eat in the outer shed of this Keezhmel house. In the end, they laid the leaves for the meal in the paddy-threshing room, where food was served to people of other faiths.

Without any of the rituals prescribed for Brahmins, both Bhavathradhan and Gothrakutty finished their meal. Even the leftover rice and curries, after serving them, could not be given to the servants who collected and distributed the remains. In the end, all of it was thrown to the dogs.

Bhavathradhan narrated in detail to Namboothiri Govindan what had happened during the Mappila rebellion. There had always been enmity between the wealthy Namboothiri households and the tenant Muslims, stemming from the arrogance of wealth. The dismissal of workers and the collection of outstanding rent had made the tenants and the landlords bitter adversaries.

If one were to recount what happened at the Kangkothu house: there, the steward Samu Menon had a fierce enmity with the Mappilas. It was Bhavathradhan Namboothiri who had accompanied Samu Menon to collect the outstanding rent owed to the Kangkothu house. When the rebellion broke out, the Namboothiri woman of the Kangkothu house, who had run and hidden for safety, was left unharmed by the rebels. But it was the steward Samu Menon and Bhavathradhan whom they chased down and caught.

Samu Menon had a beautiful daughter—Chinnammu. A young Muslim named Moidhu, who loved her, secretly abducted her and kept her hidden. When this came to light, ten or fifteen Mappilas went there. They caught and tied up Moidhu, who tried to stop them. Then, one by one, they entered the room where Chinnammu was kept. Chinnammu died.

Bhavathradhan, who had aided Samu Menon in his oppressive attempts to collect the outstanding rent from the Mappilas, was not spared either. The leader of the Mappila group, Kangkothu Ahmad Kunji, was the one who caught Bhavathradhan as he tried to escape and hide. The Kangkothu clan had many members in many villages.

Of all the branches that had arisen, only one was known to have converted to another religion—Pavathradhan, as he was called. It was known that Ahmed, who once stood before him with a raised knife, had formerly been a Namboothiri. This much Ahmed understood. But Ahmed did not kill Pavathradhan. Instead, he captured him, converted him, and made him a Muslim. Thothrakkutti too had to endure several acts of violence. In the end, she too converted. Thothrakkutti, now called Amina, recounted all these stories in detail to the Brahmin women of the Keelmel, Paalathol, and other families. Hearing these tales, they were stunned. After staying for a few days with the Keelmel family, Pavathradhan and his daughter departed. No one knew where they went. No one asked, either. Chennadan gave them a little money and sent them on their way. They left. Chennadan stood watching as the father and daughter walked away, one behind the other.

From the moment he heard Pavathradhan Namboothiri’s story, Ganapathi Namboothiri was left astonished. Ever since he had taken charge of the temple administration, enemies had arisen in the community. These were not the olden days. There was no longer any such thing as Brahmin devotion. On all the lands belonging to the community, it was Christians who now did the farming. A time might come when they would refuse to pay rent. As the temple administration gained in power, enemies would only multiply.

The elder and the younger brother sat together and discussed. In the end, Ganapathi Namboothiri decided to resign from the post of temple administrator. He sent word to Chennadan to inform him. Chennadan could not believe it. Even Kallaaru Mooppan suspected some deception in Ganapathi Namboothiri’s resignation. The whole village came to know of it. Why was Ganapathi Namboothiri relinquishing his administrative duties? Everyone asked.

He must have thoroughly cleaned out the temple, leaving nothing behind. It was Nattacheri Padmanabhan who said this. Now, for the daily running of the temple, they depended on the generosity of the sons-in-law at the temple’s boat jetty.
He had to plead. After the riots broke out in the north, some said that Ganapathi Namboothiri was living in fear.

Seelanthippillai Paramu Vathiyar’s daughter, Unnachiyammai, was married to the paddy store supervisor, Eechara Pillai. Eechara Pillai’s maternal uncle, Madhupillai, too, had for a time served as a supervisor of the paddy stores. He belonged to the Ezham Pillai family of Kuttamangalam. After the land survey was completed, the lands belonging to the government were demarcated and once again classified for cultivation. Those lands were the Maharaja’s direct property. To collect the rent paddy from these lands, paddy stores were set up in each region. The person responsible for overseeing these paddy stores was the paddy store supervisor. Before Madhupillai retired from his post, Eechara Pillai had joined the paddy store as an accountant. He had no great greed for paddy or money. He was a man of clean words, with good habits. The son-in-law, in fact, had more public support than the maternal uncle. Once, the son-in-law spoke to his uncle.
“I... I have chosen my wife myself.”
Until that day, no son-in-law had ever spoken so to his maternal uncle. Though Madhupillai was a little startled, he listened calmly.
“Who is the girl, son?”
Without any shyness, Eechara Pillai replied, “Seelanthippillai Vathiyar’s daughter.”

The house of Kochittooli, wife of Paramu Vathiyar, was a mud hut that he himself had built. A hut roofed with the leaves of the native atti tree. The uncle pointed to the future that awaited his nephew: “You will have to live in that mud hut.” That is, if Eechara Pillai stood by Seelanthippillai Paramu’s daughter, he would henceforth be set apart from the Ezham Pillai family. But Eechara Pillai was ready to sacrifice anything.

he was ready to do. That marriage took place. Eechara Pillai stayed with his wife in her house itself. In due course, he became the official overseer of the paddy granary. He became a man supported by many. In those days, when the villagers wanted an example of ideal conjugal life, they would point to the marriage of Eechara Pillai and Unnachiyamma. Everyone had a good opinion of Unnachiyamma. On top of that, she was the wife of the master. She was a woman who never deceived anyone. When his wife wished to have ten marakkal of sowing land in her own name, Eechara Pillai bought her fifty marakkal of sowing land in her name. The money for this included Unnachiyamma’s own earnings as well.

Yet, even with all this, Unnachiyamma was not allowed to enter the kitchen in her husband’s house. Once, when she went to the Ezham Pillai house, she was served rice only in the southern shed. Eechara Pillai too sat there with her and finished his meal. In this way, Eechara Pillai too was set apart. After that, he never went near his own house again. On the spot where Unnachiyamma’s mud hut once stood, he built a beautiful house. Paramu and his wife Kochidooli were happy. The joy of seeing their daughter living comfortably with a good husband. Unnachiyamma gave birth—a baby girl. Paramu took the child in his arms and named her Kunjumalu. She grew up as her grandfather’s beloved granddaughter.

Chennattu Kunju, in his youth, appeared rough in the eyes of the villagers. He would not care even for the Sthanis. For the sake of the family’s needs, he would say anything; he would do anything. The Chennattu family had no notable strength in terms of relatives or kin. Nor did they have property. Kunju’s maternal uncle, Achomachhar, was an innocent man. When he died, the family’s entire property was only fifteen marakkal of sowing land. The profit from that...

It was Kochchunangi, Kunjhu’s sister, who had to fill the stomachs of her eight children and everyone else. Kunjhu would never let them go hungry. He toiled hard on his fifteen marakkal of paddy land. Ploughing the fields, rolling the heavy water drum—he did it all by himself. He would also go to work in the fields of others. He enrolled Kochchunangi’s children in school and made sure they studied. Her younger son, Kesavan, became a renowned Kathakali performer. That too was Kunjhu’s cherished wish. Some pieces of land that had been lost during their maternal uncle’s time, he managed to reclaim. Thus, as the Chennattu family began to regain its greenery, the rough Kunjhu began to appear in the eyes of others as the resourceful, clever Kunjhu.

He desired Kunnumalu, the daughter of Eechara Pillai. Eechara Pillai, the head of the rice granary, was a prominent official in the village. Was Kunjhu worthy enough to marry his daughter? Who would have the courage to go and ask for the girl’s hand there! Kunjhu himself went before Eechara Pillai and said humbly, “You must get Kunnumalu married to me.” Eechara Pillai was not agitated. But he could not give an immediate reply. He only said that he would think it over and let him know. Kunjhu left. Eechara Pillai discussed it with his wife. Kunjhu was a resourceful man. It is only the resourceful who can be a little rough. He had come, driven by desire. Eechara Pillai had faith that Kunjhu would take care of her well. Unnachiyamma hoped that whoever married Kunnumalu would be a man of good conduct. The reason was that Kunnumalu had no maternal uncle to look after her. Her brothers were younger than her. Unnachiyamma herself had lived under her husband’s care. From the time Seelandhipillai Paramu Pillai brought Kochchittuli into the family and took care of her, it had been a household under the father’s supervision. The family of Athipuraykkal still needed that tradition. The fact that Chennattu Kunjhu was a man of orderliness was something Eechara...
Pillai’s opinion. Thus, the marriage was concluded.

Once the alliance with Athippuraykkal was established for Chennattu Kunchu, that family’s fortunes rose. The supervision of the Athippuraykkal lands now became Kunchu’s responsibility. After every harvest, Kunchu would purchase ten or fifteen marakkals of land in the name of Unnachiyammai. Why did he not buy it in the name of Eechara Pillai? Kunchu had an answer for this. If he bought property in Eechara Pillai’s name, then one day, perhaps, Eechara Pillai’s sons-in-law might claim that all this property belonged to their mother’s brother and demand inheritance rights through the marumakkathayam (matrilineal) system. To prevent such an obstacle, Kunchu bought the properties in the name of Athippuraykkal Unnachiyammai. After Eechara Pillai’s time, the properties should go to Eechara Pillai’s children—that is, to Kunnumalu Amma and her siblings. Even in practical matters, Eechara Pillai appreciated Kunchu’s prudence. The villagers too agreed that he was a man of resolve and foresight.

Kunchunayar registered the Koilpuram farmstead, which had ten marakkals of paddy land, in Unnachiyammai’s name. It was said that a family once lived in that farm, which now lay overgrown as the Thazhampudhar forest. The land had an obscure history, unknown to the villagers. They called it waste land. But Eechara Pillai knew that Kunchu would never make a loss in matters of property. Kunchu’s wish was to build a farmstead there and settle his wife and daughter, Gauri. As soon as he expressed this, the Pulayars cleared and leveled the land. With Kunnumalu Amma’s money, a small house was built there. Kunnumalu Amma and her daughter moved in.
Thus, Chennattu Kunchunayar settled his wife in her own...
Taking someone from their own house and settling them in another, by building a new house, was something unheard of in the village until then.

It was Kunjunayar’s sister, Kochunangi, who most strongly opposed and grumbled about this. The Chennattu family’s property had grown, yet there was always pressure. Kochunangi had eight children—not little ones, but grown, with no end to expenses. It was only through Kunjunayar’s hard labor that the large family managed to get by. Still, Kochunangi kept grumbling. Why should her brother give away property to his wife’s family? Her worry was that the family of Kunjunayar’s wife, taken from the Chennattu house, was now thriving and living in comfort. She even spoke of this to many people.

Even Kunjumalu felt a twinge of resentment in her heart. There was a sense of grievance that her husband was buying property for the Chennattu people using a share of the profits from the farming done on the lands at Athippuraykkal. Unnachiyamma, too, had such thoughts. But Eecherapillai would not agree to this. On one side were his own sisters and family, on the other, his wife’s people. Thus, both families harbored suspicions about Kunjunayar. Sometimes, he even had to hear some pointed remarks. Kunjunayar paid them no mind. He cared for his wife, and just as much, he looked after the affairs of his birth family. All three meals, he continued to take at his birth house. At night, by the light of a burning torch, he would go to Koyirpuram. In this way, he never neglected any of the old customs. In the marumakkathayam system, eating at the wife’s house was against tradition. Besides, the Athippuraykkal people were of a lower caste.

Kunjunayar’s daughter, Gauri, sometimes went with her father to the Chennattu house. Kochunangi, her aunt, would pay special attention to her, seat her separately, and serve her food herself. The reason was that she worried her own children should not eat after touching Gauri. Going to her father’s house...

When she returned home, Gauri would recount the happenings of that house to her mother. From these stories, Kunjumalu understood that the food at her husband’s ancestral home was not satisfying. One night, after much insistence from Kunjumalu, Kunjunayar ate the meal served by his wife. It was not proper; yet, for the sake of his wife’s insistence, he yielded. Kunjumalu complained to Kunjunayar about the nature of Kochunangai, who, even for the elder brother who earned and provided for the household, did not serve enough rice to fill his stomach. What the wife said about her sister-in-law was true; but Kunjunayar did not wish to create discord between the sisters-in-law. Whatever it was, after this incident, Kunjunayar began to have his dinner regularly at his wife’s house. Kunjumalu’s mother would cook the dishes her son-in-law liked, steaming and serving them with care. Kunjunayar would sit and eat together with his daughter. Thus, Gauri was blessed with the fortune of dining with her father.

The time had come for Eechara Pillai to retire from his position as supervisor. He had to measure and hand over the government paddy stock to the agricultural tahsildar. Six thousand marakkals of paddy were found to be missing from the granary. The matter was extremely serious. The noose was tightening. Eechara Pillai was an officer who had never broken his oath. Then how had so much paddy gone missing? Had those who worked under him conspired? The good man was bewildered, unable to find any clue or evidence. He had saved money in the name of Unnachiyamma of Athippuraykkal. Eechara Pillai knew well that it was not wealth earned by misappropriating government funds. But who would believe that? The tahsildar gave him a week’s time. The missing paddy had to be procured from somewhere and brought to the granary to make up the deficit. In the end, he sold some properties in his wife’s name, bought six thousand marakkals of paddy, and delivered it to the granary. That responsibility was thus discharged. He also retired from service. Eechara Pillai, contrary to the ways of the world, along with his wife...

He loved his children as well; in due course, he added their names to his property. In the end, when he was forced to use a portion of that property to settle his debts, he was deeply grieved. Yet, when it came to selling the property in her own name to pay off her husband’s debts, Unnachiyammai felt no hesitation or regret. Her only desire was to live in peace of mind with her husband. But fate decreed otherwise. One night, quite suddenly, Eechara Pillai died.

Mother and children wept. In those days, it was only when the maternal uncle died that one was expected to mourn. There was no necessity for the mother and children to weep if the father died. Yet, at Athippuykkal, Unnachiyammai fainted and collapsed. The children, thinking their mother too had passed away, began to cry. Those two could not live apart from each other. Such was the depth of their love. Neither would go anywhere without the other. Even after death, they would not be separated. Their bond was so strong that everyone feared Unnachiyammai too would soon follow her husband. No one was near Eechara Pillai’s corpse. But everyone gathered around Unnachiyammai, who seemed to be drawing her final breaths.

The time for Eechara Pillai’s funeral kept getting delayed. Meanwhile, from his own family in Ezham Pillai, some of his sons-in-law arrived with a few men. They had come only to take away the body. Their real aim was to establish their claim as heirs to the property Eechara Pillai had earned. But the people of the community intervened. They firmly declared that, with Unnachiyammai lying unconscious in this state, Eechara Pillai’s body could not be taken away.
Eechara Pillai’s eldest son-in-law, Madhavan Pillai, insisted that he could not return without his uncle’s body. Madhavan Pillai’s purpose was to claim his father’s property as his inheritance.

Understanding what was happening, Kunnumal too joined in that commotion directly. “We will not give up our father,” she declared, without the slightest hesitation. The place itself was astonished to hear her words. A large number of people from the community had gathered there. When it became clear that all of them were on Kunnumal’s side, Madhavan Pillai and his associates, after shouting threats about taking the matter to court, left the place.

After that, Eechara Pillai’s final rites were conducted at his wife’s house. Unnachiyamma, who lay in a stupor, knew nothing of all this. On the twentieth day after her husband’s death, Unnachiyamma too departed from this world.

Summons from the court came to Kunnumal and her minor brothers. The plaintiff was Elampillil Madhavan Pillai. His argument was that the properties acquired in the name of Eechara Pillai’s wife, Unnachiyamma, should, according to marumakkathayam, pass to the Elampillil family, and that the true heirs to the property were Eechara Pillai’s nephews. Chennattu Kunjunayar, who was well-versed in court matters, had foreseen that such a case would arise. That was why he had made sure that all the properties Eechara Pillai bought with his earnings were registered in Unnachiyamma’s name. Yet, even that did not resolve the problem. Where did Unnachiyamma get the property from? The counter-argument was that it came from her husband Eechara Pillai’s earnings. If that argument was to be completely demolished, it had to be proved that Unnachiyamma had at least some property inherited by right. Though the case was to be argued through lawyers, the mind behind everything was Kunjunayar’s. It was necessary to establish that Unnachiyamma had inherited some property by tradition. While pondering the way to do this, he remembered that in the Athippuraykkal family, for generations…

Chennadan learned the old story, which he had only heard spoken of before, from Kunjumalu Amma. According to the tale he heard, Unnachiyammai’s mother, Kochittilikkal, had a house in Alappuzha—a house known by the name Varyantra. Chennattu Kunjunayar went to Alappuzha and found the Varyantra estate house. He bought that estate house from its present owner. Thus, he obtained the original deed of the property. It was a palm-leaf manuscript. The palm-leaf record was a receipt showing that Varyantra Kochittuli had given seven hundred gold coins to a certain Govindavariar of that time. Kunjunayar leapt with joy. It was now clear that Unnachiyammai of Athippuraykkal had seven hundred gold coins as her own property. If it could be proved in court that she had used that money to buy some property, and that it had multiplied so that Unnachiyammai became the owner of four hundred marakkals of land, then the case would be won—so Kunjunayar believed.

In the case conducted against the wealthy Madhavan Pillai of Ezhamplillil, Kunjunayar won. The verdict declared that all the property acquired in the name of Athippuraykkal Unnachiyammai was indeed property belonging to the Athippuraykkal family. Many later judgments were based on the justice of that verdict. It became a principal ruling in the law of matrilineal inheritance.

The time had come to enroll Kunjunayar’s son in school. But that year, by a government order, children of the Ezhava caste—considered untouchable—were also permitted to study alongside children of the higher castes. The government had issued this order, disregarding all matters of touch and contact. Chennadan was astonished when he learned of this directive. Kunjunayar’s old-fashioned, conservative ways of thinking were not prepared for such a change. He went to see the first standard teacher to inquire about the details. The teacher, a Brahmin, was also opposed to admitting untouchables into the school.

But what could be done? The other young teacher who was there, as soon as he learned that such an order had come, ran all over the village, gathered the children of the Ezhava caste, and enrolled them in the school. The teacher of the first standard could not stop this. Kunjunayar understood his helplessness. He inquired who was the teacher who had made the effort to admit the untouchables. That was Vedippurakkal Kunjannayar. Chennadan knew that he was somewhat arrogant. Once, he had come to the temple and struck the bell that was installed in front of the sanctum. The right to strike the bell and pray belonged only to the Brahmins. His act seemed to question that very right. How would children ever turn out well in a school where such a teacher imparted lessons? Whatever it was, Kunjunayar decided not to enroll his son in a school where he would have to sit and study alongside untouchables. When Chennadan’s wife, Kunnumalu, returned home after not enrolling Manikandan in the school, she quarreled with him. That was a time when all of Kunnumalu’s brothers had finished their schooling and were staying in Alappuzha, Kottayam, and other places, pursuing higher studies. It was Kunjunayar who had made all the arrangements for their education. Kunnumalu’s desire was to have her son Manikandan educated like them and placed in a good position. On the days when he went to school, even if he came home at noon or in the evening after bathing, Kunnumalu would suggest that any pollution from sitting with the untouchables would be washed away. Her view was that they too must run along with the world, keeping pace with its speed. In the end, Chennadan, though unwilling, enrolled Manikandan in the school. On the way home, his thoughts were only about how the world was turning upside down. There should not be caste differences. There should not be untouchability. Where would all this end, he wondered, and his mind grew weary.
Chennadan convened the old first-date meeting.

In the temple’s drama hall, those who had gathered all criticized the move to admit Ezhavas to the school. Vedippuraykkal Kunjanna Nair, too, was present there. He was the first to speak, addressing the progress that education would bring to the village. Now, with the increase in the number of children at the school, there was not enough space in the building. Until a new building could be completed, the government had ordered that the fifth and sixth standards be suspended. This would affect the higher education of the children in the village. Therefore, Kunjanna Nair appealed to those assembled to build the new structure. But everyone opposed this request. They accused him of having increased the number of children by forcibly admitting Ezhavas, and said that his real aim was to break down caste differences.

Kunjanna Nair’s proud declaration that he was a follower of Gandhiji startled some of them. In Chennattu, Kunjunayi believed Gandhiji to be an avatar of the Kali Yuga. All together, they drove Vedippuraykkal Kunjanna Nair out of the drama hall. Yet Kunjanna Nair did not lose hope. He went to meet Kochuraman Vaidyar, the prominent Ezhava of the village, and sought his help for the construction of the new school building. Kunjanna Nair said that he was following the principles of Sree Narayana Guru, who fought against caste discrimination. But Kochuraman Vaidyar was one who wished for caste differences to remain. Therefore, he could not agree with Kunjanna Nair’s way of thinking.

At the very least, a hall the size of a long room must be built. If not, two or three classes of the school would be lost. No one else in the village was concerned about this. Kunjanna Nair seemed caught in confusion. The temple possessed property, though at present it had no paddy in hand. Now, there was no lease—
The full amount had not been collected. A lawsuit was underway for the outstanding dues. A considerable sum was also being spent on the legal proceedings.

Even so, there was not going to be any major obstacle in constructing a building for the school. Kunjhan Nair went to the Palathol family and met Ganapathi Namboothiri. Wasn’t he now the administrator of the Devaswom? Ganapathi Namboothiri thought, “Let the Ezhavas too learn to read and write.” After all, even the Shudras had now begun to read and write, contrary to the Vedas! And yet, no decline had come of it. Not only that, many families had advanced. Now, let the Ezhava too be educated. Ganapathi Namboothiri decided that the Devaswom would bear the expense of constructing a school building.

Behind this, there was another motive as well. Chennattu Kunjhan Nair and his associates opposed admitting Ezhavas to the school. This was an opportunity to confront them directly. Ganapathi Namboothiri felt he should make use of it.

Within the temple grounds stood an old wild jackfruit tree. If it were felled, it would provide enough timber for the school building’s beams. The construction work began swiftly. Chennadan and his associates gathered together and boiled with rage. “Ganapathi Namboothiri is treating the Devaswom’s property as his own,” they complained. There was no one to listen. The community had lost its leaders.

Varattu Sori Kunjukkayimal and E-pidikkum Krishnan Pillai had both passed away. Now, who was the eldest in the Konoth community? No one knew. The current eldest was an Ayyappan Pillai working in the house of some Christian. He could do nothing. Kunjhan Nair and his associates decided to file a case against Ganapathi Namboothiri. Nattasseri Padmanabhan provided the funds. A complaint was lodged. Including Chennadan, fifteen people were listed as plaintiffs. They demanded Ganapathi Namboothiri’s removal from the temple administration. The government...

An administrator was appointed, and a human messenger was sent for this purpose. Meanwhile, within ten days, the construction of the school building was completed. Thus, the first defeat befell Chennadan and his associates. The work undertaken by Kunjhan Nair and Ganapathi Namboothiri was carried out and finished. But the village split into two factions. In many places, there were violent clashes and riots.

One day, early in the morning, news spread throughout the village: Ganapathi Namboothiri’s boatman, Paachu, had been stabbed to death on the road north of the temple. Until then, the village had never witnessed a murder. There had been a suicide once before—someone had hanged himself. But this was the first murder. Paachu lay dead, stabbed. There had been an argument between Paachu and Muthalathu Raman. Muthalathu Raman was Chennadan’s henchman. With a single stab from Raman, Paachu died. The police arrived. Chennadan and his associates fled and went into hiding. The police went to their houses and harassed the women. Ganapathi Namboothiri had the police do this. He made good use of the opportunity to strike at his adversaries.

A case was decided in the High Court, ordering the appointment of a receiver. Chennadan and his associates won. When the time came to take charge of the temple ornaments, the paddy in stock, the money, and all other assets after proper accounting, the entire village gathered there. The temple, which had been administered by the Sthanis for centuries, now came under the management of the receiver. There were those who mourned this change. Those who had been opposed were delighted. But Ganapathi Namboothiri showed no hesitation. His swift and sharp actions astonished Chennadan and his associates. In the end, the Devasthanam passed from the hands of the villagers, and even those who had stood with Chennadan could not help but feel a sting.
Sri Narayana Guru was building a temple for the Ezhavas. The Guru himself came and consecrated the idol. In that...

Kunjanna Nair was engaged in organizing the Ezhavas for a collective cause. He also took part in the sambandhi feast held at the house of Kochu Raman Vaidyar, a prominent Ezhava figure. That is, Kunjanna Nair sat and ate as an equal with the Ezhavas. It was news that shook the entire village. Kunjanna Nair’s next endeavor was to establish a post office in that village. He went around the entire village, collecting signatures for a petition. Though Chennadanan and Kanakkulavan initially refused, they too signed in the end. Was it not something the village truly needed? Finally, permission for the post office was granted. It was started in an old building belonging to the Devasthanam. Since it was under the responsibility of the temple receiver, court approval was also required. Permission was granted to run the post office for one year. Only if the income generated could cover the expenses would the permission be extended.

But no one sent letters to anyone from there. Nor did any letters arrive. Only a few letters related to the court would come. After a month, the accounts were tallied. The income was only three rupees. The government’s expenditure was twelve rupees. The postmaster and Kunjanna Nair discussed how to increase the income. The postmaster came up with an idea. When his salary arrived that month, he bought five rupees’ worth of postcards and envelopes from his own pay. Kunjanna Nair suggested that the postmaster himself use those postcards and envelopes to write letters to everyone in the village. The content of those letters was a request that everyone should write letters. In those letters, he described the importance of the post office. The postmaster himself delivered the letters in person. One of them reached the girl next door to him. That led to some disputes and commotion.
The next month, fifteen rupees’ worth of postcards were sold from the post office. Only one person bought them—

Vettippurakkal Kunjannayar. To the Ezhavas who distilled arrack, he wrote—‘Arrack must not be distilled, arrack must not be drunk, arrack must not be given to others.’ This was the essence of the letter, echoing the plea of Sri Narayana Guru. In the letter received by Chennattu Kunjannayar, the message was that temple entry was the birthright of all Hindus. The one who had written and sent it was Gandhiji. In the letters written to those who had received a school education, it was stated that freedom is our birthright, and that foreign rule must end. Even the Christians in the village received letters. They gathered and discussed. Though the ruler of our land is our own Raja, the real authority rests with the representative of the British Emperor. He is a Christian who follows the Vedic path. Some among the Christians felt that they must act to thwart the Hindu agitation to drive him out. Chennattan could not accept the aim of allowing the untouchables to enter the temple. In another letter that heated up Chennattan and his associates, there was a question and an answer. What must the Nayars do to prosper? They must implement individual property rights. To Chennattan, this seemed like a plan to destroy all the remaining joint families at one stroke and level them to the ground. That is, all the property in the family must be divided proportionally according to the number of heads. Each person could then take their share and go their separate way. After that, there would be no such thing as a family. If so, then who would protect and care for the women? Their husbands must protect them. Would such a thing happen in Nayar households? It is Kunjannayar who has been protecting and caring for his sister, Chennattu Kochunangai, all these years. Kochunangai bore eight children. There is a man who fathered them—Kunjiramasar. He has given nothing to her or her children to this day. If individual property rights come into force, would it mean that the husband would be responsible for protecting his wife?

The property that Kunjunayar had earned for the Chennattu family—when it came to dividing it according to individual ownership, Kochunangai, her children, and their offspring would each receive a share. Would he have to buy it from them and descend to the Chennattu way? When he pondered this, Kunjunayar found himself in a state where no solution or decision seemed attainable.

Kunjumalu’s younger brother, Athippuraykkal Raghavan Pillai, had secured a position as a teacher. He had a new aspiration: to establish a plantation in the eastern range of hills. Kunjumalu, Raghavan Pillai, and their other brothers would often discuss this together, and Chennattu would listen in. Kunjumalu too agreed with the idea. All the Christians in the village had become wealthy by buying plantations in the eastern hills and cultivating them. But it required money. When Kunjumalu argued on behalf of Raghavan Pillai to partition the family property, Chennattan said, “All your brothers are grown men. In their youth, I took care of their upbringing myself. I have finished that duty. I have earned and provided property for the Athippuraykkal family. From now on, you must look after your own affairs. Apart from what is needed for family expenses, it is decided that the remaining paddy will be sold to buy a plantation.” Raghavan Pillai bought a plantation at Erumelil. When agriculture flourished there, Kunjumalu dreamed that grand two-storied houses would be built at Athippuraykkal and Koyirpuram as well. Once, when he returned, Raghavan Pillai took back his sister’s ten-sovereign gold necklace. It was the necklace made for Eechara Pillai’s daughter. Raghavan Pillai’s honeyed words could charm anyone. Poor Kunjumalu trusted her brother.

The situation in Kunjunayar’s Chennattu family was not very satisfactory. The eldest son-in-law, Kochukittan, never followed his mother-in-law’s guidance. He never had time to involve himself in any agricultural work. Always, his only pursuit was to follow behind Vedippuraykkal Kunjannayar.

Work. He took part in the efforts to establish the Nair Service Society and to implement individual property rights, which were initiatives undertaken by Kunjannan Nair. He had resolved to marry a woman he desired, buying her a saree and arranging the wedding. Chennadan knew about this. The woman was the daughter-in-law of a man who had once testified against Chennadan in a case he had filed. Yet Chennadan gave his consent. If individual property rights were to be established, then as the family head, a fifteenth share of the property Kunjannan Nair earned would go to Kochunangai and her children, as well as to his own children—that is, five or ten marakkal of land. The prevailing sentiment among Kochunangai and her children now was that the family head could go wherever he wished.

Kunjannan Nair, the only son of Kunjachi, the maid of the Palathol house. He grew up eating the leftover rice brought from the house where his mother worked. But one day, while still in school, he told his mother, “I don’t want the old rice you bring from there.” After that, he never ate it again. Kunjannan was a diligent student. He had a good character, was modest and disciplined. He got a job as a teacher in the very school where he had studied. After that, he no longer sent his mother to work as a maid. He cared for and protected his mother. Kunjachi, who was well-liked by everyone and had earned a good name for herself, had only one wish—that her son should get married. But Kunjannan Nair, who had taken on social responsibilities, never found the time for such things. In the end, Kunjachi died without seeing her son married. Her body was laid out in the shed and

He did not perform any of the final rites for his mother, except lighting the funeral pyre and placing her ashes in the urn. Kunjan Nair had no faith in such rituals. Because he did not carry out the funeral ceremonies, the women in the neighborhood felt that Kunjachi’s soul would wander, lost and without direction.

One day, Kunjan Nair was nowhere to be found. Only later was it discovered that he had joined Gandhiji’s ashram. His house had now become a reading room. The young men who had once been his followers would gather there. There, they would hold discussions about the country’s independence and about individual property rights.

Vaikom temple, famed as the southern Kashi, had now become the center of a satyagraha. A satyagraha had begun there to win the right for the untouchables to move freely in public places. Kunjan Nair, who had gone north to Gandhiji’s ashram, was now returning to take part in the satyagraha. The elders in the village were afraid that all the youth might join the satyagraha. They tried to forcefully prevent children from going to the reading room at Vadippuraykkal. Their belief was that anyone, no matter how good, who set foot there would become a rebel. But now, many of the young men spent their days and nights there. Newspapers would arrive there. As soon as the postman delivered the paper, everyone would gather to read it together. Chennadan and his associates would hold meetings at the house by the canal. It was an action that would shake the entire country. Soon, the untouchables would demand entry into the temples as well. Chennadan’s opinion was that the authorities should bring in the military to beat, crush, and trample the satyagrahis. But the others who were with him...

He did not become as agitated as they had expected. Countless changes were taking place in the world. A great world war had come and gone. Many more changes were yet to come. All these could only be known through the newspapers. In Eswara Namboothiri’s opinion, children should not be prevented from reading newspapers. Satyagrahis were pouring into the village like a mountain flood. Could a flood be stopped by building a sand embankment? These were people who would not retreat even if beaten to death. It was the upper castes who were leading the satyagraha. The Congress was the great force behind it. Gandhi himself was under great pressure in this matter. To fight against caste discrimination, the Ezhavas had their own organization—the Sree Narayana Dharma Paripalana Sangham. Namboothiri women did not need to cover their faces with palm-leaf umbrellas as a veil. The old custom of Namboothiris having sambandham with Nair women should be abolished. Widow remarriage should be made a reality.

Chennadan and the Vattalikkal listened to all this, their tongues hanging out in astonishment. Fearing that a great danger was about to befall the land, they gathered at the house of Palathol to discuss how to escape from it, and parted ways after sharing a meal. Yet, some good came of it; the enmity between Chennadan and Ganapathi Namboothiri came to an end. Not only that, both factions decided to unite and act together to reclaim the temple affairs from the receiver administration. Through their respective lawyers, the two groups withdrew the case, and the receiver administration was to come to an end. With the court’s permission, a man named Krishnan Pillai was appointed as the administrator. Even the title of the office changed—the new name was “Manager.”

The untouchables began to walk on the public roads. It was Parayan Idyappan who walked first. Perhaps someone had incited him; or perhaps he had decided on his own to begin walking thus. By nature, he was stubborn. He was born in the lineage of Cheramannan Thiruvanchan. In the village, it became an event of great significance.

Big arrangements were underway at the reading hall. There was to be a reception for Vaikkam Satyagraha participant and jail-returnee Vedippuraykkal Kunjan Nair! For the first time ever, such a welcome event was being held in the village. Many did not even know what it was. A large crowd gathered, including women. After the reception, a discussion meeting was organized. Kunjan Nair spoke passionately about Harijan upliftment, freedom, and such matters. Athippuraykkal Raghavan Pillai presided over the function. Manikandan felt immense pride—his own maternal uncle was giving a speech. When the meeting ended, he held Raghavan Pillai’s hand and walked with him to the reading hall. There, at the communal feast that followed, he sat and ate beside his uncle.

When he returned home, he saw his father standing there, bristling with anger like a tiger whose cub has been threatened. Chennadan questioned Raghavan Pillai’s action of making his son eat together with an untouchable caste. In the end, after a quarrel, Chennadan stormed out, and it was Manikandan who followed him and calmed him down. Though many women in the community insisted that Koyirpurathu Kunnumalu and her daughter should be ostracized, nothing of the sort actually happened.

Manikandan’s schooling at the village school came to an end. Now he had to be admitted to the English school. From Ambalappuzha’s seashore, it was a ten-naazhikai walk back and forth to the English school. Manikandan was not lazy about walking. To admit him to the English school, Cheannadan enquired about the procedures from Sridharan Unni. It was an expensive affair. In those days, it was the maternal uncles who had to admit their nephews to school and see to their education.

Chennadan knew well that Raghavan Pillai would never do any of those things. No matter how difficult it was, Chennadan was determined that Manikandan must learn English. He also had to see that his own son-in-law, Kochukittan, studied English. If Kochukittan studied and got a job, then his younger brothers would be protected and secure. Vettikkattu Nanukkuruppu had made his son-in-law Parameswaran study English. Now, Parameswaran was a police inspector. Parameswaran had married the daughter of a peishkar, a man of collector’s rank. Now, the Vettikkattu family had risen to a high position.

But, after having worked as a cook for great officials and making his son-in-law study, when Nanukkuruppu grew old, Parameswaran treated his uncle as if he were a mere servant. Nanukkuruppu felt no sorrow in this. Had not his son-in-law risen to a great position? That was enough. The old man, who consoled himself that the family had prospered, withdrew and lived quietly.

The rough Cambridge cloth that Chennadan had brought from Alappuzha was not suitable for Manikandan. When he tried it on, Chennadan felt it was too big. Still, he decided it would do. Kittakkaniyar prepared and brought a fine palm-leaf umbrella. Manikandan tied his veshti, put on the shirt his father had sewn for him, took the palm-leaf umbrella in hand, and set off to study English. Among those who studied with him, many joined English schools in distant towns. Some stopped their studies altogether.

Manikandan wrote a letter to his maternal uncle, Raghavan Pillai, who was then at the estate in Erumeli. He wrote that he needed suitable clothes and an umbrella. A reply came from his uncle, saying he would bring the clothes.

In the newly established court by the Maharaja, arguments and counterarguments about individual property rights were ongoing. Everything said by the supporters and opponents appeared in the newspapers. It was widely spoken that individual property rights would soon become law. Anticipating this, Raghavan Pillai expressed his eagerness to sell certain properties belonging to Athippuraykkal. When he came, he did not bring the clothes meant for Manikandan. He did not care at all about his son-in-law joining the English school. Now, the estate needed some more money. For that, land belonging to Athippuraykkal had to be sold. His younger brothers, Govinda Pillai and Kesava Pillai, did not object in the least. They had no thought of speaking against their elder brother. It was Chennadan who spoke up for Kunjumalu. Now, if family properties were to be registered, it had to be shown that it was for family necessity. The new law stated that buying new property for the family, spending from family assets, or selling and registering properties was not allowed. Therefore, for the needs of the estate at Erumeli, selling some land here by writing a bond was not wrong, Chennadan said very matter-of-factly.

It was only then that the scheming Raghavan Pillai had done all this time came to light. The estate he had bought at Erumeli was not family property. He had bought it in his own name. Chennadan had suspected this earlier, which is why he intervened now. He had taken family property, to which everyone had rights, and bought an estate in his own name. It was Raghavan Pillai’s attempt to usurp family property. When Kunjumalu Amma realized the true nature of the younger brother who had sweet-talked her and cunningly taken away her jewelry, she was overcome with despair. Without even consulting her husband, she had handed over her jewelry to her brother-in-law. Because of the wind that blew in the name of individual property rights, from now on, with no affection left, everyone would only think of their own...
They will take care of the matter. In this wind, the very foundation of the family would crumble. “Let it be, let it go,” said Chennadan, consoling his wife.

Raghavan Pillai was adamant that the property should be sold and the money obtained. Or, he wanted a separate share, a portion of the property to be his alone. From now on, it would not be family property; the assets must be divided into six parts. Kunjumalu Amma had two younger sisters and three younger brothers. The sisters had many children. Kunjumalu herself had two children. If the property were divided according to the individual share system, Raghavan Pillai would get only one thirteenth of the share. His argument was that this was property earned by his father and given to his children; it was not property belonging to the Athippuraykkal family. Therefore, his contention was that it would suffice to divide the property among the six children of Eechara Pillai, the overseer of the paddy granary.

But earlier, when the sons-in-law of Eechara Pillai argued in court that the properties of Athippuraykkal Unnachiyamma were actually earned by Eechara Pillai, it was Chennattu Kunjunayar who ran about, argued the case, and ensured that none of those properties were lost. It was Kunjunayar’s efforts that led to a final verdict, according to which all the Athippuraykkal ancestral property belonged to Unnachiyamma; it was family property. Because of such a court verdict, the Athippuraykkal properties were protected. Otherwise, the sons-in-law of Eechara Pillai would have taken them all away. But Raghavan Pillai refused to accept any of this. His argument was that the court verdict was one that was obtained by suppressing the truth. He filed an appeal. Even Kunjumalu Amma’s sisters sided with Raghavan Pillai. Although, if the individual property system were implemented, they would have received a larger share, still, they did not join in filing a case against Raghavan Pillai. Kunjumalu Amma was left alone. In the end, in the Koyirpuram where Kunjumalu resided...

Only the house and the farmhouse fell to Kunjumalu’s share. The four hundred marakkal of land and the other farmhouses were divided among the brothers. Thus, the Athippuraykkal family ceased to exist. Kunjumalu was left without even a strip of land to cultivate.

All over the village, lawsuits and disputes raged in the courts, as the law of individual property rights was enforced. Because the Maharaja, out of his goodwill, had signed it, it became law. The Chennattu family had only fifteen marakkal of land. All the wealth that came later was earned by Chennadan’s own labor. But according to the law of individual property rights, everything had to be divided by shares. The children of Kochunangai and their children would each get a share. One share would go to Kunjunayar as well. At most, ten marakkal of land would be his portion.

All these years, he had been known as Chennadan. But when the division was done, he was reduced to being just Kunjunayar. Once he had held plenty of paddy and money in his hands and wielded authority. It was good to get some property; at least there would be no shortage of kanji for a meal. But he decided he wanted no more disputes or quarrels.

He called his sister Kochunangai and said, “I am handing over the keys right now. I am giving up the land and the farmhouse. Tell your children. If they want to split and hack everything into pieces, let it be so. Otherwise, if all of you want to stay together, let that be so. Whatever you think I deserve, give me that.”

Kochunangai had not expected this. The sight of the brother who had protected and cared for them all these years leaving the family moved their hearts to tears. After the division, what guarantee was there that Kochunangai’s children would look after her?
Chennadan bought a copy of the law of individual property rights, signed into effect by the Maharaja’s own hand. Manikandan read a section of it to his father.

He brought it to attention. If the family property had been earned by the husband, then one-fourth of it would rightfully belong to him. Cheennadan sincerely congratulated Manikandan for his intelligence in discovering that such a share existed. Following this division, one-fourth of the property earned by Kunjunayar for the Cheennattu family would belong to Kunjunayar himself. But even here, fortune did not favor them, said the vakil’s clerk after examining the documents. The reason was that, although the deed stated that Kunjunayar had provided the money to purchase the property for the Cheennattu family, the wording of the document was such that the property could be interpreted as belonging to the family. In the end, all that Kunjunayar received from the family was the seven and a half marakkal of land he had earned through hard labor. Thus, that chapter too came to an end.

In this way, much property was lost for the sake of the family. Similarly, Padmanabhan of Nattacheri, who had earned considerable property for the family, also spent a few days wandering about with Keshu and Vaithaava, only to receive a single share in the end. Thus, many families were ruined and disappeared.

Now, Kunjunayar was living in Koyirpuram; he was the head of a household consisting of his wife and children. But with what was he to manage the expenses? All that Kunjamalu Amma received was the farmhouse at Koyirpuram. Kunjunayar had only seven and a half marakkal of land. Household expenses had to be met; Manikandan had to be sent to school. Manikandan remembered the time when his father had cultivated the lands at Athippurakkal and Cheennattu. How had things come to this now? It was all because of the new law brought by the Maharaja! Manikandan hated the Maharaja who had enacted such a law. He did not participate in the Ponnuthampuran Thirunal celebrations at school. Yet, through this law, an event occurred that brought Manikandan some happiness: his father—

She had come to stay with them permanently at home. For Manikandan, this felt like a good change. Yet, his father had grown very thin. Mother said it was because of worry. It was something that had happened all over the land, not just to one person. What use was there in worrying? Mother would try to console father.

Manikandan was clever in his studies. Viswanathan was his closest friend—civilized in both appearance and manner. Manikandan scored high marks in language subjects, but was poor in mathematics. There was not a single day when he did not get beaten by the math teacher. He would not attend the math classes held after lunch. Once, when Viswanathan had come to Manikandan’s house, he mentioned that Manikandan never came to the math class after lunch. Kunjumalu Amma scolded her son. Unable to contain her anger, she shoved a lump of hot cow dung into the mouth of the crying Manikandan. Kunjunayar too scolded him. After that, Manikandan began going to school even after lunch.

It was during a visit to Viswanathan’s house that Manikandan drank tea for the first time. Viswanathan’s mother was the headmistress of a school. Viswanathan showed her some poems written by Manikandan. She liked them. Later, during the annual day celebration at her school, Manikandan recited one of his poems. The poem was about beggars.

When he began to eat the rice he brought from home to school, he would often see some beggars around the dining room. Many times, Manikandan had given his food to them. Among those beggars, one was covered all over with scabies. Another was a woman afflicted with leprosy. Yet another, with a swollen belly and a shrunken, caved-in chest. When she walked, foul-smelling water would trickle down her thighs from behind. One day, she stood in front of the school...

Manikandan saw the dead body lying there. That became the subject of his poem. When he finished reading the poem, a long applause arose. When it became known that his son was writing poetry, Chennadan too was pleased. Yet Kunjunayar said, “He writes only about these beggar children. Is there any merit in that? What if he wrote devotional poems instead?” Kunjunayar consoled himself, thinking, “Let him write like this for now—later, he will write devotional poems and stories too.”

In the evenings, Manikandan would not come straight home from school. He would go to the reading room of Vedippuraykkal Kunjan Nayar. There, bhajans would be held. He would join in the singing. Once, Kunjunayar learned of this and went there himself. The place had a sign that read “Gandhi Ashram.” They sang the song “Raghupati Raghava Raja Ram” there. Kunjunayar too was entranced by the song. The bhajan was so filled with devotion. That day, Kunjunayar did not scold his son. Yet he offered advice: “Do not mingle with the young men who gather at Vedippuraykkal. Telling lies all these days that you never went there is a great sin. No matter how many mantras you chant after telling lies, it will do no good.” Manikandan accepted his father’s advice in his heart.

Manikandan passed his exams every year. Meanwhile, Viswanathan’s mother was transferred to another town. In this way, Manikandan lost that friend. There was another who loved Manikandan in his class—a girl named Sarada.

For Vedippuraykkal Kunjan Nayar, life was in a way like that of a renunciant. Only the ochre robe was missing. He cooked and ate by himself. He would eat vegetables boiled with salt. He touched neither tea nor coffee. He would rise very early in the morning. Most of his time was spent in chanting the Lord’s name and reading scriptures. On a small plot of land on the western side of Vedippuraykkal, he did some farming. There

He did not like women coming to weed the fields. He would not even speak with those born as women. In some ashram up north, he had learned yogic postures— He had learned them for the sake of self-restraint, To conquer lust and anger. But none of this brought him any benefit. He did not attain mental unity. He wished to live as a celibate, But his mind would slip away. At dusk, he would dream as if someone was standing at the threshold calling him; It would be the young woman from the neighboring house.
