Sometimes, it would seem as if he himself had reached her bedroom and was standing there. Now and then, the memory would return of once seeing a woman’s nakedness while she was bathing in the Kodanthara pond. Crowds would gather for the prayer meetings led by Kunjanna Nair. The mental agitation that arose during the prayers would become visible for all to see. He sometimes felt that sermons delivered with distracted prayer bore no fruit. He undertook a ten-day fast with unbroken chanting of the divine name. Chennadan and his companions also took part in that chanting. When Kunjanna Nair lay fasting, people would come to see how his body seemed to glow like burnished gold. After breaking his fast, there was a unique power in the sermon he delivered. He began not only spinning thread and holding prayers, but also the work of village advancement and Harijan uplift. The temple, which had been under receiver administration, was fully reclaimed, and a committee chosen from among the community took over its management. The temple regained its former prosperity. That year, Kunjanna Nair himself oversaw the temple festival.

When the village was afflicted by a rabid dog menace, the ashram’s Balasena group hunted the dogs. They chased down and killed many dogs, both rabid and healthy. Kunjanna Nair could not tolerate this. Even rabid dogs, he argued, should not be tortured. Suren, a member of the Balasena…

Thiran could not understand it. Even Kunjanna Nair was unable to explain to him the fundamental principle of non-violence. When he learned that Manikandan, despite having declared that he would not go to the ashram, was in fact coming there every day, Kunjanna Nair admonished Manikandan with words of wisdom. No matter how justified the need, one should not lie, he said. Without lying, Manikandan argued that he could not come there. Yet, he could not avoid coming to the ashram. His coming there was not for anyone else. It was for the sake of the country’s freedom. Kunjanna Nair could not refute Manikandan’s arguments. At many such moments, his mind faltered. It felt as if he was retreating from the convictions he had regained through fasting. Even now, his mind was not clear. From somewhere, desires and attractions reached out their hands. Was Gandhiji failing? Was it impossible to live like Gandhiji? Kunjanna Nair had seen great leaders who had renounced all comforts and sought non-violence. He himself could not adhere to it. He needed yet another purification. Even among those who came to the ashram, there was a certain lack of zeal. How could he inspire them, instill enthusiasm and vigor in them?

Another event shook the village. Some Pulayars who had converted to another religion now attempted to become Hindus again. These were people who had worked as servants for the Christians at the riverbank. The Christian landlords, joining together, tied them to coconut trees and beat them. Many were beaten so severely that they were close to death. Chennattu Kunnu Nair and his associates ran to the ashram and reported this outrage. Everyone, in one voice, demanded that this wrong must be avenged. But Kunjanna Nair, warning that this could turn into a communal conflict, somehow calmed them and sent them back. Surendran and Manikandan together went to visit the homes of the Pulayars who had been beaten.

That was a great consolation to them. A young Pulayan said, “From now on, I am not a slave, nor am I Kunjathan. I want a name that is neither Hindu nor Christian.” Though Surendran could not fully grasp the meaning of his words, he felt it was necessary to bring together such people.

Manikandan passed the final exam at the English school as well. He sought a way to secure a job that would fetch a salary of ten chakrams, stamped with the seal of Sri Padmanabhan. It seemed as if Kunjumalu Amma’s life was finally bearing fruit. But Manikandan’s heart was set on joining college. That was an expensive affair. There was not even enough income for household expenses. Kunjumalu Amma sent him to his maternal uncle. His uncle, Raghavan Pillai, had an estate at Erumeli. His dwelling was there too. To reach it, one had to walk through the forest. On the way, he saw the vast estates of the local Christian landlords. At last, he reached the place where his uncle lived.

It was advice against joining college that came from Raghavan Pillai. Disheartened, Manikandan turned back. On his way back, he wandered the streets of Kottayam town. He knocked on many doors, seeking a job. There, at Parayathara, he met Paachu. Paachu was working at a hotel, sending money every month by money order to his mother and sisters for their expenses. Paachu, who toiled day and night, was a good-hearted man. None of Manikandan’s efforts to find work bore fruit, and he returned to his village.

His father and mother resolved that Manikandan must be admitted to college. Kunchu Nair felt that, come what may, his son must be given higher education. Carrying a trunk worth two rupees on his head, Manikandan set out for Thiruvananthapuram. Surendran too came to see him off. His mother, with eyes brimming with tears, prayed—

Kondal. After joining college, Manikandan searched for and found a place to stay. An old house in the Nandankode area. There, the family of a middle-aged man named Govindapillai resided. He allotted one room in that house for Manikandan. He had to arrange his own meals separately.

The college opened. That day, Manikandan met Viswanathan. Old friends thus came together again. It was Viswanathan who told the others that Manikandan wrote poetry, and so the other students came to know of it. Viswanathan stayed in the college hostel. There was always a flock of friends gathered around him. Manikandan, however, was friends only with Viswanathan. Though he spoke to everyone, he never laughed or made merry; as much as possible, he kept to himself. The old liveliness and easy mingling were gone.
It seemed to Viswanathan that Manikandan had changed completely.

A few days later, there was a Congress convention at Thampanoor. Manikandan stood beside Viswanathan. When a speaker uttered some absurdity, Viswanathan laughed aloud. That day, Viswanathan took Manikandan to another place. A small room. There, someone was teaching a few others. It seemed as if a guru was answering the questions of his disciples. Manikandan, too, became one among that group. Two or three days a week, there would be study classes. Among those who came there were students, workers, and Congressmen. From the discussions that took place there, Manikandan felt he gained a new light. An individual way of thinking began to blossom. He came to understand the causes of the sufferings of the deprived. In that new light, Manikandan wrote a poem. At a gathering in the college, he read that poem aloud. His resonant voice echoed through the hall. That poem held both rhythm and melody. Viswanathan was astonished. The audience...

They were immersed in poetry. But when the gathering ended, the head of the Malayalam department at the college called him aside and reprimanded him. He warned that the poem he had read bordered on treason, and that he could be expelled from the college for it. In the end, he sent him away with a stern warning not to write such poems that incite students to revolution anymore.

He became popular in the college. The daughter of the chief secretary would stand gazing at him. At the next college gathering, the poem he read was about the nakedness of a woman. The head of the Malayalam department was angry with Manikandan that day too. “Your poem is obscene,” Viswanathan was the most offended. He called him in and scolded, “Hey, you good-for-nothing!” “You have been taking part in training classes—how could you stoop so low?” That was Viswanathan’s question. Manikandan could not understand what crime he had committed.

Manikandan came home for the holidays. By then, Surendran had already gathered the Parayars and Pulayars in the village and formed a trade union. Some people from outside came and conducted training classes about the great strength of the working class. Though both of them studied Marxism, he was able to understand the difference between the two. Surendran would go to the Pulayar huts and eat food from them. Mixing with them was his way of life. He would proudly say that he had become class-conscious. He would wander from one Pulayar hut to another, from one Parayar hut to another, drinking their sour gruel, and Kunjunayar, not wanting Manikandan to be influenced by such company, separated him from Surendran.
Surendran had both father and mother. He was the eldest among the children born to his father’s fourth wife. Even after that, his father married again. All five wives were still alive.

They lived. It was his mother who raised Surendran. His schooling came to a halt. At first, he immersed himself in Kunjannan Nair’s ashram, and later, in labor activities. Suddenly, he felt the urge to get married. He saw a girl too; a girl without parents. Surendran married Ponnamma. The reason for this sudden marriage, he confided only to Manikandan.

When he went to the Pulayar and Paraiyar huts for trade union work, his mind often wandered. There were grown women everywhere. He married only to prevent any untoward incident from happening there. Manikandan felt that the training Surendran had received was not quite complete.

Surendran suddenly had the idea of organizing a meeting for agricultural laborers. The whole village would oppose it. Already, rumors were circulating that the laborers were going to demand higher wages. The laborers themselves had not yet gained self-awareness. They were used to being subservient to the landlords. Even so, he decided to hold the meeting.

Kunjannan Nair’s Gandhi Ashram now throbbed with life. The number of people coming for prayers had dwindled. Kunjannan Nair felt that a more spirited Congress conference was needed to convey the intensity of the freedom struggle to the people. It would be an opportunity for the people to act. At the working committee meeting to organize the conference, Kunjannan Nair
He spoke. He urged that the actions be intensified.

The speech filled those present in the assembly with enthusiasm. To ensure the Congress conference was a success, prominent Christians like Vattathara Grigory and Paruthikkattu Thomas came forward and took the lead. They felt it was best for the Congress to intervene to prevent the Parayars and Pulayars—agricultural laborers—from uniting. But the government issued a prohibitory order against holding the conference. There was talk of gunfire and lathi charges being used. This only fueled the determination of Kunjanna Nair’s leadership group.

The people came forward to conduct the conference. Some Congress leaders from North India were also expected to attend. The whole town was in a festive, joyous mood. Yet, beneath it all, there was an undercurrent of fear.

On the morning of the previous day, Kunjanna Nair hoisted the flag. Fixing his gaze on the fluttering flag, Chennattu Kunjanna Nair stood for a long time, eyes closed in reverence, hands joined in prayer. That evening, under Kunjanna Nair’s leadership, the subject determination committee was to meet. They wrote and prepared resolutions to be proposed and passed at the meeting scheduled for the next day. The pandal was crowded with people.

Suddenly, they saw some red lights shining on the northern side of the river. They were the police boats. Three boats came rushing in. A large force, armed with rifles and wearing iron helmets, landed.

From the stage, Kunjanna Nair raised his voice: “Bharat Mata ki Jai!” Some of the workers echoed his cry. The police officer ordered them to stop the shouting. Kunjanna Nair, with all his might, shouted the slogan to its highest pitch. It touched the sky.

An order was issued to arrest Kunjanna Nair. No one knew from where it came. Black stones came flying into the pandal. Some police officers were hit by stones. The police rampage began. People scattered and fled in all directions. Gunfire erupted. The whole town trembled. Kunjanna Nair and several others were arrested and taken away. Death was...
It was a night that issued a summons.

Only Kunjanna Nair had spent long days in prison. He did not wish to come out on bail. One dawn, the police brought Kunjanna Nair to the Gandhi Ashram and left him there. The whole village was relieved. Everyone went to see him. He was seen in a very weakened state. He spoke nothing to anyone. That day, citing some urgent reason, Kunjanna Nair went to the town of Alappuzha and did not return that night.

The next morning, in a branch of the mango grove to the south of the ashram, a man was found hanging. It was Kunjanna Nair. Within a short while, the entire village had gathered there. From his body, they found a letter. According to the legal will written by Kunjanna Nair, he had left the Vedippuraykkal paddy field and the house in Puthupparambu as inheritance to Karthiyayani and to the child in her womb.
chapters.summary: Chennadan struggles with changes to temple traditions and land laws, while Ganapathi Namboothiri’s controversial leadership sparks unrest.

chapters.title: Fortunes Rise, Fortunes Fall
paragraphs: The hill becomes a valley; the valley becomes a hill. All the old, great families have been ruined. Some houses that were once hidden from view now shine forth. Among them is Malancheri. Once, there was only a thatched hut there. Now it has become a sturdy house built of wood. All this rise was due to a son who had prospered.

Malancheri Pappi’s son, Gopalakrishnan, works in Malaya. Money comes in abundance. For Pappiyamma, there is also Levadevi, who lends gold and gives loans. When there is a bit of a crunch to send money for the studies of her son Manikandan, who stays in Thiruvananthapuram and studies, Chennattu Kunjannayar will go to Malancheri. In this way, all the gold in the house found its way into Pappiyamma’s box. Kunjannayar, the thatched...

He finished counting the small change he had. When that was not enough, the little profit that Kunjumalu earned from raising the cow helped them get by. Yet, many times, even that was not sufficient to set things right. Only then would he have to go in search of Pappiyamma. But now, he did not have even a tiny gold coin left to pawn. Without gold as collateral, Pappiyamma would not lend a single paisa to anyone. Such was her custom. Was it not the hard-earned money her son had made toiling on the far shore of the sea? She was anxious that it should not be squandered recklessly. Even so, when Kunjunayar came to ask, she could not send him away empty-handed. The reason was that, in her youth, Kunjunayar had been her secret lover. Even at this age, she had not forgotten it. In those harsh, hungry days, whenever she needed help, it was he who gave it. That was before Kunjunayar married Kunjumalu Amma. Though the time had come when such memories ought to fade, in Pappiyamma’s heart, Kunjunayar still had a place.

Pappiyamma’s son had come back from Malaya. It became news in the village. Word spread that Gopalakrishnan had returned with three trunks full of money. To all who came to see him, Gopalakrishnan handed out money—ten, twenty-five at a time. There was no stinginess with money. For Pappiyamma, the work was unending. She had to prepare tea for all the visitors. There was no end to the cooking of meat and fish. The liquor bottles were being emptied one by one. To everyone who came, Gopalakrishnan would tell stories about life in Malaya. They were stories worth listening to, full of flavor. Over there, he had a job as an overseer in the estate of a white sahib. In Malaya, most of the laborers were Chinese. Kunjunayar, too, went to see Gopalakrishnan. Gopalakrishnan said he would take Manikandan with him to Malaya. If one went to Malaya, one could earn money. But it was a land of utter savagery.

It was from the changes that had come over Gopalakrishnan that Kunjunayar realized what a solitary life it was. When it was time to leave, Gopalakrishnan took out some notes and handed them over. Though they were without fragrance, Kunjunayar accepted them. If she had known that life there was like this, Pappiyamma said, she would never have sent her son there.

Now, Vattathara Krikary is the biggest farmer in the village. Paruthikkattu Kocheuseppu and Aathumali Anthoni are even bigger farmers than him. To put it briefly, it is the Christians who cultivate field after field in the village. They own lands; lands that once belonged to other families. Besides those, there are lands they have taken on lease from Devasthanam and from Srinivasaiyyar of Mangombu. For their agricultural needs, they even borrow paddy from Srinivasaiyyar. Adding up the principal and the interest, everyone was forced to repay a large sum. Pattar filed a case demanding the return of both principal and interest. Krikary and his friends got caught in a great predicament. Krikary argued that if farming was to continue, the government must bring in a law to stop the relentless repayment of such debts. Where did this Pattar get so much paddy and money? Krikary began to question the unaccounted wealth of Srinivasaiyyar. All the property he had amassed belonged to the people of the village. He multiplied his wealth by lending at interest to the poor farmers who took land on lease for cultivation. Summoned on the petition filed by Srinivasaiyyar, Krikary went to the madam and met the swami. Opening a thick account book...

Srinivasaiyar was watching. Grigory shouted and threatened that as soon as the petition was filed, the court would not immediately deliver a verdict, and even if it did, permission could not be granted to auction the properties. Even after hearing this, there was no disturbance in Srinivasaiyar. Everything would happen in its own due course—that was the Pattar's reply. He did not have the authority to waive the principal amount lent as a loan. That was the position of the Math. Nothing could be written off there. He did not have the power to do so, Pattar said. As Grigory left, he felt that what Pattar said was not dry obstinacy. The Math distributed money for agriculture, trade, and industry. Only when the money was returned and the accounts settled would loans be given again. If agriculture was to continue in the village, the Math had to remain strict in this way. Grigory understood this economic doctrine that had been followed in the Math for centuries.

A debate arose in the legislative assembly about the law to write off agricultural loans. Grigory worked entirely behind the scenes for this. He approached the Diwanji and made a representation. He gathered the indebted farmers and released a statement. The moneylenders, learning of this, united and appealed to the government. They too made a representation to the Diwanji. Until a favorable law was enacted, Grigory decided to halt all agricultural work. Transactions came to a standstill. It could be said that agricultural work across the land had come to a halt. The laborers fell into severe hunger. In the end, the government decided to take steps to provide relief to the farmers from the burden of debt. The law was being prepared in the legal department. Grigory was tirelessly working in the background for this.
The Diwanji’s sixtieth birthday celebration was approaching. From village to village, farmers’ associations made grand arrangements to welcome the Diwanji.

Grigar wanted to arrange a reception in his own village as well. This was an opportunity to please the Diwanji. He discussed it with the other farmers. The Diwanji still harbored resentment over the Congress meeting that had been held earlier. This reception could serve to dispel that bitterness. On that day, they had criticized the Diwanji harshly. Now, everyone agreed there was nothing wrong in honoring and praising him.

However, the Congress youth who heard about this decision opposed it. In that gathering were Thomas, son of Kochauthayi from Paruthikkadu; Philip, son of the Karikari from Vattathara; and Varghese, son of Anthony from Aathumala. All of them were Congressmen. Their decision was to create confusion at the meeting if the Diwanji was brought to the village and given a reception. But they did not say this openly. When their fathers pulled them aside and questioned them, they did not even bother to answer. Nor did they say what they planned to do. Sridharan only replied that he could not say. The others kept their mouths shut. That was how their opposition was revealed. In those houses, a great rift opened between fathers and sons. The mothers were caught in the middle, struggling.

Grigar and his associates feared that if the Diwanji was invited and given a reception, those young men would create serious trouble. In the end, they decided not to invite the Diwanji to the village. Still, the Diwanji’s sixtieth birthday celebration was conducted with great pomp. Heavy police presence was arranged to keep the gathering from descending into chaos.

Months later, the Debt Control Act was passed in the legislative assembly. The law stated that it was enough if agricultural debts were repaid in installments. Court proceedings would be suspended for the time being. For the farmers, this was a temporary relief. But in some families, it caused distress. The tenants...
The money that had been spent on paddy was not being recovered in any way for the household. Nothing that was supposed to come in as income was coming in.

For someone who had lived his whole life striving for one ideal after another, it was only natural that there should be experiences that could not be written out fully. He wrote in detail about his childhood, about how the country was in those days, and about the frequent changes that had come after. Kunjunayar was a man who had shaped his own life solely through his own efforts. He had brought a ruined family back to the shore. He had saved and stabilized the family of his mother-in-law. When individual property rights came, all that was shattered. He was cast out from his own family. He loved his wife. Even to his wife’s family, he was a bearer of burdens. He educated his daughter. Now, his son’s advancement was the only goal left in his life.

Manikandan absorbed every word of that letter into his heart. It seemed to him that his father had said everything he needed to say in that long letter. What about after his father’s time? Is it only when life comes to an end that one feels compelled to write like this? Manikandan could not help but think of his father’s death.

He could not even bear to look. Manikandan felt as if he wanted to cry out loud. It was night. He had to leave for the village. Hadn’t his father written that he must not return to the village? There, in connection with the Diwanji’s sixtieth birthday celebration, the elders and the youth had split into two factions. There was no conversation. There was no quarrel; yet anything could happen at any moment. The father’s only wish was that his son should not get entangled in any of this. Father would have known that the controversy surrounding the sixtieth birthday celebration was intensifying in Thiruvananthapuram as well. A commotion could erupt in Thiruvananthapuram, too. Father could not even bear to imagine the police taking his son away. The only wish of both father and mother was that their son should study and find himself a job.

Now, before the father’s eyes, only a future shrouded in darkness appeared. The result of a lifetime spent reading the Puranas was evident throughout that letter. That was why Kunjunayar was able to write in such a way that it left an impression on the mind. The foundations of dharma described in the Puranas, and the deep-rooted beliefs, were all shaken. In the past, he had been able to distinguish between right and wrong. Now, all that clarity was gone. The hope he had for his son had cast a shadow of darkness over that father’s heart.

The next day, Manikandan was greatly unsettled. Even though Viswanathan called him to the student union meeting, he did not go. Until midnight, he wandered restlessly through various parts of the city. Even when he returned at night and lay down in his room, sleep would not come. His mind was filled with the words from the letter his father had written. The next morning, the owner of that rented house, seeing how dejected he looked, inquired about his well-being. Manikandan said nothing. With kindness, the house owner gave him some hot kanji. That day too, Manikandan did not go to college. In the evening, Viswanathan came running to see him. Manikandan took out the letter his father had written and handed it to Viswanathan.

He handed it over. Viswanathan did not have time to read it all. His life was pressed by urgency. He was involved in student agitations. Because Manikandan insisted, Viswanathan read the letter in haste. He did not fully absorb what he read. It was not a time when he could reflect on its meaning. Still, Viswanathan did not fail to notice a few sentences. A father's advice that his son should not get entangled with the police! Viswanathan realized that the letter was written by a man who, unaware of the changes brought by time, had not prepared himself to adapt to them. His mind told him that this letter would make Manikandan retreat from the path of revolution. After reading it, seeing Manikandan's face, drained in mind and body, Viswanathan said, "You are a coward."
Viswanathan had given Manikandan a name—coward! It seemed to Manikandan as if the whole world was calling him by that name. He began to despise himself. He even called himself once—coward!

There was unrest at the college. Someone had broken and smashed the statue of the Diwanji. The whole country shuddered. The police entered the college and carried out a lathi charge. There was no movement of people on the streets. Police everywhere. All his friends, including Viswanathan, were involved in dangerous actions. For Manikandan, standing aside from everything seemed shameful. What else was he but a coward? He had read a great deal in the party’s training classes. At those times, his mind had been stirred to rebellion; his eyes had been opened. He had developed a passion for criticizing every problem of life. Back then, he wrote poetry; sharp, powerful poetry—now, poetry would never come to him again. Impossible. Coward!
It must have been Viswanathan who broke the Diwan’s statue. The police were searching for him. One day, at the house where Manikandan was staying...

The police came to the house as well. They came knowing that he was a close friend of Viswanathan. Standing before the inspector’s sharp gaze, Manikandan trembled like a tender leaf. He was forced to speak about all his connections with Viswanathan. To save himself, he told a few lies as well. The police searched every corner of that room. Fortunately, there were no party-related books there at that time. When they saw the political textbooks, the police asked, “Are you a politician?” When the inspector picked up Maxim Gorky’s *Mother*, Manikandan’s heart pounded. The inspector gave a stern order that if Viswanathan came there, the police must be informed at once. He told the owners of the house as well—if Viswanathan came there, or if they failed to inform the police of his arrival, the house would be turned into a field of ruin. After that, the police patrolled around the house several times. The owners of the house became afraid. They did not have the heart to ask Manikandan to leave. But they had no choice. Manikandan took his box and descended the steps from that rented house.

The Second World War. Germany invaded Poland. Now, to attack and capture a country did not even take a day. England declared war against Germany. Germany bombed London. Though the war was being fought in Europe, Krikar wondered what good or ill might come of it for him. The price of paddy was rising every day. He waited, hoping for the price to rise further, watching for the right moment to sell. But a request came from the government. Farmers had to declare to the authorities how much paddy they possessed. After counting the members of each family, and subtracting what was needed for their own consumption and for agricultural work...

The remaining paddy would be taken over by the government. Only a very low price would be given for it. They were about to introduce rationing arrangements for rice. All these were laws that shattered Krikary’s mental fortress. Paddy could not be transported without permission. If anyone broke the law, the police would come and seal their paddy storehouses. Krikary had four thousand marakkals of paddy in his possession. He sold his paddy at the current high price. Paruthikkattu Kochauthan did the same. Even the rubber that had been lying around, unwanted by anyone, he sold at a good price. In his opinion, war was a good thing. The parish priest at Mathakoyil shared the same view. In that region, all the true believers had profited from the war.

At the sermon following the end of Mahabali on Sunday, the priest said: “It is out of compassion for the true believers that the Lord has sent Hitler, His divine messenger; that He has caused this war.” Some Christian youths could not tolerate the priest’s ignorance. Paruthikkattu Thamachan, Gauriyar of Thunbeghat, and others were very angry and spoke to the priest about this. Gauriyar raised a hue and cry that the priest, who was both a traitor to the people and a fascist, should be jailed. The priest did not understand any of this. Only later did he realize that what he had said was against the British government and that all he had spoken was sheer foolishness. The priest, weeping openly, sent for the elderly Christians of the diocese and begged forgiveness, saying that he had praised Hitler out of joy at seeing the true believers get five or six paise. They comforted the priest. To them, criticizing a priest seemed a grave sin.

But the matter did not end there. Surendran, Gauriyar, and Thamachan joined together and put up a notice for a public meeting—an anti-fascist public meeting. Seeking to prevent it, they approached the police for help.

Krigari approached one of his relatives, the Collector. He went with hope, but returned in fear. Even to think of stopping that gathering was considered treason; it was an act against the British government; if anything was done, it would mean going to jail—the Collector warned him and sent him away.

From many houses in the village, young men joined the army. The British government recruited and took them away for military service. Even the families at home did not know to which country their sons were being sent. Every month, their letters and money orders would arrive. There must have been at least six hundred families in that village—they would all wait for the arrival of the postman. But while waiting like that, sometimes it would be the telegraph boy who came—bearing the news of death for one among them. When the news of death arrived at one house and the wailing reached its peak, in the next house there would be a rush for a young man to leave and join the army. Wars were raging in many parts of the world. When signing the money order, the mothers’ hands would tremble. If a letter arrived, it was the postman who had to read it aloud for them. If it was a telegram, the postman would simply hand it over and vanish in an instant. He did not have the strength of mind to witness the scenes that unfolded in a house when the news of death in a telegram became known.

Because of the law of private property, in the fragmented Konothu estate, there were six thatched huts. In one of them lived Kaurikkunjamma. Her sons, Vasudevan and Krishnan, were both in the army. Every month, their allotments kept coming. On Mondays and Thursdays, the postman would pass that way. On those days, his midday meal and rest would be at Kaurikkunjamma’s house. The postman had no wife; no children either. Kaurikkunjamma treated him like a husband.

She would serve him. Even if there was no rice anywhere in the village, she would somehow procure it, paying whatever price was asked, and prepare a meal for the postman. She would cook his favorite curries and wait in anticipation for his arrival. She would draw water for his bath. With reverence and devotion, Gaurikkutty would tend to the postman. The postman was a good man, a man with a heart. Not only Gaurikkutty, but everyone cherished the postman who brought letters and money orders from sons, brothers, and husbands serving in the army. Yet, no mother or wife ever forgot the figure of the postman who brought the telegram. To share in that dark moment was a burden for the postman as well.

The war spread and raged. Like a forest fire, it swept across the world. In that fiery pit, people fluttered and fell like moths. Each day, the postman would dutifully deliver the letters and money orders that arrived. There was no shortage of days when he brought telegrams as well. The dread of the distant war lingered in his satchel. The fortunes brought by the war were of the same kind.

One day, the meal Gaurikkutty served the postman seemed tasteless to him. He did not answer any of her friendly questions. That night, too, the postman was sunk in deep sorrow. Gaurikkutty’s heart began to burn with irritation. The postman said nothing.

Gaurikkutty’s son Vasudevan and Seeratta Gopalan had once gone together to enlist in the army. That day, only Vasudevan was taken. Gopalan had returned. But now, he had become a wealthy man. He was in the business of buying paddy, milling it into rice, and selling it. Because it was wartime, there were restrictions on moving paddy and rice from one place to another. Yet, Gopalan secretly bought paddy in large quantities, milled it into rice, and sold it. For that, he had to bribe the policemen.

Every month, he continued to pay a certain sum. Whatever may be said, Seeratta Gopalakkaimal was now a wealthy man. From now on, the Seeratta family would rise in status. Long ago, in the outer fields, when Beerukannu Mudalali ruled as the landlord, the Seeratta estate house had belonged to them. Now, he was striving to reclaim that house. At present, it was in the possession of Abdul Razak, a descendant of Beerukannu. The old structure, with its granite foundation and the serpent-worship shrines, still remained. Other than coming to the estate to pluck coconuts, none of Beerukannu’s descendants had ever caused any harm to the property. Now, Gopalakkaimal had the financial strength to buy it back. Razak, too, was willing to return it. But no matter how much Gopalakkaimal paid to reclaim the Seeratta ancestral home, could it ever become the old Seeratta family again? For now, only he, his wife, and his children would live there. How could it be the Seeratta family without the Seeratta women?

Whatever it may be, because of the war, Gopalan had become a rich man. There were others like him as well. Parayathra Paachu, who once worked in a hotel in Kottayam clearing betel leaves from the tables, had also become wealthy now. It did not take long to become rich. By supplying wooden goods needed for the war, he had suddenly become a man of means. Both Seeratta Gopalakkaimal and Parayathra Paachu, along with all their family members, prayed to the gods that the war would go on and on. But the mothers of the boys who had joined the army prayed day and night for the war to end, calling out to the gods without rest. Vasudevan had joined the army only after asking his mother’s permission. But the younger son, Krishnan, had gone without telling or asking his mother. Money orders from both of them arrived without fail. Yet, for some months now, Kaurikkunjamma had noticed a change in the postman’s manner.

He did not even eat with satisfaction. When asked what the reason was for this inability, his only answer was that there was nothing. Even to the anxious inquiries of that mother about her children, he gave no reply. One day, slinging his leather bag over his shoulder and taking his large umbrella, the postman descended the steps before dawn. As he left, he turned once to look back at that house. That was not his usual habit. Gaurikkunjamma’s heart fluttered like a worm.

The next Thursday was to be his day to come again. On that day, she prepared the food he liked and waited for him. He did not come. He did not come the following Monday either. Only later did she learn that the postman had resigned from his job and left the village. No one knew where he had gone. One and a half years ago, a letter arrived for Gaurikkunjamma, informing her of the deaths of Vasudevan and, a year later, Krishnan. It was a letter sent by the postman.

There was no rice or paddy to be had in the village. The big landlords had paddy stored in their granaries. They sold it at high prices, at night. The Parayars and Pulayars, who worked in the paddy fields, were paid their wages in cash. The age-old custom of giving paddy as wages had ceased. The agricultural laborers’ union was compelled to take up certain forms of protest. At least half of the wages must be paid in paddy. The party said this would not happen unless the laborers went on strike. To aid the war against fascism, the laborers must unite. If so, how could the laborers eat rice or pongal even once a week? This was Surendran’s question to the landlords’ granary.
The only way to break the chains is through struggle.

Surendran could not understand the party’s decision that a struggle could not be conducted. The workers had resolved to strike without disrupting the union. It had become a dilemma. Perhaps it would become necessary to set aside the party, or else the union would be weakened. The workers found themselves unable to comprehend that, while they starved, the capitalists reaped enormous profits in the name of war. Should they side with the capitalists, or act according to the party’s directives? “If I lead the struggle, I will be expelled from the party,” Surendran declared at a workers’ meeting.

At that moment, Sotha’s daughter, Pappa, raised her voice: “Wherever comrade is, there we will be too.” The party demanded an explanation from Surendran. There were several accusations. The most serious of these were actions contrary to the party’s code of conduct. Three or four clear charges stood out. One was based on a complaint from Kuttappan, Pappa’s husband. Surendran had kept Pappa as his wife; even when Kuttappan called, she refused to go with him. It was true that Surendran had been close to Pappa since childhood. But Pappa herself said, if the party people asked, she would not consider that accusation significant. She declared firmly that she did not go with Kuttappan simply because she did not like him.

Next, there was the matter of Neeli, Kannan’s daughter—her child was said to be Surendran’s. No one could ignore this. Thus, the first accusation was that Surendran had improper relations with all the young women in the village. He was ready to accept that charge. He felt that, as someone who had broken with class, this too was part of his journey.

The second accusation was that he had organized a strike in violation of party policy. Even though, through that struggle, the workers had received partial wages in paddy, the fact remained that organizing the strike was against policy.
The party’s position was that, at its core, it was not right.

The third accusation was the most significant. He had failed to foster a bond between the workers and the party. Instead, a personal dominance of Surendran had come to prevail among them. Surendran could not understand this accusation at all. As far as he knew, he had never done anything against the party. Even after the party’s district secretary explained these charges, Surendran still did not feel he had committed any crime. Pappa too said the same thing. Surendran had been of more help to the workers than the party itself. He was always with them. Whether it was to bring a nurse for someone’s childbirth, or to fetch a doctor when illness struck, or to mediate when a dispute arose—at every place, for everything, he was there as their support. How could that be a crime? But the party could not tolerate a situation where, without Surendran, there was no party.

“Vellayane Veliyeru”—“White man, quit!”—never before had such intense fervor been heard in the freedom struggle. The agitation to drive out the British. The idea that India must expel them had taken root. It was not Gandhi who first said it; it was the soul of India itself. The land of Bharat had shuddered and risen. The freedom struggle had gained a passion it had never known before. To Surendran, this seemed like the final battle towards a determined goal. Yet the party was saying not to participate in this great movement. He could not decide what was right. In many parts of the country, the agitation had turned violent. Gauriyamma and Thamas were arrested. He himself could do nothing alone. Surendran was shaken by the party’s decision to stand aside from the “Quit India” movement. Something had to be done. But at the same time, he must not go against the party. He wandered through the fields and bunds, like a mad dog.
Across the country, violent actions were being taken against the British government, and he too wanted to take part in them.

In a field where fifteen thousand marakkals of paddy were cultivated, the bund was breached and water rushed in. The paddy stalks were swaying in the wind; it was the season of ripening. This was a field jointly farmed by Paruthikkadan and Vattathara on a sharecropping basis. All the paddy grown there was declared as being for the needs of the army, and the owners sold it on the black market. Not a single grain harvested there was given as wages to the laborers who worked in those fields. Because of that, if an opportunity arose, Pappa was seized by the urge to destroy that agriculture, even if it meant breaking the bund and letting in the floodwaters.

Surendran did it. He spent an entire night, waist-deep in water, trying to create a crack in the bund of that pond. That embankment was so strong. He set about the work with fervor. If he finished it that night, his part in the struggle would be done. The crowbar struck swiftly. At first, water began to trickle out like a thin stream. The crack gradually widened. He ran from there. After running a short distance, he heard the roar of the floodwaters behind him. The pond’s bank had collapsed, and the fields were submerged in the flood. He felt a sense of relief. The satisfaction of having done something. Even if he was sent to prison, it did not matter. He went to Sotha’s hut, called out softly to wake Pappa, and told only Pappa about what had happened. Pappa’s reply was immediate!
“Good! That’s exactly how the property of those ruffians should be destroyed.”
In the days that followed, the police arrested many people. But the police never suspected Surendran.
Chennattu Kunjunayar lived for almost a century. It was not an ordinary period. He witnessed countless changes. The untouchable...

Temple entry was granted to the oppressed; they found places in schools to study alongside others; caste distinctions crumbled. The reverence for Brahmins faded away. Brahmin supremacy itself was destroyed. Kunjunayar never visited any temple. In his youth, he had seen families swollen with the pride of wealth. Now he saw them collapsing. The social order in which he was born and raised had been turned upside down. There had been changes in the methods of agriculture. There were changes, too, in the ways property changed hands. The codes of dharma and the foundations of life, as he had understood them from reading the Puranas, had all changed. The struggle against monarchy was raging fiercely. Kunjunayar had no thought as to what the times to come would be like. Yet, in that long letter, it was only about how his son’s generation should live that the father reflected. When he finished writing and sent it to his son, he felt as though all his duties were done. His body grew weak. Kunjunayar fell to his bed. From beside his deathbed, Gopalan Nayar from the neighboring house read aloud the Bhagavatam. Every passage read was by heart to Kunjunayar. He himself, in his younger days, had pointed out that only up to the Ekadasha Skandham need be read. For five days, as Kunjunayar lay bedridden, Kunjumalu Amma sat by his cot, draining water and remaining there. That chaste woman, having made her resolve, stood firm. Without her husband, everything was intertwined for her. As the portion was being read that enumerated those who are closest to God, Kunjunayar’s breath ceased as he listened. Kunjunayar had died; yet Kunjumalu Amma was still alive. That should not be. When they thought to lay Kunjunayar down below, spreading sacred ash and darbha grass, Kunjumalu Amma stopped them. “No; as long as I am alive, he cannot be dead,” she said. A little while later…

She slipped and fell from where she had been sitting; her breath stopped. It was as if Kunjunayar had gone ahead alone, and after a while, returned to take his wife along with him—such was her dignity in death.

In the southeast corner of the house plot at Koyirpuram, two funeral pyres burned one after the other. Manikandan performed the last rites for both of them. He had known that his father would die; it was clear from that letter. But he had never expected his mother to die. She had died as she wished. Unable to bear separation from her husband, that mother had left her son and gone away. Can anyone die simply by willing it so? There is no answer.
In the village, people whispered that Kunjumalu Amma had waited by Kunjunayar’s bedside with poison. No one had seen her drink it. Whatever the truth, even in death, she followed her husband.
Manikandan would often take out his father’s letter and read it. He had memorized it by heart. Again and again, it would weaken his spirit.

After Viswanathan was released from prison—where he had been held for breaking the statue of the Diwanji—he came to see Manikandan. When they saw each other, both their eyes filled with tears. Manikandan described to him the scene of his parents dying together. Viswanathan could not believe it. When Manikandan said he was not ready to return to college, Viswanathan advised him not to ruin his life.
The letter sent by Kunjunayar had made Manikandan a coward. The love for his parents had affected the young man like a narcotic, and seeing this, Viswanathan grew angry and left.
Viswanathan had dedicated his life to the struggle for independence. Even after independence, there would be struggles. He had decided what this country should become. To create a new era...

Manikandan, too, possessed the eagerness to take part in that struggle. Yet, someone—or something—held him back. He would dream of marching toward a vast battlefield, a mighty army numbering in the millions. At the head of that great host was Viswanathan, and Manikandan followed close behind. When bullets rained down, the hand must not tremble, the flag must not fall. Thus, in his dreams, Manikandan took part in the freedom struggle with fervor. This was his vision.

After that, Manikandan never went to Thiruvananthapuram again. All his books remained there; even the notebooks where he had penned his poems. Since then, there was no more reading, no more study. The “White Man, Quit India” movement was blazing everywhere. The leadership of the student wing was in Viswanathan’s hands. Manikandan’s eyes longed to see Viswanathan, even just once. He led the struggle, always evading the police. Manikandan’s ears yearned to hear Viswanathan’s stories. Even at night, Manikandan could not sleep. The doors of the house were always left open. Manikandan felt as if he was performing penance, waiting to see Viswanathan.

One dawn, as he stepped out into the yard, a great noise reached his ears—a roar like the sea surging and crashing beyond the shore. Later, he realized it was the sound of floodwaters rushing through the paddy fields of Makkaal, fifteen thousand strong, as the sluice gates were opened. The police began rounding up everyone they could find, questioning all who crossed their path. Who had done this? Manikandan felt as if it was he himself.

He imagined the police coming to arrest him. He shut his door and stayed inside his room. One day, lighting a lamp and sitting before it, Manikandan took a vow: “Until India attains freedom, I will not shave my beard.” It seemed to him that this vow echoed throughout the land.

Pappiyamma of Malancheri was no longer alive to hear that sorrowful news. Gopalakrishnan, who had been in Malaya, was killed by the Japanese. This was what those who returned after the war said. But before she could learn this story, Pappiyamma had already passed away. All those who had gone to Malaya with Gopalakrishnan had joined the INA. In some battlefield on the border of Burma, they all perished. To Surendran, this seemed a matter of pride for his village. Yet, he himself could do nothing. He hoped that in the future, he would have the opportunity. What was to be gained now was not true freedom. Power was merely shifting hands, from one set of masters to another. Crores of Indians were still bound in the chains of servitude. Until they attained true liberation, the struggle would continue. That, Surendran convinced himself, was the real struggle.

It was decided to partition India into two. Rivers of blood flowed. The intensity of partition culminated in the slaughter of hundreds of thousands. After independence, a land registration took place in that village. In the outskirts, there was a sale deed transferring the land in the name of Abdul Razak Seerattagopalakkaymal to Seeratta Mana. At a time when rivers of blood flowed in the streets of North India as a result of communal riots, Abdul Razak returned to a Hindu, the ancestral owner, the land that his family had held for generations. Though Razak’s younger brother, Suleiman, opposed this action of his elder brother, it made no difference. Suleiman had decided to go to Pakistan. But the riots in the North prevented that from happening. Razak felt that things should remain as they were in the old generations. Once, Hindu, Muslim, and Christian had lived in unity. The religious fanaticism that had grown in the minds of the educated youth unsettled Razak. On the midnight of August fourteenth, as all slept...

Were they awake? It was a night when India ought not to sleep. Yet, it did not seem as though the whole of India was wide awake. In the villages, the people who did not even know what freedom meant must have been sleeping soundly. But they too had been part of the struggle for freedom. At midnight, the flag of the British throne was lowered. The tricolour flag, adorned with the Dharma Chakra, was hoisted. Mahatmaji was not in the capital to witness it in person. Perhaps he did not come because he was saddened by the pain of Partition?

That day, special pujas were held in temples and other places of worship across the country. Manikandan came out that day. Surendran wandered here and there in the village. This day was marked by a unique significance. Tomorrow’s dawn would be different. In the end, even the Britisher boarded a ship for his country at that midnight hour. Exactly at twelve, the conch was blown. The bell was rung at the Matha temple. There were fireworks as well. Standing at a corner of a deserted field, Manikandan shouted until his throat was raw. “Bharat Mata ki Jai!” That cry echoed across the sky. There was great commotion at the police station. Surendran saw the policemen, dressed in uniform and holding rifles, salute the tricolour. He remembered how those very men had once set fire to a tricolour flag and torn it to shreds. From that flag, this new flag has arisen.
chapters.summary: As fortunes shift in the village, Kunjunayar struggles to support his family while generational and political rifts deepen.

chapters.title: The Barren Fields Remain
paragraphs: After independence, the first election came. Paruthikkattu Thomas was the Congress candidate. The leaders liked Thomas very much. He was a man of good repute. He knew exactly how to do what was needed, when it was needed.

I know. But there are those who struggled even more than him for freedom. Among them is Gauriyar of the Begkal fields. Now, he stands apart from everything. Some whispered that he withdrew because he did not get a place as a candidate and that he would rise in anger. Others believed it was because of his Communist leanings that he kept away. Whatever the reason, Gauriyar became inactive. Many leaders tried to bring him back into the field. It was of no use. With the coming of freedom, Gauriyar felt he had done all that he needed to do. That was his stand.
Still, how could someone who had gone to prison in the “White Man, Quit!” struggle suddenly become so inactive? It remained an unanswered question.

The candidate of the Left was a man named Sadanandan. Sadanandan, who had stood in the front row wielding a sickle in his hand at Punnapra Vayalar. There is a mound at Vayalar now, is there not? That mound was made by gathering together the corpses, piling them up, and covering them. Inside it, there are only fragments of bones. From there, a torch was lit and carried in procession around that electoral constituency. It was a procession of the dark-skinned, a deluge of blood-red flags.

The slogans they shouted awakened the workers. Land belongs to those who till it; do not think of evicting them from the land. These were the new slogans. The election field grew hotter by the day. When looking at the list of voters, both parties felt fear. The speeches of the Left emboldened the workers: Stop the evictions. Raise the wages of the laborers. Vattathara Krikary and Paruthikkattu Kochousepp lost their patience. They tried to intimidate the agricultural workers in their own fields. Some tenants whose names were written in their registers did not have the courage to say to their faces, “We will not vote for the Congress.” Many of them, from their own fields...

They vanished as if by magic. On election day, the landlords dressed them in new clothes and gave them plenty of food, then led them to the polling booths. By eight o’clock, a long queue had formed at the polling station. All of them were ‘open votes’—none could read or write; their eyesight was poor. To the question, “Whom do you want to vote for?” the answer was, “For Thamas.” Their landlords were seated right there. Because of that, many could not voice what was truly in their hearts. Surendran, who sat inside the polling booth as Sadanandan’s agent, had to suppress a feeling of disdain. Pappa came to cast her vote. Surendran’s mind was troubled. He feared that the name “Thamas” might escape her lips. “Who are you going to vote for?” The reply burst out like a firecracker—“Sadanandan.” The very building seemed to tremble. Pappa repeated the name once more. Those who came after her too loudly declared Sadanandan’s name. A crack as thin as a hairline in a great dam had brought down the entire edifice. Yet, in that election, it was Thamas who won.

The agricultural labor union’s struggle had become renowned. The agitation was for higher wages. Surendran doubted whether the laborers would stand united as one. He did not have full faith in the Communist Party either. But everyone was astonished. Not a single laborer went to work. In the fields of the Vattathara landlord, in the fields of the Paruthikattu landlord, and in the fields of others, the season for starting agricultural work had already passed. Vattathara Krikori went to Surendran’s house to speak with him directly. That house had not been thatched. It was a crumbling, dilapidated dwelling. There, Surendran lived. His wife, Ponnamma, and their children were in perpetual hunger. There was neither movement nor sound there. Even the children showed no signs of life or restlessness. Krikori had heard that Surendran was living in utter poverty.

But he had not expected it to come to this extent. An idea occurred to him. If he helped Surendran a little, he could win him over. How to help? Perhaps if he arranged for some repairs to be done on the house? But Surendran was not one to ask for such things. Even when his wife, Ponnamma, was asked in various ways, she never spoke of the hardships her family was enduring. Finally, when the matter of repairing the house was broached, her reply came sharp and sudden! “No need.” It fell on Krikary’s ears like a bombshell. Krikary’s trick had failed.

To make the workers withdraw from the strike, Krikary and his associates devised many strategies. None of them bore fruit. No work was happening in any of the fields. The workers were lying hungry. As the strike dragged on, Surendran grew anxious. A reconciliation meeting was held under the leadership of the Collector. That too yielded no result. In the end, Krikary and his associates, without any formal negotiation with the union, decided on their own to increase the wages. The next morning, the workers returned to work. The laborers received higher wages. Yet, the fact that the strike ended without any settlement talks with the union was, to Surendran, a matter of deep embarrassment.

The panchayat elections arrived. Surendran filed his nomination as the Communist candidate in one ward. Opposing him was Vattathra Philipose. Philipose was ready to buy every vote with money. In a pamphlet printed and distributed by the Congressmen, Surendran’s acts of transgression were described in detail, with evidence. In Sirattai, a young woman named Kunjamma became an orphan. She had no one to support her. At night, she slept on shop verandahs. One night, as she writhed in labor pains on a shop verandah, Surendran took her to the hospital. The delivery did not happen. Somehow—

The stomach had to be cut open quickly. When the doctor asked, it was Surendran, as the husband, who wrote and signed the consent letter. The operation was performed; the child died. The mother survived. According to the signed document, Surendran became her husband. The pit notice accused that it was Surendran who had made that woman, who had been wandering as a street vagrant, pregnant. Such were the hundred and more accusations. But the workers did not abandon him. Surendran became the panchayat president.

It was through Surendran’s efforts that, for the first time in the village, roads were laid and electricity arrived. For that, he went to Thiruvananthapuram and met with ministers. Even though the Congress coalition ministry was in power, Surendran did not hesitate to meet them and organize welcome ceremonies for them. His only ideal was that the needs of the village must be fulfilled. The capitalists like Vattathara Karikkari and others had to cooperate with Surendran’s activities. Even though he was a communist, they came to like Surendran. Through him, many more things could be done for the village. A good hospital was needed. A higher secondary school should come. Work that would never cease.

There was no difference of opinion within the party about the good deeds Surendran was doing. But the party saw as a problem his friendly relations, in practice, with class enemies. People like Pappa distanced themselves from him. She too accused him of having fallen into the web of the vote enemies. Surendran was deeply pained.
How many fields are there in this village! Of what is produced there, more than half the paddy belongs to eight or ten households.

It is accumulating only in the rooms. More than half the cultivated lands in the village are in their possession. Agricultural methods have been modernized. Now, the yield is many times greater than before. Today, they farm using money as capital. Agriculture has almost become an industry. The values associated with private property and inheritance rights are also changing. When did this situation arise, where a few have land and many have none? Who made the laws that a man owns the land he has fenced and tilled, and after his death, it belongs to his heirs? Surely, it must have been in the youth of the gods that boundary stones were first planted for land. When did the concept of truth come into being? How many, how many have interpreted it! God, truth, justice—all these change with every era. They will continue to change.

In earlier times, a certain classic figure, Kochupillai, would come, demarcate the properties, settle disputes, record them in the register, and issue pattas. Even before that, property transfers had taken place. In those days, if one lit a kuthuvilakku lamp, placed soil and flowers on the tip of a plantain leaf, and added water, it was considered that the land had changed hands. After Kochupillai came, it became necessary to register any transfer of land. One could say that truth was born from these transactions. The old phrase, “There is no money to repay the debt,” stamped by the ancient creditors, was itself an incarnation of truth. Through that, land transfers continued to take place.

Now, another slogan is being heard: “The land belongs to the tiller.” The tenants believe that soon a law will come forbidding the payment of any rent. Vasudevan of the Balathol house would visit the homes of all the tenants. He would speak of his urgent needs. Sometimes, he would return home with only four or five marakkals of paddy. Because there was no money to pay immediately, he would return to his family with empty hands.

All the original sums due have now become obsolete. The slogan “Land belongs to the tiller” has become a reality. Now, only the formal approval of the law remains. Leasehold properties are being divided among the children as if they are the true owners, just like those who currently possess them. From now on, there is no need to give any share of the land to the original landlord. There is no need to return the property either.

First, the Communist ministry came to power. The laborers benefited. The police did not interfere in labor disputes. Contrary to the fears of the conservatives, temples and shrines were not demolished or razed to the ground. Some Communists from the village also participated in temple administration. That government did not last long. The ministers in that government were the respected leaders who had led the national struggle. They were not hirelings. They were not corrupt in their conduct. Even so, confusion arose against that ministry. The idea that a government should be formed for the sake of society emerged afterward. Such experiments also failed. In the next election, the Communist party contested alone. It was certain that if the Communist party came to power again, the law of hereditary tenancy would be enacted. In Paruthikkadu, Vattathara, and all the lands of the great landlords, there were tenants. It was impossible even to imagine a situation where all those lands would have to be registered in the tenants’ names. The whole village was abuzz with talk. There was talk that Surendran would be fielded as the Communist party’s candidate from that constituency. That was the plan of Grigory and his associates. If Surendran became the candidate, they were ready to bear the expenses for it.

They made themselves ready. The reason was, if Surendran returned victorious, at the very least, they could fulfill some minimum needs in all matters—this was their expectation. Surendran still lived in a thatched hut. Even his daily meals were a struggle. Poor fellow, let him at least taste a little prosperity, thought Krikari with compassion. But the party could not even consider making Surendran, who was friendly with class enemies, their candidate. It was Sridharan who became the Communist Party’s candidate. Whoever the candidate was, the party’s votes did not diminish. Every worker held the belief that they would win.

The son of the elder Pulayan, known as Valiyakunjathi, looked at Krikari’s dark face and said, “Yes, boss, we are going to rule.” Krikari trembled. Times had changed; the days of being called ‘Thambaran’ were gone. He could not bear being called ‘boss’ instead. Perhaps, from now on, even Pulayars might call the landlords by name. Krikari’s sense of dignity faltered. How much money would it take to kill this arrogant fellow? No matter how much, it did not matter; honor was what mattered. A few days later, the rotting, bloated corpse of Karuthai floated away, merging with the river.
Sridharan won the election with a large majority. The Communists secured a decisive majority to form the government.

Now, Manikandan was residing in a choultry in Thiruvananthapuram. The watchman there, Koya, had given shelter to this young man, who was both educated and intelligent. Koya held respect for Manikandan, who was a college graduate and a poet.

He would provide food for him. He would arrange a vacant room for him to sleep in. Manikandan was living in a dream world. He spoke only with Goya. Now, he had taken a vow: “Only after socialism comes to the country will I grow a beard.” All day long, he wandered the length and breadth of Thiruvananthapuram. On the pale full-moon nights, in the solitude of the beach at Kazhimukham, he would compose poetry, his mind united with the silence. The divine melodies of nature reached his ears.

He dreamed of a government of the working class coming to power. Landlordism must come to an end. With the new Communist ministry ascending to power, it seemed to Manikandan that a new light had dawned in the country. Now, its face was clear to him.

On a new moon night, at the beach in Kazhimukham, he met a stranger, someone he had never seen before. Immersed in a blissful poem, Manikandan’s gaze fell upon a young man who seemed to have come in search of solitude. Perhaps he too was a poet. Perhaps he was a lover afflicted by despair. Manikandan yielded the beach to him and walked away.
The next evening, the newspaper carried a report: A young man had committed suicide at the beach in Kazhimukham.

Let us say that the old Kodanthara Moothassan, the Konnothu Vallyachan, and Seerattakaimal are coming to visit this village today. They are resting now in the world beyond, are they not? But where is this “world beyond”? In heaven, or in hell? They did not sin enough in their lifetimes to be consigned to the netherworld for eternity. They only took a little of the god’s property, and that too, in trivial ways. Somehow, let us imagine that, in some interval, they are coming to visit this village, and here are those who remain...

In the glow of electric lights, it was as if their eyes could no longer truly see. The ancient mango trees that once touched the sky were all gone. Every one of them had been cut down. Now, only new hybrid grafted mango trees stood in their place. What remains here to speak of the village’s antiquity? Nothing at all. Everything is new. Today, there are no Kodanthur, no Konothu, no grand eight-tiered houses of Seeratta to be seen. Once, every family had its Gandharvans. They too have vanished. The gait and attire of women have changed. Men no longer wear the traditional kudumi. The eyes of the old community leaders, wearied by the sight of textile shops and pawnshops, have grown dim and fixed in their gaze. The paddy fields are nowhere to be seen. Everywhere, it is only money.

The textile merchant, after closing his shop for the day, bundled up the money he had earned, pressed it to his chest, and set off for home. On the way, someone lay in wait, assaulted the shopkeeper, and snatched away that bundle of money. They had witnessed this scene.

For some days, the corpse of a bearded man who had been wandering about the village was seen floating down the river, leaping and bobbing in the current. In the eastern hills, on the estate of the Vattathrakkaran, a Tamil woman working as a coolie was saved by Philipose. It was her lover’s corpse that drifted away in the river.

In this village, there were no longer any Anantharavar—no sons-in-law or kin by marriage. There were no sisters to sustain such relationships. Only wives and children remained. The tharavadu family system had disappeared. The wife was the slave of the husband; or the husband, the slave of the wife. New families, new customs; life as a whole had utterly changed.

Today, there are people in the village working in government jobs. There are those working abroad. The number of those who cannot read or write has dwindled. School education has become commonplace. There was a time when many could not read or write English. At first…

The school that was started here was nothing more than a thatched hut. That thatched hut had a history of its own. Does anyone remember Suppaiyan? Suppaiyan Saar, who fell in love with Seelanthippillil Kalyaniyamma. It was Suppaiyan who first brought the word "Saar" (Sir) to this village. Today, every superior is addressed as "Saar." That was Suppaiyan’s gift to the village.

Nattacheriy Ramachandran Pillai’s son, Madhu, had completed his M.Sc. in Chemistry. He wished to study further, but Ramachandran Pillai could not afford it. Madhu’s younger sister, Nalini, had passed her B.A. She needed to be married off and sent to her husband’s home. If only Madhu could get a job, the family would be saved. Ramachandran Pillai and his wife had but one dream—a job for Madhu, a marriage for their daughter! But Madhu shattered all their dreams. In the Christian family of Aatrukkadalil, there was a girl named Rosakkutty—she too was a college student. On the very morning the bridegroom’s family was to come and see her, Rosakkutty was nowhere to be found. She had eloped with Madhu.

Seeratta Gopalakkaimal too had educated his son. But the boy did not get a job. Now, in his old age, Gopalakkaimal kept the family afloat by parboiling, milling, and selling rice. The heat of the husk fire in the oven was unbearable. If he turned away for a while, the heat on his body would subside a little. His son Damodaran was always reading something or other. Gopalakkaimal never called him for help, never disturbed him for any task. The boy was educated. That old man, who had built a life from nothing, would sometimes, as he sweated in the heat of the husk fire, grumble about his hardships and losses. One day, would Damodaran fall, burnt by the flames? Would it have been better if he had strangled him at birth?
The foundations that once stood strong in Seelanthippillil...

All the fields had collapsed and fallen into ruin. There were no evening lamps lit there anymore. Pamupillai now worked in a company in Kochi. In that family, only his sister Gauriyamma and one of her daughters remained. In the village, no one knew anything about individual property rights; there was not enough property to divide among heirs. Paramupillai had not married. With his help, Gauri continued to live in the old house at Seelanthippillai, along with an elderly maternal aunt. The rooms there were no longer filled with paddy; what was preserved there were only bundles of palm-leaf manuscripts. That house, a hundred years old, was on the verge of collapse. Once, when Pamupillai thoroughly inspected the house, he saw that termites had eaten into the main beam of the roof. The house could collapse at any moment. The termites had started their work from the manuscripts stored on the floor. For several generations, there had been no one to open that room. How many manuscripts must have fallen prey to the termites!

One day, in Seelanthippillai, a fire burned for hours on the southern side. From many corners, earth and scraps of palmyra leaves fell into that fiery pit. Only at midnight did the fire subside and die out. Thus, antiquity burned and turned to ash.

The Land Reform Act would soon come into effect. Only four days remained. From that day forward, no one would own land individually. All lands would belong to the government. There would be no more lessors; no more landlords; no more tenants. The ten cents of land surrounding the leased plot would belong to the tenant. No family could own more than fifteen acres of land. For the implementation of the land ceiling law, a Land Tribunal office had been established.

It is coming to the village. It is only through the efforts of Panchayat President Tenant Surendran that permission has been obtained to bring the office here. But the Collector has stated that the necessary land and building for the office must be arranged and provided free of cost. Surendran was plunged into distress. There was no other way; for the time being, the Panchayat hall would have to be given to the Land Tribunal. The President’s opinion was that the Panchayat could convene wherever it wished.

Just as Kodanthra Moothathasan had come upon hearing about the donation of the Erumathra Madam to the Kalasiper, Panchayat member Narayana Panicker came running as soon as he heard this news. The members did not know what the Land Tribunal was. Surendran explained it to them. It was the office established to implement the land reform act: to register those who had been evicted from tenant lands and allot them ten cents of land each; to register and grant pattas to tenants for the land they cultivated; to acquire surplus lands and distribute them to the landless—officials empowered to do all this were coming. At that time, they would have to be properly received and attended to; Narayana Panicker understood this as well. Panicker recalled the stories he had heard about the survey that had taken place long ago. From now on, everything was going to be turned upside down. After all, it was a government matter—let it happen, Panicker consoled himself.

Everyone, including Paruthikkattu Kochouthayam and Vattathara Karikari, was afraid. Tomorrow, the sun would rise on a world shaped by the new land reform law. One who had a thousand marakkal of land would be left with only eight hundred and fifty marakkal. On the other hand, one who did not have even a needle’s point of land would get ten cents of fertile paddy field. The landlords, who had always received tenant rent and tenant paddy in every village, would be left with nothing. The tenant would become the owner of the land. Such a great change had never happened before. Kochoutha, that night, did not close his eyes for a moment.

The next day, as the east brightened, he heard a voice from somewhere. Inquilab Zindabad. A large group of young men, carrying measuring chains, iron rods, and sickles, marched in rows, shouting the slogans of revolution. Around the leased land, they measured out plots of ten cents each, marked the boundaries, and fenced them off—thus, the tenants took possession. Kochauth, frightened, went inside and locked the door.

Now, apart from the plot where the Palathol family house stood, they had no other property. All the lands that had been let out on lease had come into the hands of the tenants. For the past several years, the family had been surviving on the meager income from the temple rituals. Even in the temple, there was no income. If those who were supposed to pay rent to the family had given even a tenth of it, the house would have flourished—there had once been uncountable properties. How did they all vanish? That is the question to be asked. Did the people of the house ever do any farming? Did a single drop of sweat from the people of the house ever fall on the fields? Agricultural land belongs to the cultivator. It is not for those who merely eat and idle away. This may sound harsh. But over time, many harsh things become just; and many just things become harsh.

It was Krishnan Namboothiri who was able to understand this change of the times. When the house fell into ruin, there were some who showed compassion to those who remained there—not anyone else, but the Pulayas and Parayas who were the tenants of the land. Whenever there was no rice in the house to boil gruel, Krishnan kept a record of the paddy they brought and gave on many occasions. Even though they did not give it as a loan, should it not be returned someday? After deducting what was due to the heirs of the tenants, he wrote off the remaining small plots of land to them and thus, in a way, fulfilled his responsibility before he died. Krishnan Namboothiri believed that one who borrows a debt would never attain salvation in any birth.

Now, Vasudevan was the head of the household. His wife, Arya Antharjanam, and daughter, Subhadra, lived with him. His son, Krishnan, who studied in college, joined the Communist party, and later, feeling that the party lacked revolutionary fervor, became a Naxalite. Many young men from villages like Kadukathra Kunnukkutty became involved in the activities of that new movement. It was all a secret. They did not know one another; their movements were unknown to each other and could not be discovered. Krishnan would come home at any time—that is, he would arrive in the middle of the night. At any moment, he would vanish without a trace. Therefore, Vasudevan could not find out anything about his son’s activities. There was no income from performing rituals at the temple. He continued the pooja only out of the belief that one should not succumb to the greed for karma. By law, a small amount of money could be obtained as compensation for the properties held by the tenants. If that was received, he thought, Subhadra could be married off. But Vasudevan had no certainty as to when it would come through the Land Tribunal.
In this situation, one night, Krishnan returned home. As usual, he spoke to his mother about the poverty of the household.

He needed to speak to his son. The next day, after returning from the temple when the puja was over, the son spoke to his father: “You must recite the sacred thread mantra for me. I want to become a Brahmin.” Vasudevan could not believe his son’s resolve to become a Brahmin. The boy had decided to assist his father in the work of archana and thereby uplift the family. But simply wearing the sacred thread would not make one a Brahmin. This was something that required strict observance of rituals from a young age, with steadfast discipline, to attain the proper state. Krishna had already committed many acts that were forbidden, enough to disqualify him. Even if the purification rites were performed, would the villagers believe it? That too would cost money. Krishna said that he had the necessary money with him. The fact that his communist son now wished to become a Brahmin again seemed to Vasudevan a sign of better times for the family.

The next day, Arya Antharjanam asked her son for a rupee. There was no salt in the house that day. The previous day, Vasudevan had received a little rice from the offerings at the temple. Even if gruel was made from that rice, wouldn’t salt be needed? That was why she asked for a rupee. Krishna had money in his possession—not in cash, but as a large bundle of gold ornaments. But that belonged to the Party. It had been entrusted to him for safekeeping. Krishna’s mind was tossed about in turmoil. What if he took one gold coin and converted it into cash? The household was starving. Rice had to be bought. No one needed to know—he would simply do it; let forgiveness come later. According to the Party’s rules and the law, it was forbidden. Such restrictions were a torment.

A curiosity arose in Krishna to know exactly what was in that bundle. He untied it and looked inside. There were old ornaments and ancient gold coins.
