It was the kind of property some rich man had kept safe, not needing to sell or convert it. The person who had entrusted it to him had not even counted or checked it properly. There was a chain made by stringing together old coins. What if he took one coin from it and sold it?

If ever there came a situation where he had to return it, it would be impossible to find out that a coin was missing. But Krishna knew this was a terrible beginning. Once fear is gone, one would be tempted to take one after another. What would happen if the party leadership came to know of this? Ordinarily, even if one joined the party and later left due to a difference of opinion, one would be branded as having been killed. A slight slip of the tongue was enough. He would become a class enemy. Then he would be included in the list of those who must be destroyed and eliminated. If that was the case, what would be the fate of someone who actually misappropriated party property? For several days, Krishna had been troubled by such thoughts.

In the end, he did it. He sold a gold coin and bought rice and groceries needed for the household. He bought some cloth for Thunga. Days passed. Now, there was no shortage of food at home. Next, Subhadra had to be married off. Krishna told his father that he had the money needed for that. From where? Vasudevan had to know. Even though Krishna did not openly say that it was money stolen after killing some rich man, Vasudevan understood. Whatever the circumstances behind that misdeed, it could not be justified. Vasudevan was an old-fashioned Brahmin. He had no doubt that everyone born on this earth would inevitably reap the fruits of their deeds. To enjoy this property was a sin. Return it, Vasudevan advised his son.

Krishna could not do as his father said. The reason was, to return it when the party did not need it would be a violation of discipline. He did not have the mind to keep it safe until it was asked back. How could he watch his family starve when there was money in hand? He sold the coins one by one and helped his family. Vasudevan could not digest that food. His own

The blood in his body had become impure. One day, he called his son and told him that he was preparing to end his own life. He also instructed him on how his funeral rites should be performed. Not a single coin from the money in his son’s possession should be spent on this matter. For several days, he lay without food or water. In the end, that life departed. Suicide achieved through sheer willpower!

All the funeral rites were conducted exactly as father had said, using only the money given by the villagers. Those who had leased the lands of the Palathol house all contributed and helped. Thus, the bond between the tenants and the Palathol house came to an end.

A few days after Vasudevan’s death, Subhadra’s wedding took place. Krishnan hurriedly arranged and completed everything. He would go to the temple to perform the archana. Now, Arya Antharjanam had only one remaining wish—that her son’s wedding should also take place.

But then, one morning, the temple was not opened. The Devaswom staff came to the house in search of Krishnan. All the doors in the house were found open. Arya Antharjanam lay collapsed, unable to speak. In the backyard, they saw Krishnan hanging from a tree branch. During the postmortem, a letter was found, written by him, stating that he had ended his life of his own will.

Kadukkathra Kunjukuttan no longer left the house. Always lying on the bed, never speaking to anyone. If his mother called him to eat, he would go and sit down, eat whatever was served. How many days could one live like this? He wished to leave the Naxalite organization. But was it possible to leave that organization? For one who leaves, and for those who permit the leaving, both are class enemies. Would they let a class enemy go? Kunjukuttan did not know.
Later, in the newly formed ministry, Viswanathan also became a minister. Many old friends attended the oath-taking ceremony.

Many had come to congratulate him and share in his joy. Only one had not come—Manikandan. Viswanathan wished to see him. Manikandan was someone who ought to have been in a position greater than his own. Viswanathan longed to rescue him from his present state. But now, not even the caretaker of the choultry where Manikandan had stayed knew where he was.

When the second Communist ministry came to power, Koya had suggested a way for Manikandan to make a living. After all, the ministers were all known to Manikandan. That was all Koya had said. That very day, Manikandan had left the place. He never returned.

Manikandan wandered from city to city. Occasionally, he would come and go from the villages as well. With his grown beard and mustache, and hair spreading wildly in all directions, no one recognized him. Everywhere he went, Manikandan saw others like himself. Once, in a choultry, he saw two people—a man and a woman. Their appearance was filthy, pitiable. The sight of those young ones seemed strangely familiar. Wasn’t it Madhu and Rosak Kutty? Manikandan walked on. His mind wandered through the fourteen worlds spoken of in the ancient legends. No path was clear to him. Sometimes, after walking and walking, he would find himself at a narrow street corner. Even from that needlepoint, there was only one direction to run. Which world was he heading to? There was no certainty. Manikandan had become a part of that endless road.
At the old Kodantra house site, construction work for a factory building was underway. All around...

Everything has become a town. Another of Surendran’s dreams is coming true. What all has he not done for the sake of the village? Surely, the village owes a debt to Surendran. But now, he is no longer the old Surendran. He has built himself a grand house. Today, his family shines with great influence. He holds a good share in the factory. There is even a car for him to travel in. Unlike before, Surendran no longer has the time to help with the needs of the villagers. That is why, in the last panchayat election, he had to struggle so much to win. The election demanded money; it even came to the point of having to buy off some members. Where did all this money come to him from? Did he begin to earn income by making his desire to enrich the village his initial investment, and then turning it into a business? When did he start taking his first bribe? For those with money, whatever task needed to be accomplished, it was enough to approach Surendran. Even in matters of evicting tenants from land, he did not hesitate to help the landlords. Some said the old Surendran was dead. This is the new Surendran. This Surendran is changing within himself every day.

Today, Surendran has a great adversary in that village—Saleel. His own son. Surendran’s son by Paappa. It was eighteen or twenty years ago. Paappa became pregnant. That was the time when she was living apart from her husband. She gave birth to a male child. She never told anyone who the father of the child was. But everyone knew it was Surendran’s child.

Now Surendran has to face that Saleel. A strike began among the workers building the factory. The union secretary was Saleel. His approach was somewhat different. The workers stood united. The contractor...
There were many discussions with the union. He did not fall for any bait. The factory work continued to be paralyzed. In the end, Surendran decided to speak with Saleel.

Surendran felt that Pappa had developed an intention to defeat him. He was ready to do anything for her and for Saleel. Would any woman, who becomes pregnant without a husband, refuse if the man responsible for her pregnancy came forward and offered to marry her? He told her that he would accept the child, that he would provide for her, that he would arrange for her to live—and whatever else she might ask. To everything, Pappa had only one answer: No. Raising her left hand, palm open, she uttered that word, and even now Surendran hears it in his ears. Pappa had fashioned for Surendran an adversary. He admitted to himself that he was not merely a communist, but a Naxalite. He declared firmly that there could be no compromise with the class enemy.

Surendran had entered the field. With the help of the police, he crushed the strike. Saleel had to spend a few days in jail. The factory work was progressing again. An advertisement appeared in the newspaper, stating that people with higher education and qualifications were needed for employment. Kadukkaathra Kunjukkuttan, who had been a Naxalite, also applied for a job there. His father and mother insisted that he should even sell ten marakkals of land and pay a bribe if necessary to secure a job there.

The Naxalite movement had sown fear throughout the country. Those who were murdered were the rich and the landlords. Everyone in the village was afraid—what if, in the middle of the night, those people came with axes and knives? When they heard that somewhere in the north, a landlord had been hacked to death inside his own house, Thunbekkalavan was terrified. It was Philip who was most affected by this fear. To the east...

In the estates of the Thodarchi hills, he had violated the chastity of several women laborers. He was a man who hesitated at nothing. He believed that punishing a laborer was the right of the master. He had killed a laborer named Murugan with a single blow. Now, for his own safety, he was forced to spend his days and nights armed, with a gun and other weapons at his side. He had even appointed guards around his house. Day by day, fear consumed him. In the end, he took his own life.

In the village, all the fields now lie barren, untouched by cultivation. No one has the mind to sow paddy. Vattathra Krikari, Anthoni of Aatrukkadavu, and Kochouseph of Paruthikkadu have all grown old and feeble. Even now, when they see the floods rushing through the Kaalaar river, their hearts leap. The floodwaters that come tumbling down from the eastern Thodarchi hills roar with the wild sound of the forest. But in the fields of Kuttanad, that mountain flood has not flowed for many years now. The reason is that the irrigation channels for the fields have now turned into beds of black stone. This is the agricultural reform the government brought in, to enable two harvests a year by controlling the floodwaters. The silt and debris that used to come with the river floods now go straight to the sea. If only that water flowed through the fields, the yield would increase by tenfold. In the days of the mountain floods, the farmers forgot about the ponds. Nothing that nature gives by its own accord is wanted by man anymore. With chemical fertilizers and poisons, the soil has turned barren.

The Karthika wind blew earlier than usual. The positions of the stars that signaled the season for sowing in the soil had gone awry. The three old men gathered, looked into each other's faces, and sat in silence. Times have changed; nature itself is changing. In no field is there any work being done. No one is willing to farm.

There was no eagerness to come forward. There was a reason for this. The last three harvests had not yielded good returns. If no one engaged in farming, how would the people of the land drink the gruel made by boiling rice? That was Krikari’s doubt. Even those who had obtained leased land had grown weary of farming. The vast paddy fields had become the property of many. The karisal lands of Mangalassery had been leveled here and there and turned into house plots. Houses had sprung up in all those places. The remaining land was left uncultivated; it had become wasteland. The sixty-four naal of seedling land now belonged to forty people. Pattas had been issued to everyone. Yet, no one farmed the land.

Within the village boundaries, Krikari owned a hundred marakkal of land. When laborers went there to work, Poovachaal Paili stopped them. That land had been temporarily registered in Paili’s name as a benami when the land ceiling was fixed. Now, Paili was not ready to give it back. There were many others who had lost their land in this way.

Since when did man begin to love the land? That love, which had endured for thousands and thousands of years, had turned into greed, into thirst, and had become the cause of countless wars! The history of man is the history of his greed for land, the history of his thirst. Mother Earth, who gives everything. That mother is full of compassion. Yet, whether by conquering and seizing the earth or by transferring it, the problems of humankind have not been solved. Let the earth be as it is. Accept that whatever grows on the earth is meant for everyone.

Today, no one remembers Klassiper Kochupillai. No one knows Chain Measurer Nagam Pillai either. Kodantra Moothassan and Paruthikkattu Olatha too—all of them seem to have risen from the dead and wander the old fields and boundaries of Kuttanad where the ancient lands remain. Even in their time, and in the time of the generations before them, the people must have risen from the dead and wandered those boundaries. Thus, looking back...
If we look back, we can discover the time when man loved the land.

The children and grandchildren of Vattathara Krikari are now living in foreign lands. The fields that remain here are of no interest to the children of those three old men. The earth has become barren. Man’s love for the soil has vanished. Yet, a question arises: “Don’t all these people need to eat?”
It was Paruthikkattu Sochchoth who asked this question.
